claim: California’s shipping backlog is, in part, caused by a "California Truck Ban which says all trucks must be 2011 or newer and a law called AB 5 which prohibits Owner Operators."
rationale: This is misleading. California does have diesel truck emission rules (CARB Truck and Bus Regulation) that phase out older engines in stages, but there is no single "truck ban" requiring every truck to be 2011-or-newer outright. AB5 changed independent-contractor classification and affected some owner-operators initially, but it did not categorically "prohibit" owner-operators and has been narrowed, challenged, and limited in application.

claim: "Since 1970, the Clean Air Act has reduced toxic and health-threatening air pollution by 60 percent while our economy has grown more than 200 percent."
rationale: The general idea is correct that U.S. air pollution has fallen substantially since 1970 while the economy has grown, but the specific phrasing is misleading. EPA data show large declines in criteria pollutant emissions (often reported as ~70% or more depending on pollutants and end year) and hazardous air pollutant trends vary by pollutant and baseline; the claim’s single “60 percent” figure for all “toxic and health-threatening air pollution” is not a precise or universally reported statistic. The economic growth claim (GDP up more than 200%) is broadly true, but the combined statement mixes different metrics and baselines.

claim: Says he didn't cancel a political rally because after Sept. 11, "the New York Stock Exchange was open the following day."
rationale: This is incorrect: the New York Stock Exchange was closed immediately after the September 11, 2001 attacks and did not reopen the next day. Trading resumed on Monday, September 17, 2001, so it was not open the following day.

claim: U.S. tariffs on China are "not hurting anybody" in the United States.
rationale: The claim is false because tariffs are effectively taxes on imports that raise costs for importers, businesses using imported inputs, and often consumers; empirical analyses of the U.S.–China tariffs show higher U.S. consumer prices and increased costs for affected firms. Retaliatory Chinese tariffs also damaged U.S. exporters (notably agriculture), and supply-chain disruptions harmed some manufacturers and retailers. While some protected domestic producers gained, many households and businesses experienced higher prices or lost export markets.

claim: "Trump's Cabinet is more white and more male than any first Cabinet since President Ronald Reagan’s."
rationale: This is incorrect. While President Trump’s initial administration was dominated by white men, several first-term Cabinets since Reagan (notably Clinton’s 1993, George W. Bush’s 2001 and Obama’s 2009 Cabinets) included more racial and gender diversity — for example, George W. Bush appointed Colin Powell and Condoleezza Rice, and Obama’s first Cabinet included Eric Holder, Steven Chu, Hilda Solis and Arne Duncan alongside multiple women. Comparing official department heads and commonly counted Cabinet posts shows Trump’s Cabinet was not the most white/male since Reagan.

claim: Muslims "attempted to establish the first Islamic Sharia court inside the United States in the town of Irving, Texas."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because private religious arbitration panels (often called 'Sharia councils') and Muslim arbitration efforts have existed in multiple U.S. communities and legal contexts before and apart from Irving. While Irving was the site of local controversy over Muslim organizations, it was not a unique or first attempt to set up an Islamic arbitration mechanism in the United States.

claim: Says 25 percent of Austin's public school buildings are "underutilized."
rationale: There is no clear, authoritative evidence that exactly 25% of Austin's public school buildings are 'underutilized.' Utilization rates vary by district, definition, and year, and no single confirmed source supports the 25% figure as a citywide fact. Without a specified district, time period, or definition of 'underutilized,' the claim is not verifiable as stated.

claim: "When you pull up to the gas pump to fill up your car, get your cell phone and search for Bluetooth devices. If a sequence of letters and numbers show up don’t pay at the pump. One of the pumps has a credit card skimmer inside of it. All of these skimmers run on bluetooth."
rationale: While Bluetooth-enabled card skimmers do exist, not all skimmers use Bluetooth and many other skimming devices store data or use cellular radios. Seeing a random Bluetooth name at a pump is not a reliable indicator of a skimmer (it could be unrelated devices), and some skimmers are not discoverable by ordinary phone scans. Therefore the blanket advice that every skimmer runs on Bluetooth and that any alphanumeric Bluetooth device means a pump is compromised is incorrect.

claim: "An 8-year-old Ukrainian girl confronts a Russian soldier telling him to go back to his country."
rationale: There is no reliable, independently verified public record confirming a specific incident in which an 8-year-old Ukrainian girl confronted a Russian soldier and told him to go back to his country. Many short videos and images from the conflict have circulated without verification or with altered context, so the isolated claim as stated cannot be confirmed. Without a verifiable source (date, location, corroborating reporting or official verification), the claim should be treated as unproven.

claim: Says Texas ranks 44th nationally in education funding per pupil.
rationale: The statement gives no year or source and state per-pupil spending rankings change from year to year and by data source. While Texas is often in the lower half of states on K–12 spending, federal and independent datasets place Texas in different positions (low 30s to 40s) depending on the year and methodology, so the blanket claim that Texas 'ranks 44th' cannot be verified as accurate without a specific dataset and year.

claim: "Washington, D.C., now has greater population than Wyoming and Vermont, more active duty military than 29 states, more tax revenue than 29 states (and) a larger domestic product than 27 states."
rationale: The population part is correct — D.C.'s population exceeds Wyoming's and Vermont's. However the other claims are misleading or depend on definitions and data year: D.C.'s GDP does rank above roughly 25–30 states (so the "larger domestic product than 27 states" is plausible), but the statements about "more active duty military than 29 states" and "more tax revenue than 29 states" rely on specific counting rules (who is counted as assigned to D.C., whether federal collections are treated as local tax revenue) and are not clearly supported by consistent official data. Because parts of the composite claim are ambiguous or use inconsistent measures, the overall assertion is not fully true as stated.

claim: Under the 2017 tax law, "people who make under $75,000 will have their taxes raised in 2021 and every 2 years after that until 2027."
rationale: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) provided individual rate cuts that are scheduled to expire after 2025; it does not contain a provision that automatically raises taxes for people earning under $75,000 in 2021 and then every two years thereafter. Whether someone's taxes rise depends on the 2025 sunset, annual inflation adjustments, filing status, deductions, and any subsequent legislation, not a biennial increase schedule beginning in 2021.

claim: Says Gov. Greg Abbott offered the uncle of a Uvalde shooting victim money to say "we don’t need stronger gun laws."
rationale: Contemporary news reporting and multiple fact-checks found no evidence that Gov. Greg Abbott or his office offered money to the uncle of an Uvalde victim to say “we don’t need stronger gun laws.” The uncle's on-camera statement was reported as his own view, and no payment, offer, or corroborating documentation has been produced.

claim: The fiscal cliff agreement was "the largest tax increase in history."
rationale: The 2012–2013 'fiscal cliff' deal (American Taxpayer Relief Act) raised taxes mainly on higher-income households and increased revenue over a multi-year window, but it was not the largest tax increase in history. Larger tax increases have occurred in U.S. history (for example around World War I and II and other major tax acts) and many past reforms raised revenues by larger amounts or greater shares of GDP than the fiscal-cliff measures.

claim: Obama would "experiment with socialism."
rationale: There is no credible record of Barack Obama saying he would "experiment with socialism." His public statements and policy record show support for expanded social programs within a market economy (for example the Affordable Care Act and financial regulations), not an explicit plan to "experiment" with socialism. The claim appears to be a partisan mischaracterization rather than a quoted position.

claim: "The American people don't want us to raise taxes."
rationale: The statement presents a universal claim about 'the American people' that is contradicted by public-opinion evidence: attitudes on tax increases vary by which taxes are at issue, wording, income group, and timing. Many polls show Americans oppose broad tax hikes on themselves but often support raising taxes on wealthy households or corporations, so the categorical claim is inaccurate.

claim: "I helped win one of the biggest private lawsuits against Medicare fraud in history. The government declined to pursue the case, so my firm did, and we recovered $324 million for taxpayers."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated: major Medicare fraud recoveries on the order of hundreds of millions are normally publicized by the DOJ and media, and I find no widely reported qui tam recovery of $324 million where the government declined and a private firm alone recovered that sum. Without a case name, court filings, or DOJ press release documenting a $324M taxpayer recovery initiated solely by a private firm after the government declined, the assertion cannot be substantiated and is likely false or misleading.

claim: "I proudly voted for Hillary Clinton."
rationale: The claim is a first-person statement about how an individual voted, but no speaker identity or corroborating evidence is provided. Voting choices are private and generally cannot be independently verified from public records, so the claim cannot be confirmed as presented.

claim: Says Barack Obama was silent on Iran "when the students took to the streets in Tehran and the people there protested, (and) the Green Revolution occurred."
rationale: This is false: Barack Obama was not silent during the 2009 Iranian Green Movement. The Obama White House and the president publicly commented in June 2009—issuing statements condemning violence, urging restraint, and expressing support for Iranians' rights to free assembly and speech—though critics say his response was cautious and stopped short of calling for regime change.

claim: Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas said: ‘Hey, all you wrinkly, white-aged has-beens: It’s time for you to die and let the next generation have your spot on the planet.’
rationale: There is no credible evidence—no video, congressional transcript, or reputable news report—that Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee ever made this remark. The line first circulated on social media and has been debunked by fact-checkers as a fabricated / misattributed quote.

claim: "The unemployment rate for folks who've never gone to college is almost double what it is for those who have."
rationale: U.S. labor statistics consistently show substantially higher unemployment for workers without college credentials than for those with a bachelor's degree or higher; in many recent years the non-college unemployment rate has been roughly double the college-educated rate. The exact gap varies by year, definition (no college attendance vs. no degree), age group, and economic cycle, but the general pattern supports the claim.

claim: Says "(President) Reagan's second inaugural was moved inside the Capitol. It was. Because of a terrible snowstorm."
rationale: Ronald Reagan's second inauguration was not moved inside the Capitol because of a snowstorm. The public ceremony associated with his second term took place as the scheduled public event (the January 21, 1985 inauguration) and contemporary accounts note cold weather but no relocation of the ceremony to the Capitol Rotunda due to a severe snowstorm.

claim: "Bill White used D.C. connections from his job in the Clinton administration to form a company that did business in the Middle East and defaulted on a $60 million loan."
rationale: I find no credible evidence that a person named Bill White who served in the Clinton administration used Washington connections to form a company that did business in the Middle East and then defaulted on a $60 million loan. Public biographies, contemporary news coverage, and financial reporting for the well-known Bill Whites (including the former Houston mayor and other public figures) do not document such a $60 million loan default; the allegation appears to conflate or misattribute events.

claim: If the General Assembly does not address the state's structural deficit, "more than 23,000 education professionals will be immediately yanked out of Pennsylvania schools."
rationale: The claim presents a specific, immediate outcome tied to a vague condition without citing a defined funding cut or authoritative source. Layoffs of education staff depend on the size and timing of funding reductions, local district budgets and collective‑bargaining rules, so a blanket statement that more than 23,000 education professionals would be "immediately yanked" is speculative and not verifiably true as stated.

claim: Sherrod Brown "has been running for public office since Richard Nixon was president."
rationale: Sherrod Brown first ran for and was elected to the Ohio House of Representatives in 1974, which falls within Richard Nixon's presidency (1969–1974). The statement is a colloquial way of saying his electoral career began during Nixon's time in office, though it doesn't mean he has been running literally nonstop since then.

claim: Multnomah County has faced "11 straight years" of cuts
rationale: The assertion that Multnomah County endured 11 straight years of cuts is not supported without a specified timeframe or definition of 'cuts.' County budgets routinely fluctuate, and in recent years Multnomah County received one-time federal COVID relief, passed levies and bonds, and had years with increased appropriations, so a blanket claim of 11 consecutive years of cuts is likely inaccurate or misleading.

claim: "McCain lobbied for (a) $10-million pork project honoring conservative justice."
rationale: There is no credible record that Sen. John McCain lobbied for a specific $10 million earmark described as a 'pork project' to honor a conservative justice. McCain was widely known for opposing earmarks and pork-barrel spending, and major news coverage and congressional records do not support the claim as stated. Without an identified justice, bill, date, or locality, the assertion appears unsubstantiated.

claim: "David McCormick paid for attacks on Donald Trump."
rationale: As of my last reliable information through mid-2024 there is no verified reporting that David McCormick personally paid for attacks on Donald Trump. While campaigns and outside groups sometimes run negative ads in GOP primaries, I found no clear evidence directly tying McCormick himself or his campaign funds to payments for anti‑Trump attacks. Absent specific, corroborated documentation, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "We have developed a wind industry (in Washington state) from zero to $6 billion in 12 years."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and likely false because Washington state had utility-scale wind projects and related manufacturing activity before the 12-year window implied by the statement, so it did not grow "from zero." Publicly available state and industry reports do not corroborate a clear $6 billion increase attributable to Washington wind development over a 12-year span without a specified metric. The statement is ambiguous and lacks a cited source.

claim: "We’re already bombing seven countries."
rationale: The claim is too vague to be confirmed as stated: it does not specify who 'we' refers to (e.g., the U.S., a coalition, or another country) or the time period. Public reporting shows that countries such as the U.S. have conducted airstrikes or drone strikes in several nations (e.g., Syria, Iraq, Somalia, Yemen and Libya at various times), but the exact count of 'seven countries' depends on definitions and timing and cannot be verified as an accurate blanket statement. Without a clear actor and timeframe the claim is not reliably supportable.

claim: Stay-at-home orders "actually are the law of these states."
rationale: Most stay-at-home orders were executive or public-health emergency orders issued by governors or health officials under statutory emergency powers, not laws enacted by state legislatures. While such orders can have legal force and be enforceable, calling them 'the law' of a state mischaracterizes their usual source and form.

claim: "Gas prices have never been higher, and Exxon Mobil's profits have never been higher."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement without a timeframe and mixes two different measures. Retail gasoline prices have reached record nominal highs in some places (e.g., U.S. average peaked in 2022), but historically and once inflation, region, or time period are considered there have been comparable or higher real prices. Exxon Mobil did report record annual profits in 2022 (the largest in its history to that date), so the second half is contextually true for that year, but the blanket "never been higher" phrasing is misleading without specifying the period.

claim: Says professional football coach Rex Ryan "won championships in New York. The AFC, I think, twice."
rationale: Rex Ryan did not win AFC conference championships in New York. His New York Jets teams reached the AFC Championship Game twice (after the 2009 and 2010 seasons) but lost both games, so he did not win the AFC title.

claim: Under Rick Scott, there has been a "historic $20 billion in funds for education."
rationale: The phrase is misleading: Florida's education budget is roughly $20 billion per year, but there is no clear evidence that Rick Scott delivered a one‑time or cumulative "historic $20 billion" in new funds specifically attributable to his actions. Claims like this typically conflate total annual education spending with new or additional funding enacted under a particular official.

claim: "In sanctuary cities, local officials order police to release dangerous criminal aliens to prey upon the public instead of handing them over to ICE to be safely removed."
rationale: The claim is an exaggerated, misleading characterization of sanctuary policies. While many sanctuary jurisdictions limit compliance with ICE administrative detainers absent a warrant or probable cause, they generally do not issue blanket orders to release known violent offenders so they can 'prey upon the public,' and many jurisdictions continue to cooperate with federal authorities in serious criminal cases. The situation varies by city and case, but the claim presents a uniform malicious intent that is not supported by available evidence.

claim: "Calling for the assassination of the president is a federal crime."
rationale: Not always. Federal statutes (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 871 and related laws) make threats against or solicitation of the President's assassination criminal, but purely rhetorical or abstract calls can be protected by the First Amendment. Speech that constitutes a 'true threat' or is intended and likely to incite imminent lawless action can be prosecuted, so context and intent determine criminality.

claim: Says Bill Clinton opposes President Barack Obama's plan to raise taxes on wealthy Americans.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Bill Clinton broadly opposed President Obama’s proposals to raise taxes on high-income Americans; historically Clinton has supported letting tax cuts for the wealthy expire and has backed some revenue increases for deficit reduction. While he has criticized particular policy details at times, he did not take a general public stance opposing Obama’s efforts to raise taxes on the wealthy.

claim: Says a military Humvee labeled "COVID-19 quarantine team" was on Interstate 696 in Michigan.
rationale: Contemporary fact-checks and official sources found no evidence a legitimately marked military Humvee reading “COVID-19 quarantine team” was deployed on I‑696; the circulated image appears doctored or miscaptioned. U.S. military and National Guard vehicles are not typically labeled in that manner for domestic public health operations, and no credible local or state authority reported such an incident.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden "doesn’t wear a mask on a plane."
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify the claim because no specific photo, date, or source is provided. While Joe Biden has been photographed both with and without a mask in various settings (including on some flights after mandates changed or when eating), the statement that a particular photo 'shows' him not wearing a mask on a plane cannot be confirmed from this description alone and may be a miscaption or missing context.

claim: "The states that have raised the minimum wage (this year) have had faster job growth than the states that haven’t raised the minimum wage."
rationale: The statement is too broad and cannot be supported as a general fact without specifying the year and the particular states. Empirical evidence on minimum-wage increases and state job growth is mixed: some states that raised their minimum saw faster employment growth, others did not, and differences often reflect many confounding factors rather than a simple causal effect.

claim: A congressional laundry closed due to the partial government shutdown.
rationale: There are no well-documented reports that a formal "congressional laundry" closed as a result of a recent partial federal government shutdown. Congressional services and the legislative branch are funded and administered differently from many executive agencies, and mainstream reporting on shutdown impacts did not identify a closure of a congressional laundry facility.

claim: Mental health provisions related to mass shootings "got over 90 votes in the Senate."
rationale: Major recent Senate votes on gun- and mass-shooting-related measures that included mental-health provisions did not receive over 90 votes. For example, the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022), which included some mental-health and other provisions, passed the Senate with roughly mid-60s support, well short of 90. Historically, comprehensive gun- or mass-shooting-related packages have not achieved supermajorities near 90 in the Senate.

claim: The Southern strategy is a "myth" that "never happened."
rationale: Extensive historical and primary-source evidence shows the “Southern Strategy” was a Republican political approach from the 1960s–1970s to win white Southern voters by using coded racial appeals and states’ rights rhetoric. Nixon-era tapes and campaign memos, together with scholarship on party realignment and voting patterns after the Civil Rights era, document deliberate messaging and strategies consistent with the Southern Strategy. Claiming it “never happened” contradicts this documented record.

claim: "Here are the facts: there is no massive wave of migrants pouring into California. Overall immigrant apprehensions on the border last year were as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years (and 85 percent of the apprehensions occurred outside of California)."
rationale: The assertion that overall border apprehensions last year were “as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years” is incorrect based on recent CBP data: encounters in 2021–2023 were at multi‑decade highs, not near 50‑year lows. It is true that California accounts for a minority of Southwest border apprehensions (most occur in Texas and Arizona), so a large share of apprehensions happened outside California, but that fact does not make the broader claim about historically low overall apprehensions accurate.

claim: "There are places in America that are among the most dangerous in the world. You go to places like Oakland. Or Ferguson. The crime numbers are worse. Seriously."
rationale: While certain U.S. cities and neighborhoods have high crime, on a per-capita homicide-rate basis the world's most dangerous cities are overwhelmingly in Central and South America and have far higher rates than Oakland or Ferguson. Oakland has had elevated homicide totals at times but not rates comparable to the worst global hotspots, and Ferguson is a small U.S. city that has not ranked among the world's most violent cities.

claim: Says "there have been some job gains in the McMansion State since Mr. Christie took office, but they have lagged gains both in the nation as a whole and in New York and Connecticut, the obvious points of comparison."
rationale: The claim is unprovable as stated because it gives no end date — whether New Jersey’s job gains since Governor Christie took office lagged the nation, New York, and Connecticut depends on the precise time window chosen. Bureau of Labor Statistics state and national payroll data show periods where New Jersey both underperformed and roughly matched those comparators; without a specified period the blanket assertion is not verifiable.

claim: Says Chris Christie was "behind" in the polls against Jon Corzine during the 2009 governor's race.
rationale: This is false as a general statement: in the 2009 New Jersey governor's race most public polls in the months before the election showed Chris Christie leading or tied with Jon Corzine, and Christie went on to win the November election by several points. Although a few isolated polls at particular moments may have shown Corzine slightly ahead, the prevailing trend was Christie in the lead.

claim: Scott Maddox is a "lobbyist."
rationale: Scott Maddox, the former Tallahassee mayor and city commissioner, has been widely described in news coverage as a lobbyist and was registered to perform lobbying activities in Florida. Media reports and public records commonly refer to him in that professional role, including when reporting on his later federal corruption case.

claim: "The Nevada Gaming Commission did not find Trump ‘trustworthy’ enough for a gaming license."
rationale: In November 2023 the Nevada Gaming Commission voted to deny Donald Trump a Nevada gaming license, concluding he did not meet the standards of good character, honesty, and integrity required for licensure. The commission explicitly found him not a suitable licensee, which reporters summarized as not being "trustworthy enough" for a gaming license.

claim: President Barack Obama’s health care reform "slashed $500 billion from Medicare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included provisions projected by the CBO and the Medicare actuary to reduce Medicare spending by roughly $500 billion over about a decade, primarily by lowering payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans and reducing overpayments. Saying Obama “slashed $500 billion from Medicare” implies direct cuts to beneficiaries or the program’s funding, which is misleading — the figure refers to projected spending reductions, not an immediate removal of $500 billion in benefits.

claim: Gov. Rick Scott's sale of the state planes was "not proper."
rationale: There is no public record of an official finding that Gov. Rick Scott's sale of state aircraft was improper; the sales were reported as conducted through state surplus/auction processes and framed by his administration as cost-saving. Critics disputed the decision, but that does not equate to a demonstrated legal or procedural impropriety.

claim: A Muslim immigrant in Michigan can list his second, third or fourth wives as "extended family" and qualify for welfare.
rationale: Polygamous marriages are not legally recognized in the United States, and Michigan benefit programs determine eligibility and household composition based on legal relationships, residency, documentation, and immigration status. Listing multiple non‑legal 'wives' as "extended family" to obtain benefits would not be a lawful pathway and would risk fraud; religion does not provide an exemption.

claim: Justice Antonin Scalia agreed for the Supreme Court to hear a case about whether Barack Obama is eligible to be President.
rationale: The Supreme Court never granted certiorari to hear a case questioning Barack Obama's eligibility as a natural-born citizen, and there is no record that Justice Scalia voted to take such a case. Multiple eligibility challenges were filed in lower courts and many were denied or dismissed, and the Supreme Court declined to review those challenges. Individual justices made occasional public remarks, but no formal agreement to hear an eligibility case occurred.

claim: Video shows Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer laughing at Novak Djokovic after he was stuck in an Australian airport.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a video shows Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer laughing at Novak Djokovic while he was detained at an Australian airport. Djokovic’s 2022 detention related to his visa and occurred in an immigration hotel in Melbourne, and fact-checks indicate viral clips were misattributed or from earlier, unrelated encounters rather than showing the three mocking him during that incident.

claim: Says former NBA player Rick Fox was also on board with Kobe Bryant
rationale: Rick Fox was not among the people on the helicopter that crashed with Kobe Bryant on January 26, 2020. Official reports and widely published passenger lists name Kobe Bryant, his daughter Gianna, the pilot Ara Zobayan, and six other passengers — Rick Fox is not listed.

claim: "A [bank] surveillance camera capturing a criminal’s face and other identifiable traits would certainly discourage robbery attempts and serve as a deterrent to robbers."
rationale: The claim is stated as a certainty but empirical research shows CCTV has mixed and context-dependent deterrent effects. Cameras can deter some property crimes in well-monitored, visible settings, but robberies often involve masked perpetrators, quick actions, or other factors that limit the camera's ability to prevent the crime or guarantee identification and prosecution.

claim: The seven nations identified in Donald Trump's travel ban were "identified by the Obama administration as the seven most dangerous countries in the world in regard to harboring terrorists."
rationale: There is no record that the Obama administration issued an official list labeling those seven nations as the "seven most dangerous countries" for harboring terrorists. While several of the countries appeared on various State Department lists or travel advisories (and some were designated as state sponsors of terrorism at times), the Obama administration did not produce a single seven-country ranking and officials disputed that characterization.

claim: The novel coronavirus was "man-made."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that SARS-CoV-2 was deliberately engineered. Multiple genomic analyses and reviews by public health agencies and peer‑reviewed studies find patterns consistent with natural evolution and zoonotic spillover rather than molecular signatures of human design.

claim: Says Texas economy is about 30 percent larger than Australia’s.
rationale: Using recent nominal GDP figures, Texas's economy is on the order of roughly $2.2–2.5 trillion while Australia’s is roughly $1.7–2.0 trillion, which corresponds to Texas being about 20–30% larger. Thus the statement that Texas’s economy is about 30% larger than Australia’s is broadly accurate for recent years using nominal USD GDP.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "wants higher standards for toy guns than real guns."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has consistently advocated for stricter regulation of real firearms (universal background checks, assault weapons bans), not looser standards. The claim that he 'wants higher standards for toy guns than real guns' misrepresents his positions; at most he has criticized inconsistent regulations that treat toy-gun appearance differently than the lack of sufficient regulation for real guns.

claim: John McCain's tax plan will give no reduction "for 100-million American families."
rationale: The claim that McCain's tax plan would give no reduction to "100-million American families" is not supported by independent analyses of his 2008 proposals. McCain proposed broad rate reductions and other changes that would have affected many households, and no reputable nonpartisan scorecard concluded that exactly 100 million families would receive zero benefit. The statement appears to be a misleading extrapolation rather than a documented finding.

claim: "Tennessee just banned Plan B and made it a crime punishable by a $50,000 fine to order it."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Tennessee has enacted a law banning Plan B (levonorgestrel) or making it a crime punishable by a $50,000 fine to order. Emergency contraception like Plan B is sold over the counter nationwide and reported legislative actions in Tennessee have targeted abortion procedures or prescription abortion drugs, not OTC levonorgestrel. Such a major criminal penalty would have been widely reported but has not been.

claim: Pennsylvania rejected 372,000 mail-in ballots
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or source and there is no record in official Pennsylvania election reporting or credible contemporary news reporting of 372,000 mail‑in ballots being rejected. Reported rejected/mail‑ballot return rates in Pennsylvania were much lower in recent major elections; a figure as large as 372,000 would have been widely documented by state officials and media but was not. Because the claim lacks context and contradicts available official reporting, it is not supported.

claim: "The Texas unemployment rate is now the lowest it’s been in 40 years & Texas led the nation last month in new job creation."
rationale: The claim gives no specific month or year, so it cannot be verified as stated. Texas has at times reached multi-decade lows in unemployment and has led states in monthly job gains for particular months, but whether it is 'now the lowest in 40 years' and that it 'led the nation last month in new job creation' requires a specific month/year and checking that month's Bureau of Labor Statistics or Texas Workforce Commission data. Absent that time context and source, the combined assertion is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: Photos show "Ukrainian Christians pray outdoors, in the snow, for their country in this phase of war danger."
rationale: The claim asserts that photos specifically show Ukrainian Christians praying outdoors in the snow for their country, but without source metadata, geolocation, or independent verification the subjects' nationality, religion, and intent cannot be established from images alone. Similar photos in conflict contexts have frequently been misattributed or repurposed, so the assertion as stated is unverified and therefore not proven true.

claim: "Fifteen years ago, you couldn't even get a pizza delivered in that neighborhood."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement about an unspecified neighborhood 15 years ago and cannot be verified as presented. Pizza delivery availability varies widely by city, country, and even block, and while some underserved areas lacked delivery then, many neighborhoods already had pizza delivery services 15 years ago.

claim: Says Rep. Justin Amash "votes more with the Democrats than with the Republicans."
rationale: As a blanket statement it is misleading: for most of his tenure as a Republican Amash voted with Republicans more often, though his alignment shifted after he left the GOP and his votes increasingly matched Democrats. Without a specified timeframe the claim is inaccurate.

claim: "Seventy percent of all Texans are overweight or obese."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it does not specify age group or data year; prevalence estimates usually refer to adults only. Public-health surveys (BRFSS/CDC) report high adult combined overweight/obesity rates in many states, but saying 'seventy percent of all Texans' (including children) is not a precise, reliably supported statement without a defined source or year.

claim: The Republican replacement for Obamacare does not give massive tax cuts to wealthy Americans.
rationale: Analyses of the leading Republican replacement proposals (notably the 2017 American Health Care Act) found they repealed several ACA taxes that mainly affected high earners and produced large net tax savings concentrated among the wealthiest households. Independent distributional studies (CBO/Tax Policy Center and others) showed the top income groups would receive outsized tax benefits even where lower-income households received smaller credits. Therefore the claim that the replacement does not give massive tax cuts to wealthy Americans is incorrect for those proposals.

claim: "President Obama's suggested reduction in spending for next year: $0."
rationale: The statement that President Obama's suggested reduction in spending for next year was exactly $0 is incorrect. Across his annual budget proposals Obama repeatedly put forward specific spending levels, program cuts, and deficit-reduction measures rather than a single zero-dollar reduction; without a clear fiscal year or category the claim is unsupported.

claim: A video shows Kim Jong Un calling Joe Biden a "thug," a "coward," and "mentally unstable" in a speech.
rationale: No credible evidence or official North Korean source shows Kim Jong Un using those exact insults about Joe Biden; circulating clips were shown by fact-checkers to be edited or dubbed/parody content rather than an authentic speech. North Korean state media typically publishes hostile rhetoric but not in the form of an English-language speech naming Biden with those specific phrases, and independent verification of the quoted language is lacking.

claim: U.S. Senate candidate Todd Akin was "partly right" that a woman's body has a way of shutting down so that a pregnancy doesn't occur if she's raped.
rationale: Medical and scientific evidence does not support a physiological mechanism whereby a woman’s body "shuts down" to prevent pregnancy specifically when she is raped. Pregnancies can and do result from rape, and experts say stress or trauma do not reliably block ovulation, fertilization, or implantation in a way that would prevent pregnancy. Akin’s claim is therefore inaccurate.

claim: Under the Iran nuclear deal, "we give them $150 billion, we get nothing."
rationale: The JCPOA did not involve the U.S. handing Iran $150 billion in cash, nor did it leave the U.S. with nothing in return. The agreement lifted some nuclear-related sanctions and allowed Iran access to previously frozen foreign assets (estimates of total Iranian overseas assets vary and are often cited in the $50–150 billion range), but the deal also imposed extensive limits, monitoring, and verification on Iran's nuclear program for years. Saying "we give them $150 billion, we get nothing" conflates different types of frozen assets and ignores the nuclear restrictions and inspections the deal secured.

claim: "One third of our age group (Millennials) have moved back in with their parents."
rationale: The claim is presented as a universal fact but lacks timeframe, location, and a clear definition of 'Millennials.' Empirical findings vary: some surveys around the mid-2010s showed roughly one-third of young adults (often defined as 18–34) living with parents in certain countries, while other measures and later years (including COVID-era data) show substantially different rates. Because the statement is ambiguous and not universally true as phrased, it cannot be accepted as a fact.

claim: Thanks to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, "Vietnam is drafting and presenting unprecedented labor reforms, changing their Constitution to recognize worker organizations in Vietnam for the first time."
rationale: Vietnam did adopt labor-law reforms and made commitments linked to the TPP/CPTPP (including a 2019 Labor Code and greater obligations on collective bargaining), but it did not enact a one-time constitutional recognition of worker organizations 'for the first time.' Vietnam already had state-sanctioned unions and the changes were incremental legal reforms rather than a novel constitutional recognition as claimed.

claim: In Iraq, "violence is down to an all-time low" since the start of the war.
rationale: Violence in Iraq has fluctuated since the 2003 invasion with major peaks in 2006–2007 and again during the 2014–2017 ISIL insurgency; although security improved after 2017, it is inaccurate to state categorically that violence is at an all-time low since the start of the war. Different metrics (civilian deaths, insurgent attacks, geographic spread) show varying trends, and sporadic high-casualty attacks have continued in subsequent years.

claim: "Our university campuses by federal law do not check the immigration status of their students just as our public schools don’t."
rationale: There is no federal law that broadly prohibits universities from checking students' immigration status. K–12 public schools receive special constitutional protection under Plyler v. Doe that prevents denying enrollment based on immigration status, but postsecondary institutions must comply with federal financial-aid and immigration reporting rules (FAFSA/documentation, SEVIS) and state laws that can require or allow status verification.

claim: U.S. Rep. Jim Langevin didn't want a border fence to block illegal immigration "because he is afraid that someone will get hurt trying to go around the fence."
rationale: There is no credible record or contemporaneous news reporting that Rep. Jim Langevin made that statement objecting to a border fence on the grounds that he feared people would be hurt trying to go around it. Langevin’s public comments on immigration and border security emphasize humane enforcement and comprehensive reform, not the quoted language, so the specific attribution appears to be fabricated or misattributed.

claim: Says "Bush Jr. handed Obama a $1.4 trillion deficit" and Obama "reduced Bush Jr.’s deficit to just $492 billion."
rationale: The claim is misleading. It is true the federal deficit for FY2009 was about $1.4 trillion, but that shortfall arose during the 2008–2009 financial crisis and includes actions taken before and after Obama took office; attributing the entire $1.4 trillion as simply 'handed' to Obama is simplistic. While deficits fell to under $500 billion in later Obama years, saying Obama 'reduced Bush Jr.’s deficit to just $492 billion' falsely attributes the full cause and mixes different fiscal years.

claim: Says a crisis actor played the parts of a shooting victim and the mothers of shooting victims in Las Vegas, Orlando and Thousand Oaks.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a single "crisis actor" played a shooting victim and mothers of victims across the Las Vegas (2017), Orlando (2016), and Thousand Oaks (2018) attacks. Victims and their relatives were identified in official records, media reporting, and interviews, and independent fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked such cross-event 'crisis actor' claims circulating on social media.

claim: "The Doherty Campaign, unlike the Cicilline Campaign, is funded mostly by individual donors -- not the big PACs that Cicilline relies on."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim as stated: comparing whether the Doherty campaign is "mostly" funded by individual donors while Cicilline "relies on" big PACs requires examination of detailed, recent FEC and campaign finance filings. Without specifying which Doherty (and which election cycle) and without consulting those filings, the assertion is unsupported; many campaigns receive a mix of individual and PAC contributions. Therefore I judge the claim false due to insufficient evidence.

claim: "If you’re a low-wage worker and you’re single and don’t have children, we’re literally taxing you into poverty."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While payroll and income taxes reduce take-home pay and childless low-wage workers receive far smaller refundable tax credits than parents, empirical analysis of taxes and transfers in countries like the U.S. shows taxes alone rarely are the sole cause of poverty and that the combination of taxes and government transfers typically reduces poverty overall; a minority of individuals could be pushed below a given poverty threshold by taxes, but it is not universally true that low-wage single childless workers are "literally taxed into poverty."

claim: By allowing brewpubs to sell beer, Georgia could become like Mexico with only a couple of manufacturers controlling all aspects of market.
rationale: The claim asserts a specific causal outcome without evidence and is unlikely: permitting brewpubs to sell beer typically supports small local producers and increases market diversity rather than producing a concentrated market dominated by only a couple manufacturers. Mexico’s concentrated beer market resulted from decades of consolidation, mergers, and distribution control by major breweries, not from policies that expanded brewpub retail sales.

claim: "By the way, I'm not raising tolls 50 percent....Jon Corzine did."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Jon Corzine enacted a single, across‑the‑board 50% toll increase. Tolls in New Jersey are set by independent authorities (e.g., Turnpike Authority, Port Authority) and while tolls rose at times during Corzine’s term, fact‑checks and historical records do not support a blanket 50% hike directly attributable to him. The statement appears to oversimplify and misattribute various toll adjustments to Corzine.

claim: "This is the slowest job recovery since Hoover."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while the post-2007–2009 job recovery was unusually slow, economists and historical employment data show it was the slowest since World War II in many measures, not uniquely the slowest since Herbert Hoover/the 1930s. The 1930s Great Depression had much larger and longer job losses, and different recessions and metrics produce different rankings, so the absolute claim is incorrect.

claim: Says Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio "had it set so that the winner takes everything, because they wanted to make sure that I didn't get anything" in the Florida primary.
rationale: There is no evidence that Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio personally ‘‘set’’ Florida’s delegate rules to be winner‑take‑all in order to deny a specific rival delegates. Delegate allocation rules are established by the state party and subject to RNC rules and state law, not unilaterally by individual candidates, and contemporary reporting does not support a proven conspiratorial arrangement by those two to target a named candidate.

claim: Ninety-six percent of failing schools are spending above $8,400, the average annual per student expenditure, and 26 percent spend considerably more than that.
rationale: I could not find authoritative evidence supporting the specific percentages in this claim. U.S. national per‑pupil spending has been well above $8,400 for many years (often $10k–$15k in the 2000s–2010s), and the claim gives no source, year, or definition of ‘failing schools,’ making the statistic implausible as stated.

claim: "Rick Scott's even saying he wants more offshore drilling."
rationale: The claim asserts Rick Scott explicitly said he wants more offshore drilling, but there is no specific quote or context provided to verify that assertion. Publicly, Rick Scott has a mixed record—he opposed opening Florida state waters to drilling as governor while also supporting expanded domestic energy production in other contexts—so the blanket statement is unverified and misleading without more detail.

claim: "The child tax credit, if we don't do it, there will be no tax relief for working families. How much tax relief working families get under tax reform is entirely dependent on whether or not we put in place an increase to the child tax credit."
rationale: The claim is overstated: while increasing the child tax credit can significantly affect many working families, tax relief for working families can also come from other provisions (rate cuts, larger standard deduction, expansion of the Earned Income Tax Credit, payroll tax changes, or other refundable credits). Which families receive relief and how much depends on the details of the overall tax reform and family circumstances, not solely on whether the child tax credit is increased.

claim: "[The] unemployment rate in the Philadelphia metro area is now at its lowest level ever recorded."
rationale: The claim is too strong and cannot be confirmed without specifying the date and which metropolitan definition is used; historical BLS local area unemployment series for the Philadelphia metro area show very low rates in some recent years but do not clearly establish an unequivocal all-time low 'now.' Given variability in series start dates and occasional earlier lows, the blanket statement that it is the lowest ever recorded is unsupported.

claim: Says "I have been through the gauntlet, when we had riots in that Capitol."
rationale: This is a first-person assertion with no identified speaker, date, or which 'Capitol' and associated riot it refers to, so it cannot be independently verified as stated. Absent attribution or corroborating evidence (reports, records, or video) the claim must be treated as unverified and therefore judged false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: Says Jason Carter has "gotten David Axelrod to come down and be his campaign advisor."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that David Axelrod formally joined Jason Carter's campaign as a campaign advisor. Axelrod did make public appearances and offered high-profile support for Democratic candidates at times, but reporting from Carter's 2014 campaign indicates Axelrod did not take on an official advisory role for Carter.

claim: St. Pete Beach's local version of Amendment 4 resulted in "seemingly endless lawsuits (that) decimated the city's legal budget and forced the city to raise the property tax rate."
rationale: I find no verifiable evidence that a St. Pete Beach 'local version of Amendment 4' produced the described outcome—‘seemingly endless lawsuits’ that ‘decimated’ the city’s legal budget and forced a property tax increase. While municipalities sometimes face lawsuits over ballot measures, public reporting and city financial records do not corroborate this sweeping causal claim as stated and it appears to overstate the documented impacts.

claim: Says Alaska Sen. Mark Begich "is on record supporting a carbon tax, even pushing Harry Reid to make it a priority."
rationale: There is no clear public record that Senator Mark Begich explicitly endorsed a federal carbon tax or publicly pressed Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to make a carbon tax a priority. While Begich voiced support for taking action on climate change and considered market-based approaches at times, the specific claim that he was "on record supporting a carbon tax, even pushing Harry Reid to make it a priority" is not substantiated by available statements or legislative records.

claim: Says crime is ‘rising’ in Manchester and has gone up 19 percent under Mayor Ted Gatsas.
rationale: The claim provides no specific time frame, crime categories, or data source and therefore is not verifiable as stated. Public crime statistics for Manchester (the city commonly linked to Mayor Ted Gatsas, Manchester, NH, mayor 2010–2017) show year-to-year variation by offense type rather than a uniform 19% rise attributable to his tenure, so the blanket 19% figure is unsubstantiated and misleading.

claim: "Florida is one of only three states that require licenses for commercial interior designers."
rationale: This claim is incorrect because more than three U.S. states have some form of registration, certification, or licensure that affects interior designers working on commercial projects, and the rules vary by state. The statement oversimplifies and miscounts state regulatory regimes, which differ by scope and have changed over time.

claim: Says Gov Tony Evers’ administration deemed dentists non-essential
rationale: Evers' COVID-era 'Safer at Home' orders and DHS guidance did not categorically label dentists as non-essential; they generally limited elective/non-urgent procedures while allowing emergency and essential dental care to continue. The administration followed public-health guidance (and ADA recommendations) to postpone routine dentistry temporarily rather than permanently deem dentists non-essential.

claim: "The average American is working through the month of May just to pay off the government."
rationale: This echoes the Tax Freedom Day idea but is inaccurate: the typical ‘Tax Freedom Day’ for combined federal, state and local taxes in recent decades has fallen in April (occasionally early May), not that Americans work the entire month of May solely to pay taxes. Saying the average American is working through all of May to pay the government overstates the usual tax-burden timing.

claim: Says he would be first CPA to serve as Texas comptroller.
rationale: The Texas comptroller's office has existed for many decades and several past officeholders and candidates have had accounting or financial credentials, so an unqualified claim of being the first CPA is unlikely to be true. Without a specific name and timeframe, the assertion is not supported and conflicts with the historical likelihood that at least one prior comptroller held a CPA or equivalent accounting credential.

claim: "Drunk" Nancy Pelosi "was removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or congressional record that Nancy Pelosi was drunk and removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans. Viral videos and social-media posts making that claim have been debunked or shown to be taken out of context; Pelosi has not been ejected from House proceedings for that reason.

claim: As first lady, Clinton would travel to places that were "too small, too poor or too dangerous" for the president.
rationale: As First Lady, Hillary Clinton publicly stated she would go to places that were “too small, too poor or too dangerous” for the president, and the remark has been widely reported and attributed to her. Her role included frequent overseas travel and diplomatic visits to countries and regions the president did not visit, consistent with that characterization.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's Iran nuclear deal "lined the pockets of the world's number one state sponsor of terrorism with your money."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The 2015 Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) provided sanctions relief that allowed Iran access to frozen assets and renewed oil revenues, but those were Iranian funds and commercial oil proceeds, not U.S. taxpayer dollars; calling Iran the "world's number one state sponsor of terrorism" is a political characterization rather than an objective ranking.

claim: "Suez Canal blocked by huge container ship named Evergreen. Evergreen shipping is most likely a cover for human and sex trafficking" by Hillary Clinton.
rationale: While the Ever Given, a ship operated by Evergreen Marine, did block the Suez Canal in March 2021, there is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton said Evergreen shipping is 'most likely a cover for human and sex trafficking.' The claim that Evergreen is a trafficking cover is a baseless conspiracy theory not supported by reputable reporting or public statements from Clinton.

claim: "The Katy Freeway, or Interstate 10 west of Houston, is the widest freeway in the world, with up to 26 lanes, including frontage road lanes."
rationale: The Katy Freeway (I-10 west of Houston) was reconstructed to include as many as 26 lanes at its widest point when main lanes, managed/HOV lanes and parallel frontage (feeder) roads are all counted, and numerous news and transportation sources have described it as the widest freeway in the world. The claim rests on that commonly used lane-counting method rather than a single standardized international measurement.

claim: The Banking Committee voted a 1,336-page bill "out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments, with the understanding that before the bill came to the floor, we would reach this bipartisan agreement."
rationale: There is no specific, verifiable record supporting the claim as stated: large, 1,336‑page bills are rarely reported to have been voted out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments, and major committees typically conduct longer markups or have public records if such an expedited action occurred. The assertion lacks a date, bill identifier, or source and conflicts with normal congressional committee practice and contemporary news coverage of major legislative actions.

claim: Opening the schools "is a local determination, but it’s not a state determination."
rationale: Authority over school openings is not universally only local — in the U.S. states have constitutional and statutory authority over public education and many states or governors set statewide reopening rules, even while local school boards handle day-to-day operations. Therefore the absolute statement that opening schools "is a local determination, but it’s not a state determination" is incorrect without jurisdictional context.

claim: The proposed Gogebic mine in northern Wisconsin "could be extended as long as 21 miles."
rationale: Public descriptions and permit materials for the Gogebic Taconite proposal describe a specific mine footprint and project area far smaller than a single 21‑mile continuous excavation. The 21‑mile figure appears to be a misinterpretation of the length of a regional mineral belt or potential exploration area, not the length of a contiguous open pit or mine that would be constructed as proposed.

claim: "If we pass immigration reform, it will make wages go up on average $250 for the average household."
rationale: The claim gives a specific dollar effect ($250 per household) but does not identify which immigration reform, the time frame, or the modeling assumptions that produce that figure. Empirical studies and official analyses show that labor-market effects of immigration policy are heterogeneous, typically small on average, and sensitive to assumptions, so a single precise nationwide $250 increase cannot be verified without a cited source. Therefore the unsupported, precise numeric claim is not factually established.

claim: "Never in American history has so much been spent at one time. Never in American history will so many taxes be raised and so much borrowing be needed to pay for this reckless spending."
rationale: The statement makes an absolute claim ('never') that is contradicted by historical episodes of concentrated federal spending and borrowing. For example, U.S. wartime mobilization in World War II produced much larger federal outlays relative to GDP and required massive borrowing and tax measures, and other periods (New Deal/Great Depression, 2009 stimulus, 2020–21 COVID relief) involved multitrillion-dollar packages. The predictive 'never will' is also unfalsifiable and overly absolute given different measures (nominal dollars vs. share of GDP).

claim: Says Ayn Rand said, "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me."
rationale: The line is widely attributed to Ayn Rand online, but there is no clear primary-source citation in her novels or essays that confirms she wrote the exact wording. Without a verifiable appearance in Rand’s published works, the attribution is unreliable.

claim: A DeKalb sewer project "will create up to 4,000 direct jobs per year at peak production, many of which will be set aside exclusively for DeKalb residents."
rationale: I could not find independent evidence that any DeKalb sewer project will generate 4,000 direct jobs per year at peak production nor that many of those jobs will be set aside exclusively for DeKalb residents. Large public works often publish optimistic job estimates that mix direct, indirect, and induced jobs, and exclusive resident-only hiring is generally limited by labor law and typically expressed as local-hire goals or preferences rather than absolute set‑asides.

claim: Every former North Carolina governor opposes "constitutional amendments Raleigh lawmakers put on the ballot this fall."
rationale: The claim asserts unanimous opposition by every former North Carolina governor, which is a universal statement that would require public statements from all individuals who have held that office. There is no comprehensive evidence that every single former governor publicly opposed those specific amendments; public responses among former governors are typically mixed or absent, so the blanket claim is not supported.

claim: "Since 1961 … our private economy has produced 66 million private-sector jobs. So what's the jobs score? Republicans 24 million, Democrats 42 (million)."
rationale: The headline totals are misleading and not a robust, unequivocal fact. Net private‑sector job totals depend on the exact start/end months and the dataset used; independent checks of BLS payroll data and mainstream fact‑checks show different partisan splits depending on methodology, so the precise 66M/24M/42M breakdown is not reliably supported as a definitive figure.

claim: "More Americans receive food aid than work in (the) private sector."
rationale: Common measures of private-sector employment in the United States are well over 100 million people, whereas the largest single federal food-aid program (SNAP) serves roughly 35–45 million people in recent years; even adding other nutrition programs (WIC, school meals, food banks) does not approach the scale of private-sector employment. Therefore the statement that more Americans receive food aid than work in the private sector is not supported by available counts.

claim: Says protesters at the Wisconsin state Capitol on the night the state Senate passed collective bargaining changes damaged the windshield of his car.
rationale: The statement lacks a named speaker or verifiable source, and I cannot confirm any reliable report in which an identified person said protesters at the Wisconsin State Capitol that night damaged his car windshield. Because the claim is ambiguous and unsubstantiated as presented, it cannot be treated as fact.

claim: "7 out of 10 Oregon families living in poverty have at least one parent who works."
rationale: There is not a consistently supported, precise statistic showing that exactly 7 in 10 Oregon families in poverty have a working parent; estimates change by year, data source, and by whether you count all families or only those with children. While a substantial share of poor families do include at least one working adult, the claim as stated is imprecise and not reliably validated without a specified dataset and year.

claim: Says Texas schools have had "massive increases" in class sizes with Rick Perry as governor.
rationale: Rick Perry was governor from 2000–2015, and while some grades and years saw modest increases in student–teacher ratios or local class sizes, statewide data do not show a consistent or dramatic "massive" rise in class sizes across Texas during his entire tenure. Available state enrollment and staffing reports and prior fact-checks indicate changes were relatively small and uneven, not a large, uniform jump in class size attributable solely to Perry.

claim: "There are no provisions in here that substantially affect or advantage the big Wall Street bankers."
rationale: The statement is an unqualified claim of absence that cannot be verified without the specific text referred to as "here." Evaluating whether any provisions "substantially affect or advantage the big Wall Street bankers" requires reading the actual bill or document; historically, many financial or regulatory bills include provisions that do have measurable impacts on large banks.

claim: Republicans extended unemployment insurance under President Bush "when he asked to extend unemployment insurance."
rationale: The statement is too broad and misleading: while there were occasions during George W. Bush’s presidency when unemployment benefits were extended and Bush supported some extensions, extensions were enacted at different times with mixed bipartisan support and not simply as a result of Republicans extending benefits whenever Bush asked. Historical voting records show varied GOP positions and multiple actors (including Democrats) pushing for or opposing extensions, so the blanket claim overstates the situation.

claim: Says Steve Spinnett has court judgments against him for trespass and harassment.
rationale: I cannot verify that "Steve Spinnett" has court judgments for trespass and harassment based on available knowledge; no reliable, corroborating public records or reputable news reports are known to me. Because this is an allegation about an individual and I cannot confirm matching court documents or authoritative reporting, I treat the claim as unverified and therefore classify it as false for the purposes of this check.

claim: "South Korea sprays rioters with dye so they can be identified & arrested later."
rationale: South Korean police have used colored dye/marking fluids in crowd-control operations to stain protesters or rioters so they can be identified and arrested later. This has been reported in multiple incidents and is a recognized policing tactic, though it is used in specific operations rather than as a continual, universal practice.

claim: Gov. Scott Walker received a $7,300 pay raise.
rationale: The claim lacks a time frame and there is no widely reported or documented one‑time $7,300 pay raise specifically for Gov. Scott Walker. Governors’ salaries are set by statute or commission and changes are public; major media coverage of Walker’s tenure does not corroborate a standalone $7,300 raise.

claim: Says there are half as many students in one Georgia technical college than there were two years ago.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not name the specific Georgia technical college or the exact two-year period; without those details you cannot confirm a 50% enrollment decline. While some colleges experienced enrollment drops during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, a halving of students at a single institution over two years would be an unusually large change and would require institution-level headcount data to substantiate. Absent a cited source or named college, the statement should be treated as unsupported.

claim: Says Luke Messer and Todd Rokita "voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals."
rationale: Both Luke Messer and Todd Rokita voted in favor of the 2015 Trade Promotion Authority (often called “fast-track”) measure that enabled President Obama to negotiate and submit trade agreements (notably the TPP) to Congress under expedited procedures. Their recorded votes on the House TPA/fast-track bill were 'yea.'

claim: Says Amber Alerts are issued for white kids "but not Black kids in Milwaukee."
rationale: The claim as an absolute statement is false. AMBER Alert issuances are governed by race-neutral criteria (confirmed abduction, imminent danger, sufficient descriptive information) and Milwaukee/state authorities have issued AMBER Alerts for children of different races. That said, independent reporting and studies document that missing white children often receive more media attention and there are concerns about unequal attention and possible disparities in practice.

claim: "Most young Americans right now, they’re not covered" by health insurance.
rationale: Recent data show that while young adults have a higher uninsured rate than older groups, a clear majority of young Americans are insured. Typical uninsured rates for young adult age groups in recent years have been well below 50%, not constituting a majority without coverage.

claim: "Right now we’re the highest taxed country in the world."
rationale: The United States is not currently the highest taxed country in the world by common measures. International data on total tax revenue as a share of GDP show many countries—particularly in Northern and Western Europe such as Denmark, France, and Sweden—have substantially higher tax burdens than the U.S.

claim: "IDC members also get tons of campaign money from real estate, charter school, and health care lobbyists, some of whom are Republicans with connections to Trump"
rationale: Reporting and campaign finance records have long documented that members of the New York State Independent Democratic Conference received sizable contributions from real estate, charter‑school advocates, and health‑care industry donors. Some of those donors and intermediaries were Republican‑aligned or had given to or worked for Republican/Trump‑aligned campaigns or operatives, supporting the claim in general terms.

claim: "Klein did not hold a single town hall meeting (on health care) where the general public was invited to ask questions or present their views."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement about 'Klein' but provides no identifying details (which Klein, when, or where), making it unverifiable as stated. Multiple public figures named Klein have held public forums and news reporting and public records would be needed to prove a universal absence; absolute negatives are rarely supportable without exhaustive evidence. Given the ambiguity and typical patterns of public officials holding town halls, the claim is likely false as presented.

claim: "Julia Roberts claims ‘Michelle Obama isn’t fit to clean Melania’s toilet’ "
rationale: There is no credible reporting, video, or transcript showing Julia Roberts making that quote; it appears to be a crude misattribution or fabricated social-media claim. Major fact-checkers and news outlets have not documented Roberts saying anything like this, and it is inconsistent with available public statements from her.

claim: "The (health reform) legislation which Washington passed last year has made it more difficult to hire" because it’s increased costs for employers.
rationale: While the health reform did raise costs for some employers (notably those with 50+ full-time workers facing an employer mandate), empirical analyses from the CBO and academic studies find only small net effects on overall hiring and employment. Some firms adjusted by cutting hours or hiring more part-time workers, but the claim that the law generally "has made it more difficult to hire" because it increased employer costs overstates the broad causal effect.

claim: "Florida is one of only 10 states that totally prohibit a (firearm) registry."
rationale: The assertion is not reliably verifiable as stated. While Florida does have statutory limits on maintaining centralized firearm registries, the exact number of states that 'totally prohibit' firearm registries varies by source and depends on definitions (e.g., prohibiting state-run registries vs. banning all forms of records), so the claim that it is 'one of only 10' is not consistently supported.

claim: Says Paul Ryan’s budget plan "ends Medicare."
rationale: Paul Ryan's budget proposals did not immediately terminate Medicare for current beneficiaries but proposed converting Medicare into a premium‑support/voucher‑style system for future enrollees, effectively replacing the current defined‑benefit structure over time. Critics summarize that as "ending Medicare as we know it," but the plans did not cut off benefits for those already enrolled nor instantly eliminate the program.

claim: Says Charlie "Crist made it easier for Duke to take your money."
rationale: There is no verifiable context or source provided showing a person named 'Charlie' actually said the quoted line. The claim is ambiguous about which 'Charlie', 'Crist', and 'Duke' are and lacks a reliable attribution or transcript, so it cannot be confirmed as true. Without corroborating evidence, the statement is treated as unverified and therefore classified as false.

claim: If you ask Amazon’s Alexa about the origin of the coronavirus pandemic, it says "the government planned" it.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Amazon's default Alexa reliably responds to questions about COVID-19 origins by saying 'the government planned' it. Viral clips claiming this have been debunked or shown to be out-of-context, edited, or produced by third-party skills or custom responses rather than Amazon's official knowledge graph. Amazon generally routes factual queries to vetted sources and avoids asserting conspiratorial claims as established fact.

claim: "In her campaign for president, Hillary Clinton has received $100 million in contributions from Wall Street and hedge funds."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by clear evidence. Public campaign finance records and analyses show substantial donations from finance industry individuals and PACs to Hillary Clinton and allied committees, but independent tallies do not conclusively show a discrete $100 million figure solely from "Wall Street and hedge funds" to her campaign itself. Different counting methods (direct contributions, PACs, super PACs, joint fundraising, bundling, or donations to unrelated entities) produce widely varying totals, so the flat $100 million statement is not demonstrably accurate as presented.

claim: Proposition 2 on November’s Texas ballot "does not cost state taxpayers any money."
rationale: The blanket statement that Proposition 2 "does not cost state taxpayers any money" is misleading. Even when ballot language or some officials assert no direct fiscal impact, constitutional amendments or statutory changes can create direct or indirect costs to state or local governments, and authoritative fiscal analyses (e.g., from the Texas Legislative Budget Board or Comptroller) may identify potential expenditures or revenue effects. Without the specific official fiscal note it is improper to assert zero cost with certainty.

claim: The Red Sox waited "87 long years" to win the World Series.
rationale: The Red Sox won the World Series in 1918 and next won in 2004, which is an 86-year gap. Common historical accounts and media referred to the Red Sox drought as 86 years, so the claim of 87 years is off by one year.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on an assault weapons ban.
rationale: There is no clear, documented instance where Mitt Romney publicly supported a federal assault-weapons ban and later reversed that position; across his national political career he has generally opposed broad federal AWBs while supporting some targeted gun-safety measures (e.g., background checks or state-level restrictions). Claims of a "flip-flop" typically conflate support for limited measures or prior votes at the state level with endorsement of a federal assault-weapons ban, which Romney has not clearly done then repudiated.

claim: "You can’t get on an airplane, but more than 2,000 people on that list have been able to buy a gun."
rationale: Government and media reviews found that over 2,000 people on the federal terrorist watchlist/no‑fly‑type lists were able to purchase firearms during a reviewed period because the watchlist was not fully integrated into the gun background‑check system. The watchlist can bar people from flying but, historically, did not automatically block gun purchases, producing the reported ~2,000+ matches.

claim: John McCain refuses to support a new bipartisan energy bill "because it would take away tax breaks from oil companies like Exxon Mobil."
rationale: The claim as stated is not verifiable: John McCain was on record both criticizing oil company subsidies and opposing some energy legislation for various reasons, but there is no clear, corroborated instance that he refused a new bipartisan energy bill explicitly because it would "take away tax breaks from oil companies like Exxon Mobil." Without a specific bill and vote, the assertion cannot be confirmed and appears misleading.

claim: "Debt has almost doubled in Austin under Gov. Perry."
rationale: The statement is misleading and unsupported as written: a state governor does not directly set municipal borrowing, and the claim gives no timeframe or definition of 'debt.' Reported bonded and overall debt levels in Austin rose during the 2000s but did not clearly 'almost double' attributable to Governor Rick Perry's actions. Without a specified metric (total, bonded, per capita) and period, the assertion cannot be validated.

claim: Says "Harry Reid, when asked about the Republican field, said the Republican he likes the best is Donald Trump, and he said, because I can work with him. He'll cut deals."
rationale: There is no credible record of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid praising Donald Trump or saying Trump was the Republican he liked best because he could work with him. On the contrary, Reid publicly criticized Trump repeatedly during the 2015–2016 period and afterward. The quoted praise is inconsistent with Reid's well-documented public statements.

claim: Says Congress gave Wall Street "trillions of dollars of zero interest loans."
rationale: Congress did not give Wall Street 'trillions of dollars of zero interest loans.' Large post-crisis and pandemic supports were executed by the Federal Reserve (not Congress directly) and by Treasury programs (e.g., TARP, CARES) that authorized lending, guarantees, and asset purchases; these facilities typically carried interest, fees, or equity terms and many funds were repaid. While total government and central-bank support to the financial system reached into the trillions, it is incorrect to describe that as Congress handing out zero-interest loans to Wall Street.

claim: DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz "denied unemployment went up under Obama."
rationale: There is no clear, documented instance where DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz flatly denied that unemployment rose at any point during President Obama’s tenure. Public record and reporting show she emphasized that unemployment fell overall from its peak during the recovery, while official BLS data indicate unemployment did rise in early 2009 and peaked in October 2009 before declining. The claim conflates her emphasis on net improvement with an absolute denial that unemployment ever increased during Obama’s presidency.

claim: Israel has seen a "90 percent reduction in terrorist attacks" that it attributes to building a 500-mile fence.
rationale: Israeli officials and many news reports have long credited the West Bank barrier (built in the early 2000s and commonly described in media as roughly 400–500 miles of fence/wall) with about a 90% drop in suicide bombings and similar attacks inside Israel after construction. However, independent analysts note the reduction occurred alongside military operations, checkpoints, and arrests, so complete attribution to the fence alone is disputed.
