claim: "In 1992, the Democratic Party had in their platform provisions that said that illegal aliens were coming in this country, committing felonies, sent back and then they were right back across the border to do the same thing."
rationale: There is no evidence that the official 1992 Democratic Party platform contained language asserting that illegal immigrants were coming, committing felonies, being sent back, and immediately returning to do the same. Democratic platforms typically address immigration in formal policy terms and do not contain accusatory anecdotal prose of that sort; the quoted wording appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution rather than a direct platform provision. Therefore the claim that the platform explicitly said this is not supported by available records.

claim: Virginia voters are being turned away from polling locations because they were told they already requested absentee ballots when they haven’t.
rationale: While there have been isolated reports in Virginia of individual voters being initially flagged as having requested absentee ballots and being directed to provisional processes, state and local election officials reported these were limited processing errors or record mismatches rather than a coordinated program of turning people away. Voters in such cases were generally offered provisional ballots or other remedies, and there is no clear evidence of a widespread, systematic practice of denying in-person voting for that reason.

claim: Sherrod Brown "failed to pay his own taxes three separate times."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream fact‑checking that Sherrod Brown personally failed to pay his own federal or state income taxes on three separate occasions. Reporting and public financial records do not substantiate the specific claim as stated; at most, political attacks have conflated different issues or made unverified allegations.

claim: "Within a few years, we will be spending more on interest payments than on national security."
rationale: The claim is an unspecific near-term prediction and is not clearly supported. While interest costs (net interest on government debt) are rising and many budget projections show them climbing substantially this decade, whether they will exceed 'national security' spending 'within a few years' depends on the country, the exact time window, and how 'national security' is defined; public projections (e.g., for the U.S.) suggest interest could overtake some defense or discretionary categories later in the decade but not definitively in the immediate few years.

claim: "DirecTV cancels OAN after Joe Biden orders media outlets and tech giants to banish voices that deviate from the regime’s official narrative."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Biden 'ordered' media outlets and tech companies to banish dissenting voices, nor that DirecTV's decision to stop carrying One America News Network was the result of such an order. Reports indicate carriage and business decisions by providers and documented White House requests to platforms to address misinformation, but urging or communications are not formal government orders compelling private companies to drop a channel.

claim: Says Marshall Tuck "is backed by Donald Trump’s education advisor" pictured as Betsy DeVos.
rationale: There is no record that Betsy DeVos, who served as President Trump’s education secretary, publicly endorsed or directly backed Marshall Tuck. Tuck did receive support from pro‑charter and conservative donors whose views align with DeVos, but that is not the same as DeVos personally backing him, so the claim as stated is inaccurate.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "shows up in Broward County" and had a private meeting with elections supervisor Brenda Snipes.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Hillary Clinton traveled to Broward County to have a private meeting with elections supervisor Brenda Snipes. Such a meeting between a high-profile former presidential candidate and a county elections official would have been newsworthy and documented in public schedules or reliable press coverage, but none exists. The claim appears to be an unsubstantiated rumor.

claim: Says Steph Curry decided to split with Nike because the company wouldn’t allow him to write Bible scriptures in his shoes.
rationale: There is no credible reporting that Stephen Curry split with Nike because the company forbade Bible scriptures in his shoes. Curry signed a major deal with Under Armour in 2013 for business/endorsement reasons, and while his Christian faith and occasional use of scripture are publicly known, the specific claim about Nike banning verses and that prompting a split is a social‑media rumor without evidence.

claim: "President Trump has the strongest support percentage-wise in our state than any other state in the nation. He won West Virginia by almost 43 percentage points and he's been carrying close to 60 percent approval."
rationale: The statement mixes election margins and current approval without specifying timing. While Trump did win West Virginia by a very large margin (roughly high-30s to low-40s percentage points depending on the year), he has not uniquely had the single highest statewide vote share in every recent election (Wyoming and a few other states are comparably high). Also, contemporary approval ratings vary by poll and are not uniformly “close to 60%” across reliable surveys.

claim: Says Joe Biden took a knee during the national anthem.
rationale: Contemporary news coverage and fact-checkers reviewed video of President Biden at events where the national anthem was played and found he remained standing; he sometimes bowed his head or placed a hand over his heart but did not take a knee. No credible photographic or video evidence shows Biden kneeling during the national anthem.

claim: Bryan County, Ga., has "corrupted voter rolls."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence or official finding that Bryan County, Georgia, has had its voter rolls deliberately 'corrupted.' While voter rolls nationwide can contain clerical errors or outdated registrations, those routine maintenance issues are not the same as proven intentional tampering or systemic corruption in Bryan County.

claim: Congressman Scott DesJarlais "is spending his one year anniversary on vacation -- only working 6 days in all of January."
rationale: The claim makes a specific assertion about DesJarlais working only six days in a particular January and being on vacation for his one-year anniversary, but I cannot corroborate those precise attendance/vacation figures. Congressional ‘working days’ are ambiguous (floor votes, committee work, district activity), and members’ schedules vary; without independent roll-call/office records for that exact month the numeric claim is unsupported. Given the lack of verifiable evidence and ambiguous wording, the statement should be treated as false as presented.

claim: "We don’t allow filming inside of the City Hall unless there is a specific reason."
rationale: The statement is a blanket rule presented as universal, but practices differ by municipality and context. Many City Halls permit filming in public areas or during public meetings, while some restrict commercial or intrusive recording and require permits or specific reasons.

claim: "Of our 98,000 teachers who are K-12, over 53,000 of those teachers today are over 50 years old."
rationale: The claim provides no source and uses the ambiguous term 'our' so it cannot be verified; asserting that >53,000 of 98,000 K–12 teachers (≈54%) are over 50 requires specific, dated HR or department data. Typical publicly available teacher-age distributions vary by district and state and do not universally support a majority-over-50 figure, so without a cited dataset the statement is not verifiable and is likely incorrect.

claim: Wisconsin is "run by Democrats right now," so they should address election social distancing concerns.
rationale: The statement that Wisconsin is "run by Democrats right now" is inaccurate as a general claim. As of 2024 the governor is a Democrat (Tony Evers) but the state legislature is controlled by Republicans and local election administration is handled by county and municipal officials, so control is divided and not solely Democratic.

claim: Germany "is crime-riddled right now" because of migration to Europe.
rationale: Official German and EU crime statistics and independent analyses do not support the sweeping claim that Germany is currently "crime-riddled." Overall recorded crime and most violent-crime rates in Germany have been stable or have declined in many recent years; while some specific offense categories and localized incidents have involved migrants and some studies note overrepresentation in particular crime types, that does not substantiate a broad causal claim that migration has made Germany crime-riddled.

claim: "Republicans are attempting to remove Barack Obama from Georgia’s Presidential Ballot in 2012."
rationale: The claim overstates isolated actions by fringe activists and a few individual challengers as a broad Republican effort. In 2012 there were 'birther' lawsuits and local challenges seeking to block Obama from ballots in some states (including isolated filings related to Georgia), but courts dismissed those cases and there was no official statewide Republican Party campaign that removed Obama from Georgia's ballot.

claim: "Kim Jong Un dead: North Koreans calling Trump an assassin"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Kim Jong Un has died or that a widespread chorus of North Koreans are publicly calling former U.S. President Trump an 'assassin.' North Korea tightly controls information and state media would have reported a leader's death; international news agencies and governments have not verified such claims. The headline matches repeated false rumor patterns that spread on social media without corroboration.

claim: "Most of the people that work in finance make $70,000, $80,000 a year."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and unsupported: pay in 'finance' varies widely by role, experience, employer type and country, so it is unlikely that a majority of finance workers all earn in a narrow $70k–$80k band. Labor statistics and industry reports show a wide distribution with many entry‑level/clerical finance jobs below that range and many professional/senior roles well above it.

claim: Say a "left wing extremist, chases down, rams car over Trump bumper sticker."
rationale: The claim is presented without any specific facts (no date, location, names, or source) and there are no known, credible reports or corroborating evidence of a verified incident in which a 'left wing extremist' chased down and rammed a car over a Trump bumper sticker. A politically motivated vehicle attack of that nature would almost certainly be reported by multiple reliable news outlets and law enforcement, but this allegation appears unsubstantiated. Given the vagueness and lack of verification, the claim cannot be treated as true.

claim: Says "Canada has one-tenth of our population—yet it issues far more high-skilled visas (more than 150,000) yearly than we do (65,000)."
rationale: The part stating Canada is about one‑tenth the population of the U.S. is roughly correct, but the numerical comparison of 'high‑skilled visas' is misleading and unsupported. The U.S. issues far more than a simple 65,000 floor of high‑skilled admissions when H‑1B caps (65k plus a 20k master’s exemption), other work visa categories, and employment‑based green cards are counted, and Canada’s own counts depend on how 'high‑skilled visas' are defined (temporary work permits, Express Entry invitations, or economic permanent residents). The claim’s specific figures and direct comparison therefore do not hold up without clearer definitions and up‑to‑date sources.

claim: Columbia, Mo., is "one of the fastest growing cities in the region, the only city in the state to grow jobs faster than the nation as a whole."
rationale: The statement is time‑dependent and presented without a specific time period or source. While Columbia, Missouri, has experienced notable population and job growth, it is unlikely to be uniquely the only Missouri city with job growth outpacing the national rate across any commonly cited multi‑year period; other Missouri metro areas (e.g., parts of the Kansas City or Springfield regions and some suburbs) have posted faster job growth in various recent intervals. Without a specific timeframe and data source the absolute claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: "House Bill 6627 also requires the applicant to attest to their eligibility to vote, as is required by the National Voter Registration Act and used by all other states that have (automatic voter registration)."
rationale: I cannot verify that the unspecified "House Bill 6627" contains an attestation requirement; while the National Voter Registration Act does require applicants to attest to eligibility and many automatic voter registration systems include such attestations, the claim asserts a specific provision in a specific bill that I cannot confirm without the bill text or state context. Absent that confirmation, the statement that HB 6627 "also requires" this is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: In comparing mass shootings, "France had a higher casualty rate in one year than the entire two administrations of Barack Obama."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while France suffered a single-year high from the 2015 Paris attacks (roughly 130 dead and hundreds injured), the United States experienced many high-casualty mass shootings across the eight years of the Obama administrations (e.g., Fort Hood, Aurora, Sandy Hook, Charleston, San Bernardino, Orlando) whose deaths and injuries in aggregate exceed that one-year French total. Therefore it is inaccurate to state France had a higher casualty rate in one year than Obama’s two administrations without atypical definitions or selective counting.

claim: Americans "bought into climate change" in 2004-06, but then most "began wandering away from this issue."
rationale: Major public-opinion surveys do show rising awareness and concern about climate change in the mid-2000s, but the claim that most Americans subsequently "began wandering away" is an overstatement. Polling since 2006 shows fluctuating levels of worry and priority (with declines in some years, partisan divergence, and later rebounds), not a sustained mass abandonment of the issue.

claim: Video shows helicopters in Ukraine "being picked off in ambush - Short range air-to-air missile"
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that the video uniquely shows helicopters in Ukraine being struck by a short‑range air‑to‑air missile. Visual evidence from conflict videos is often misattributed; most helicopter shootdowns in Ukraine have been attributed to ground‑launched MANPADS or anti‑aircraft fire rather than missiles launched from another aircraft. Without expert weapon‑type forensics and provenance, the specific claim that a short‑range air‑to‑air missile ambushed the helicopters is unproven and unlikely.

claim: Missouri "is the state with the lowest paid workers."
rationale: This claim is false. Missouri’s wages and household incomes are below the national average but are not the lowest in the U.S.; states such as Mississippi, West Virginia, Arkansas and Louisiana typically rank lower in median wages and household income in recent federal data.

claim: "You (Hillary Clinton) get a subpoena, and after getting the subpoena you delete 33,000 emails."
rationale: Clinton’s lawyers did delete roughly 30,000+ emails they deemed personal, but those deletions were made during the lawyers’ review in early 2015 (and earlier) before Congress had issued a subpoena for her server. Multiple reputable fact‑checks and the timeline of State Department/FOIA requests show no congressional subpoena preceded the deletions, so the claim that she deleted them after getting a subpoena is incorrect.

claim: "With 40 billion dollars, Elon Musk could have given each of the 330M people living in America a million dollars and still had $7B left over."
rationale: Paying 330 million people $1,000,000 each would cost about $330 trillion (330,000,000 × $1,000,000 = $330,000,000,000,000). $40 billion is vastly smaller than $330 trillion, so it is impossible to give each person $1M and still have $7B remaining.

claim: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security warned that the SAVE "database is not a foolproof means of verifying (citizenship on) the voter rolls."
rationale: USCIS, which operates the SAVE system under the Department of Homeland Security, has publicly warned that SAVE has limitations and is not a definitive or foolproof tool for establishing citizenship for voter-registration purposes. Officials and official guidance have stated SAVE should not be used as the sole means to determine eligibility and can produce incomplete or uncertain results.

claim: Says Republican-approved changes to "make it more difficult to participate in Ohio elections include reducing in-person early voting from 35 days to six."
rationale: Republican-backed legislation passed in Ohio in 2023 significantly shortened the period for in-person early voting, cutting the long-standing multi-week early-voting window (commonly cited as 35 days) to a limited six-day period immediately before Election Day. Multiple news reports and analyses of the bill described this change as a key GOP-approved restriction on in-person early voting.

claim: "Piles of bricks are being staged in cities around the country, indicating riots are planned."
rationale: There is no credible evidence of a coordinated, nationwide effort to stage piles of bricks to incite riots. Images of stacked bricks have frequently been shown to come from ordinary construction, landscaping, roadwork, or isolated local incidents, and fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked claims of a widespread conspiracy.

claim: "The 2008 election was the first election in which voters of color comprised over 25 percent of the electorate, and that number is going up."
rationale: Authoritative turnout and exit-poll data indicate the combined share of Black, Hispanic, Asian and other nonwhite voters in 2008 was about mid-20s percentage points but generally reported just under or around 25%, so the statement that 2008 was the first election with voters of color comprising over 25% is not clearly supported. However, most sources do show the minority share has increased in subsequent elections.

claim: Takes credit for "reining in" state spending when he was governor.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it lacks any named individual or timeframe; without identifying who 'he' is, I cannot confirm whether that person publicly took credit for reining in state spending while governor. Such a statement could be true for some governors and false for others, but in this form it is unsupported. Therefore I classify it as false due to missing necessary specifics.

claim: Says remdesivir is responsible for killing patients hospitalized with COVID-19.
rationale: Randomized clinical trials and major regulatory reviews did not find that remdesivir causes increased deaths in hospitalized COVID-19 patients; trials showed reduced time to recovery (ACTT-1) and the WHO SOLIDARITY trial found little or no effect on mortality rather than evidence of harm. While remdesivir can cause adverse effects (e.g., liver enzyme elevations, potential renal effects), there is no robust evidence that it is responsible for killing patients hospitalized with COVID-19 as a general causal claim.

claim: Milwaukee’s problems include "52 percent black male unemployment."
rationale: The claim is an imprecise and misleading use of statistics. Official labor-data sources and local analyses do not show a 52% unemployment rate for all Black men in Milwaukee; that high number usually arises from misreporting a different measure (for example, the share of certain age groups who are not working or not in the labor force, or a short-term spike in a narrowly defined subgroup). Without a specified year and age definition the plain statement about 52% unemployment is inaccurate.

claim: John McCain says he never supported the privatization of Social Security, even though video shows he did.
rationale: During the 2008 campaign McCain repeatedly denied having supported privatizing Social Security, but archival video and statements from earlier years show him endorsing private/individual accounts and partial privatization. The discrepancy between his campaign denials and his prior recorded comments supports the claim.

claim: There are "approximately 20,000 annual gun purchases in Rhode Island."
rationale: The claim is likely incorrect or misleading. Rhode Island's small population (~1.1 million) and available state-level firearms reporting do not support a clear figure of ~20,000 completed annual purchases, and public data commonly cited are background-check counts (NICS) which are not equivalent to actual purchases and can vary year to year. Without a cited source or year, the 20,000 number appears unsupported.

claim: "I was the most bipartisan senator in the United States Senate."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because the speaker ('I') is unspecified and 'most bipartisan' depends on the metric and timeframe used. Different organizations (e.g., GovTrack, academic measures of co-sponsorship or roll-call behavior) produce differing rankings, so without a named senator, period, and citation to a recognized measure the claim cannot be confirmed. Therefore it should be treated as false or at least unsubstantiated.

claim: Under David Dewhurst’s leadership, the Texas "Senate passed an expansion of in-state tuition and free health care to illegal immigrants."
rationale: The claim mixes facts and is misleading. Texas did adopt a limited in-state tuition policy for certain undocumented students in 2001, before David Dewhurst became lieutenant governor (he served 2003–2015), and Texas has not enacted a law providing blanket "free health care" to illegal immigrants; undocumented immigrants remain largely ineligible for Medicaid except for limited emergency or children's services. Thus the specific assertion that under Dewhurst’s leadership the Texas Senate passed expansions of in-state tuition and free health care for undocumented immigrants is incorrect.

claim: "In many instances, (people's) health care costs are more than their mortgage costs or their rent, which, by the way, is a first in American history."
rationale: Housing (mortgage or rent) has long been the single largest household expense for most Americans; while medical spending has risen and can exceed housing for some individuals (especially the uninsured, chronically ill, or elderly needing long-term care), it is not broadly true that health care costs exceed housing 'in many instances' across the population. The claim that this is 'a first in American history' is also incorrect—there have always been subgroups and historical periods where medical bills were the dominant expense for affected households. Overall, the statement overgeneralizes from specific cases to a broad historical first.

claim: "It isn't me cutting the budget. It's the Congress' decision on sequestration. So it isn't secretary of defense or the president doing this."
rationale: Sequestration is an automatic, statutory spending-cut mechanism created by Congress (not a unilateral action by the president or a cabinet secretary) that triggers across-the-board reductions when certain budget targets are missed. While the executive branch implements the sequester (for example, the OMB and agencies apply the cuts) and the president can propose or seek to change the law, the legal requirement for those automatic cuts originates in legislation enacted by Congress.

claim: "This is the first time since Roe was decided in 1973 that a court has granted personhood status to the preborn."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because courts and legislatures have recognized legal rights or victim status for fetuses many times since Roe v. Wade (1973). State fetal-homicide statutes, wrongful-death suits on behalf of fetuses, and other decisions have treated the preborn as victims or legal subjects in various contexts long before the recent actions claimed. While the U.S. Supreme Court never conferred full constitutional personhood on fetuses in Roe, lower courts regularly have afforded fetuses limited legal protections.

claim: "In 1960, most black children were raised in two-parent, monogamous families." Today "we have only 20 percent of black children being raised in two-parent, monogamous families..."
rationale: The first part is accurate in broad strokes—most Black children in 1960 lived with two married parents (roughly three-quarters). However, the contemporary figure is misstated: recent Census and research summaries show the share of Black children living with two married parents has fallen to roughly the 30–40% range, not as low as 20%.

claim: "Every day in the United States, we are losing 15 factories."
rationale: There is no consistent evidence that the U.S. loses 15 factories every day (about 5,475 per year); official statistics on manufacturing establishments from agencies like the BLS and Census show year-to-year net changes that are much smaller and variable. The "15 a day" figure appears to be an overgeneralization or a misinterpretation of gross closures, short time windows, or differing definitions of "factory."

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown voted to keep "an extreme, job-killing Internal Revenue Service paperwork mandate."
rationale: The claim is vague and frames a subjective policy description (“extreme, job-killing”) as an objective fact. Public roll‑call records do not unambiguously show Sen. Sherrod Brown casting a single, isolated vote described in that language; the disputed reporting requirement most often cited (changes to 1099‑K reporting thresholds) was altered during negotiations and implementation was delayed, so saying he 'voted to keep' an unspecified 'paperwork mandate' is misleading. Without a clear bill, provision, and vote, the assertion cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Since 2009, "after-tax incomes are up nearly 14 percent."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and therefore misleading: it does not specify the country, the time endpoint, whether figures are nominal or inflation‑adjusted, or whether it refers to mean or median after‑tax incomes. Different reputable measures diverge—real disposable personal income per capita and median after‑tax household income have changed by different amounts since 2009—so a blanket statement that after‑tax incomes are 'up nearly 14 percent' cannot be verified as true without those details. Given the lack of specification, the claim as stated is not reliably supported.

claim: "The federal government is now on track" for the second-largest budget deficit "in 65 years."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it lacks a specified fiscal year and metric; recent deficits are large but still well below the COVID-era peak (FY2020). Historical data show FY2020 (~$3.1T) and FY2021 (~$2.8T) were the largest recent deficits, and most official projections through 2023–24 forecast deficits smaller than those peaks, so a blanket statement that the government is "now on track" for the second-largest in 65 years is not supported without more context.

claim: "New York, for all of their complaining, Gov. Cuomo's complaining, has only had a 1.5% decrease in revenue" due to the coronavirus pandemic.
rationale: The claim understates the impact: New York reported multi‑billion‑dollar revenue shortfalls and steep drops in tax collections during spring 2020 tied to the pandemic, with monthly declines in some categories reaching double digits and overall fiscal‑year gaps far larger than 1.5%. Multiple state budget briefings and news analyses documented that the fiscal impact was substantial rather than a mere 1.5% revenue decline.

claim: "Kids are less likely to get it (COVID-19). You know, they’re less likely to spread. So I think there’s some pretty good data out there that will help alleviate some of the concerns."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification. Early in the pandemic some studies found children had lower susceptibility and lower secondary attack rates, but evidence from later variants (Delta, Omicron) showed children can be infected and transmit SARS‑CoV‑2 at rates comparable to adults. Therefore the blanket statement that kids are less likely to get it and spread it is misleading without variant-, age-, and context-specific qualifiers.

claim: Roy Blunt "voted to raise his own pay 12 times" while in Congress.
rationale: The claim is misleading. Congressional pay changes can occur via automatic COLA mechanisms, omnibus measures, or votes to block versus accept adjustments, and Blunt did vote on some measures affecting member pay during a long career but did not cast twelve distinct, standalone votes simply to 'raise his own pay' as the claim implies.

claim: Greg Abbott "has campaigned with a sexual predator who has bragged about having sex with underage girls."
rationale: There are no credible reports through mid-2024 that Texas Governor Greg Abbott campaigned with a person who publicly bragged about having sex with underage girls. Such an association and allegation would have been widely reported by major news outlets, and public records of Abbott's campaign appearances do not identify a named individual matching that description. Without a specific name or reliable source, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Cannabis reform "is supported by the majority of the residents of our state, including a majority of Republicans."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it names no specific state or time period; support for cannabis reform varies by state and over time. National polling generally shows a majority of adults favor legalization, but majorities of Republicans are uncommon nationwide (though possible in some states or years), so the blanket statement is not reliably true without local, dated poll data.

claim: Wayne Powell has a "stated position of having no objection to taking `In God We Trust" off of U.S. currency."
rationale: I am not aware of any credible reporting, public statement, or official record showing a person named Wayne Powell saying he had no objection to removing 'In God We Trust' from U.S. currency. The claim appears unverified and likely arises from misattribution or a lack of sourcing. Without a clear source or context (which Wayne Powell, when, and where), the statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: The FBI lost Hunter Biden’s laptop.
rationale: Public reporting and statements indicate the repair-shop owner provided the laptop or its hard drive to the FBI in late 2019 and the bureau acknowledged receiving data; there is no credible evidence the FBI permanently 'lost' the laptop. While copies of the drive were shared with third parties (including Rudy Giuliani and the New York Post) and chain-of-custody has been disputed, that does not support the claim that the FBI lost the device.

claim: Says a change in law he carried stopped a $100 million tax increase in the Dallas school district.
rationale: The claim is vague and lacks verifiable specifics (who 'he' is, which law, and when). Without identifying the legislator, the statute, or independent reporting showing a law directly prevented a $100 million Dallas school district tax increase, the assertion cannot be confirmed. Given the absence of corroborating evidence and the likelihood that such a large, district-specific fiscal outcome would be documented, the claim is treated as false pending reliable sources.

claim: Says a gun bill before the Senate would make it a federal felony to "leave town for more than seven days, and leave someone else at home with your firearms."
rationale: There is no known federal Senate bill that makes it a felony merely to leave town for more than seven days and leave someone else at home with your firearms. Recent federal gun proposals have targeted safe-storage requirements, background checks, and prohibitions on access by minors or prohibited persons, but not a blanket felony for an owner being absent and another person remaining in the home with legally owned guns. The claim appears to misstate or exaggerate typical legislative language.

claim: Says Matt Rosendale "consistently supported land use rules that would help developers like him and hurt farmers in Montana."
rationale: There is insufficient public evidence to support the categorical claim that Matt Rosendale 'consistently supported land use rules that would help developers like him and hurt farmers in Montana.' While Rosendale has generally favored property-rights and development-friendly positions, available voting records and public statements do not show a clear, consistent pattern explicitly advantaging developers at the expense of farmers as stated. The claim is broad and appears to overstate or simplify a more complex record.

claim: The Postal Service’s financial losses result from "a 2006 law that drains $5 billion a year from post office revenue, while the Postal Service is forced to overpay billions more into federal accounts."
rationale: The 2006 Postal Accountability and Enhancement Act imposed an unprecedented prefunding requirement for retiree health benefits that required annual payments in the roughly $5–5.5 billion range, which materially worsened reported USPS losses. Independent analyses and government watchdogs have concluded those mandated prefunding payments, along with large statutory pension and retirement-account contributions, were a major driver of reported deficits.

claim: California’s Central Valley and Inland Empire "are experiencing tremendous job growth."
rationale: While parts of the Inland Empire have seen notable job gains—particularly in logistics and warehousing—employment growth across the Inland Empire and Central Valley has been uneven and, in the Central Valley especially, more modest. Characterizing both regions as uniformly "experiencing tremendous job growth" overstates the case and ignores variation by county, sector, and timeframe.

claim: COVID-19 is a synthetic version of "snake venom" that evil forces are spreading through remdesivir, the COVID-19 vaccines and drinking water to "make you a hybrid of Satan."
rationale: This claim is false. SARS-CoV-2 is a virus (a coronavirus) with zoonotic origins and is not a synthetic form of snake venom; COVID-19 vaccines and the antiviral remdesivir have documented ingredients and delivery methods (vaccines contain mRNA or vectors and lipids, remdesivir is an intravenously administered antiviral) and are subject to safety monitoring, and municipal drinking water is treated and regulated. There is no credible evidence that any of these products are being used to spread venom or cause supernatural “hybrid” transformations—such assertions are conspiratorial and not scientifically grounded.

claim: "More college graduates are living at home than in decades."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and likely misleading. While overall young adults living with parents rose to multi-decade highs (driven by economic shocks and the COVID pandemic), data specific to college graduates show they are less likely to live with parents and any uptick during recent years appears smaller and more temporary than the claim implies.

claim: The departments of Commerce, Education and Energy and the EPA saw their spending increase by between 130 percent and 219 percent between 2008 and 2010.
rationale: This claim overstates wide, multi-hundred-percent increases for entire agencies. While the 2009 Recovery Act (ARRA) did direct significant, one‑time funds to agencies such as Education, Energy and EPA, the overall departmental budgets for Commerce, Education, Energy and EPA did not uniformly rise by 130–219% between 2008 and 2010. The numbers more plausibly reflect specific program or grant lines rather than total departmental spending.

claim: "For more than 80 years, there has not been a nomination and confirmation of a Supreme Court Justice in a presidential election year. This is simply not the time to break with decades of bipartisan practice."
rationale: The factual part of the claim was true up until 2016–2019 (the last election‑year confirmation before then was in 1932), but it is no longer correct: in October 2020 Amy Coney Barrett was nominated and confirmed in a presidential election year. The second sentence is a normative argument and not a factual statement.

claim: Gov. Lincoln Chafee has imposed "a mandatory abortion fee" on all Rhode Islanders who buy health insurance through the state’s Obamacare exchange.
rationale: Chafee did not impose a universal “mandatory abortion fee” on all exchange enrollees. Rhode Island policy around the ACA required that abortion coverage, if offered, be funded through a separately itemized premium or rider and federal law prevents using premium tax credits for abortion coverage; people who did not want abortion coverage were not required to pay for it. The claim misstates the policy as a compulsory charge for all purchasers.

claim: Says CNN and other news organizations tweeted that a journalist was executed in Kabul by Taliban fighters.
rationale: I am not aware of a verified instance where CNN and multiple mainstream news organizations tweeted that a journalist had been executed in Kabul by Taliban fighters. Reputable outlets reported deaths and chaotic violence during Afghanistan's collapse, but there were no widely corroborated, on‑the‑record reports from CNN asserting a Taliban execution of a specific journalist; viral social‑media claims made that assertion and were debunked or lacked independent verification.

claim: Says "Ammar Campa-Najjar is working to infiltrate Congress" and "is being supported by CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Ammar Campa-Najjar is part of any organized effort to "infiltrate" Congress, nor credible proof that he is being funded or directed by the Muslim Brotherhood. Claims tying him to extremist organizations have been investigated and debunked by reporters and fact-checkers, and his campaign records and public endorsements do not show coordination with or control by the Muslim Brotherhood. While CAIR is a U.S. Muslim civil-rights organization that on occasion engages in political advocacy, allegations that CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood are secretly backing or directing Campa-Najjar lack substantiation.

claim: "People are less likely to just vote for party now. … They’re looking at the personalities."
rationale: The claim is an overly broad generalization. While candidate-centered politics and attention to personalities have grown in some contexts, political science and survey evidence shows party identification and partisan voting remain strong and in many places have become more entrenched rather than fading.

claim: "There's no negative advertising in my campaign at all."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that no negative advertising exists in the campaign, which is unlikely and hard to verify without a specific campaign, time period, and definition of "negative." In modern elections, campaigns and allied independent groups commonly run contrast or attack ads, so an unqualified denial is probably false unless comprehensive monitoring proves otherwise.

claim: "Nationwide tuition at public universities is up almost 300 percent ... in the last 20 years."
rationale: National data sources track published tuition and fees at public four‑year institutions and show large increases over recent decades but not a near 300% rise in the past 20 years. Depending on measure (published vs. net price, in‑state vs. out‑of‑state) increases over the last two decades are generally much smaller—often on the order of roughly 50–200% nominal and far less after inflation—so the claim of "almost 300 percent" over 20 years is not supported.

claim: Letting the Bush tax cuts expire would raise taxes on small businesses.
rationale: Many small businesses operate as pass-through entities (sole proprietorships, partnerships, S‑corps, LLCs) and are taxed on owners' individual income. If the Bush-era individual tax rate reductions and related provisions expired, owners' marginal rates and taxes on pass-through income would generally rise, increasing taxes for those small businesses. C‑corporations taxed at the corporate rate would not be directly affected, so the effect is not universal.

claim: Photo shows Bill Clinton among others not wearing a mask at John Lewis’ funeral.
rationale: The widely circulated image claiming to show Bill Clinton unmasked at John Lewis' funeral was miscaptioned or taken out of context. Contemporary news photos and videos from the July 2020 services show attendees observing COVID mask protocols and fact-checkers reported the specific unmasked photo was not from that funeral.

claim: Insurance companies have seen their profits soar by more than 400 percent since 2001.
rationale: The claim is stated without scope or timeframe and therefore is not verifiable as a general fact. Insurance industry profits vary widely by country, line of business, and year (for example losses in 2008 and other years offset gains), and aggregate industry profit data do not support a blanket >400% increase since 2001. Individual insurers or specific segments may have seen large gains, but the unqualified universal assertion is misleading.

claim: The Murray-Ryan deal "is the first divided-government budget agreement since 1986."
rationale: The Murray-Ryan 2013 deal was not the first budget agreement under divided government since 1986. There were significant bipartisan budget agreements after 1986, most notably the 1990 budget agreement under President George H.W. Bush and the 1997 Balanced Budget Agreement negotiated between President Bill Clinton and the Republican Congress. Thus the claim overstates uniqueness.

claim: "Gavin Newsom reportedly intervened at the request of Nancy Pelosi and directly ordered the California Highway Patrol to drop all charges" against Paul Pelosi for his DUI arrest.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Gavin Newsom intervened at Nancy Pelosi's request or directly ordered the California Highway Patrol to drop all charges against Paul Pelosi. CHP and the governor's office publicly denied any such intervention, and reporting by major outlets found no documentation or official action supporting that claim; the handling of the incident involved routine CHP investigative decisions and local prosecutorial choices, not a gubernatorial order.

claim: Says "I’ve been proven right" about "Hillary Clinton's radical call for open borders, meaning anyone in the world can enter the United States without any limit at all."
rationale: Hillary Clinton has not called for ‘open borders’ that would allow anyone in the world to enter the U.S. without limit. Her public positions and campaign statements have consistently supported comprehensive immigration reform with border security and pathways to legal status, and she has explicitly rejected an open‑borders policy.

claim: "An economic impact study found that for every $1 invested in pre-K in Pennsylvania, a total of $1.79 is generated in total spending within the state."
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific claim as stated because I am not aware of a widely cited, verifiable study that precisely reports a $1 → $1.79 in-state spending multiplier for pre-K investment in Pennsylvania. Economic impact studies of pre-K produce a range of multipliers depending on assumptions, methods, and whether they count short-term stimulus or long-term benefits. Without the study name, author, or year, the precise numeric claim should be treated as unverified.

claim: Data on violent crime shows Wisconsin "has become less safe than it was when Scott Walker took office."
rationale: Statewide violent-crime trends do not support a simple claim that Wisconsin is less safe now than when Scott Walker took office in 2011. FBI/UCR and state reporting show violent crime rates fell through much of the 2010s after 2011, then rose around 2020–2022 during the pandemic period; the statewide rate as reported in recent years is not uniformly higher than the 2011 level. Therefore the blanket statement that data show Wisconsin has become less safe since Walker took office is misleading.

claim: "42 percent of (Walmart’s) associates are black."
rationale: Public diversity data and EEO-1 style breakdowns for Walmart do not support that 42% of its associates are Black. A 42% figure is more plausibly an aggregate for 'people of color' or refers to a different subgroup, whereas reported shares for Black employees are substantially lower (varying by year and role, typically below 30%).

claim: Says Christopher Little has "a history of working against environmental protection by defending the worst types of corporate polluters"
rationale: I could not find reliable, public evidence that a specific individual named Christopher Little has a documented history of defending major corporate polluters or working against environmental protection. The name corresponds to multiple people (including a well-known late literary agent) and without a clear identity or credible sources the allegation is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says "of the 2,000 Portland households in the year-long (composting) pilot, 87 percent of participants reported being satisfied with the overall system."
rationale: I cannot confirm from authoritative sources that a Portland year‑long composting pilot involved exactly 2,000 households and that 87% reported satisfaction. Portland has run food‑scrap/composting pilots and surveys have shown generally high satisfaction, but the specific numbers in this claim are not verifiable from my knowledge. Because the exact sample size and percentage are unconfirmed, the precise phrasing is likely inaccurate or unverified.

claim: Says that Minnesota Democratic congressional candidate Dean Phillips doesn’t offer health insurance for his employees.
rationale: This claim is unsubstantiated: I find no credible, specific reporting or documentation that Dean Phillips categorically does not offer health insurance to his employees. Without clear, verifiable evidence (specifying which employees and which employer) the assertion cannot be confirmed and should be treated as false.

claim: "Too many dead people voted" in Michigan
rationale: Post-election audits, recounts, official statements, and court rulings found no evidence that a substantial number of deceased people voted in Michigan; investigations identified only a very small number of isolated cases often explained by clerical errors, duplicate records, or ballots cast before a voter's recorded date of death. The scale of such instances was not large enough to support the claim that "too many" dead people voted or to affect election outcomes.

claim: "Under the ruling of the Supreme Court, any lobbyist could go into any legislator and say, if you don't vote our way on this bill, we're going to run a million-dollar campaign against you in your district."
rationale: Supreme Court rulings such as Citizens United permit independent political spending by outside groups but do not authorize lobbyists to engage in unlawful threats or bribery. Saying "we'll run a million-dollar campaign against you if you don't vote our way" could be political speech in some forms, but coercive threats or quid-pro-quo arrangements remain illegal and coordination with a candidate's campaign is restricted.

claim: Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas and his wife Ginni posted a photo of themselves enjoying a $5,135 bottle of wine "as American women despair about abortion rights being taken away from them."
rationale: While Ginni Thomas did post a photo with her husband and a bottle of wine, independent fact-checking and news reports found no reliable evidence that the pictured bottle itself cost $5,135; that price figure was misattributed or taken from unrelated listings/auctions. The quoted phrase about "American women despair[ing]" appears to be commentary from others, not language contained in their post.

claim: Says Melania Trump hired exorcist to "cleanse White House of Obama demons."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Melania Trump said she hired an exorcist to 'cleanse the White House of Obama demons.' The story traces to sensational tabloid reporting and unverified claims; mainstream news outlets and fact‑checkers found no reliable confirmation and characterized the allegation as baseless or misreported. Routine religious blessings of the White House by clergy are documented, but that is not the same as an exorcism aimed at 'Obama demons.'

claim: Says taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel jumped $100 million in closed-door sessions
rationale: There is no credible public reporting or available public records indicating that the taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel increased by $100 million in secret closed‑door sessions. Major changes to subsidy amounts for public development projects in Oregon are typically reflected in public agendas, council votes, and contract documents, and reporters covering the project have not documented such a clandestine $100 million jump.

claim: "A rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months. The legislature’s failure to expand Medicaid has brought crisis to many of Missouri’s rural health care providers."
rationale: The specific rate "a rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months" is not supported by verifiable statewide data and is presented without a timeframe, making it misleading. Moreover, Missouri voters approved Medicaid expansion in 2020 and expansion was implemented in 2021, so it is incorrect to claim the legislature currently has refused to expand Medicaid; that said, prior non‑expansion did contribute to financial strain on some rural providers.

claim: A "majority of our students are trapped in" underperforming schools.
rationale: The statement is unverified as written because it lacks critical context: who are 'our students', what time period, and how 'underperforming' is defined. Whether a majority of students attend low-performing schools varies widely by district, state, and the metric used (test scores, graduation rates, growth metrics), so the blanket claim cannot be established as true. Without specific jurisdiction and a clear performance threshold, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance because of (Obamacare)."
rationale: The specific claim that exactly '20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance because of Obamacare' is not supported by clear, consistent state data. Reports from 2013–2014 show some noncompliant individual plans were canceled in Kansas, but counts and causal attribution vary and many people were offered replacement plans or obtained coverage through the exchanges or Medicaid, so the statement as-worded is misleading.

claim: "As a 27 year old staff attorney for the House Judiciary Committee during the Watergate investigation, Hillary Rodham was fired by her supervisor, lifelong Democrat Jerry Zeifman. When asked why Hillary Rodham was fired, Zeifman said in an interview, ‘Because she was a liar. She was an unethical, dishonest lawyer, she conspired to violate the Constitution, the rules of the House, the rules of the Committee, and the rules of confidentiality.’"
rationale: While Hillary Rodham did serve as a young staff attorney on the House Judiciary Committee during Watergate and Jerry Zeifman publicly denounced her years later (using harsh language and saying he had her dismissed), historical records show she submitted a resignation that was accepted rather than being formally fired by Zeifman. Zeifman’s critical comments were widely reported, but the claim’s framing that he personally fired her is misleading.

claim: Says Sen. Chuck Schumer in 2014 "helped put together and signed a $25 billion deal to fund a border wall" and now opposes Trump's $5 billion request for a border wall "just because he's a Republican." ​
rationale: There is no clear record that Sen. Schumer "helped put together and signed a $25 billion deal to fund a border wall" in 2014; he did support some border‑security measures in broader immigration discussions but not a standalone $25 billion wall deal. The claim that he now opposes Trump's $5 billion request "just because he's a Republican" asserts motive without evidence—Schumer and other Democrats publicly cited policy, constitutional and process objections rather than a pure partisan admission.

claim: "All" University of Texas "student-athletes get an iPad."
rationale: There is no evidence that every University of Texas student-athlete automatically receives an iPad. Universities sometimes provide tablets or loaner devices to specific teams, incoming classes, or for academic support, but distribution is not universally applied to all student-athletes across the entire program.

claim: Health care premiums for consumers have doubled since 2001.
rationale: In the United States, employer-sponsored and individual health insurance premiums have more than doubled since 2001. Surveys such as Kaiser Family Foundation's Employer Health Benefits reports show average family premiums rising from roughly the low- to mid‑$9,000s in the early 2000s to over $20,000 in recent years, which exceeds a twofold increase.

claim: Says "Scott Walker says he would ban stem cell research"
rationale: This statement is misleading: Scott Walker has criticized embryonic stem cell research and said he would not support funding or research that destroys embryos, but he has not broadly declared a ban on all stem cell research. Public statements and his record show support for non‑embryonic (adult or induced pluripotent) stem cell research while opposing embryo‑destructive methods.

claim: In one year, the United Nations "did 24 resolutions and 20 of them were against Israel."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported as stated: the United Nations comprises many bodies (General Assembly, Security Council, Human Rights Council, specialized agencies) and the number and subjects of resolutions vary by year and organ. No reliable record shows a UN-wide total of exactly 24 resolutions in a single year with 20 directed against Israel; such statements are typically misattributions or omit which UN body and which year they refer to.

claim: The federal government "has $3 trillion in cash flow, so we can pay our bills" and won’t default.
rationale: This is misleading. The U.S. Treasury does receive large amounts of revenue and may temporarily manage obligations with cash balances and extraordinary measures, but it does not reliably hold $3 trillion in immediately available cash and whether the government defaults depends on timing of receipts, outlays, and the debt-limit/legal context. Asserting categorically that it "won’t default" ignores those timing constraints and political/legal risks.

claim: Says Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Tammy Baldwin ranks "as the most liberal member of the House."
rationale: Tammy Baldwin was widely regarded as one of the more liberal House Democrats, but mainstream measures of congressional ideology (DW-NOMINATE, National Journal/GovTrack ratings) do not consistently place her as the single most liberal House member. Other representatives have scored to the left of Baldwin in those common rankings during her House tenure.

claim: Abortion services are "well over 90 percent of what Planned Parenthood does."
rationale: This is incorrect. Abortions account for only a small fraction of Planned Parenthood’s clinical services (commonly reported around 2–4% of total services) and represent a relatively small share of its clinical revenue; the majority of care provided is contraception, STI testing/treatment, cancer screening and other reproductive-health services.

claim: "New Jersey today has fewer employees in state government than it had when Christie Whitman left office in January of 2001, and I think that’s good. And we did it without any layoffs. We did it through attrition."
rationale: This claim is not reliably verifiable as stated. Public employment series and state payroll records use different definitions (state executive branch only vs. all state government employees, FTE vs. headcount) and show that totals have fluctuated since 2001; depending on the measure and year referenced, New Jersey has not unambiguously ended up with fewer state-government employees than in January 2001, and there were instances of layoffs and workforce actions rather than only attrition. Because the claim asserts a precise, unqualified fact about “today” and about the absence of any layoffs, it overstates what can be supported by available, variably defined data.

claim: "Barack Obama has consistently voted against tougher penalties for criminals."
rationale: Obama’s legislative record on criminal penalties is mixed rather than consistently oppositional: he has both supported and opposed measures that increased penalties at different times. Fact-checkers and legislative roll calls show votes on various bills where he backed tougher sentences as well as votes opposing mandatory minimums or certain punitive provisions.

claim: Says Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has these offshore accounts" like Mitt Romney.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public financial disclosure showing Debbie Wasserman Schultz holds offshore accounts comparable to those reported for Mitt Romney. Romney's offshore accounts were widely reported in 2012 and are documented in reporting and disclosures, whereas no reputable reporting or her official filings substantiate the same claim about Wasserman Schultz.

claim: Austin’s Pease Elementary "is a school that was created as part of the Texas Constitution."
rationale: State constitutions set up education systems and sometimes specific public institutions, but they do not create individual local elementary schools. Austin’s Pease Elementary would have been established by a local school district or board, not directly by the Texas Constitution.

claim: "68% error rate in Michigan Voting Machines. Should be, by law, a tiny percentage of one percent."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Michigan voting machines have a 68% statewide error rate; certified equipment, pre- and post-election logic and accuracy testing, and routine risk-limiting audits and recounts produce error rates far lower than that. The 68% figure appears to be a misinterpretation or misrepresentation of a specific test or statistic rather than a validated overall machine error rate, and election law requires testing and audits to ensure very low error levels.

claim: "Biden’s banking nominee demands all ‘private bank accounts’ be eliminated"
rationale: The claim mischaracterizes the nominee's proposals. The Biden banking nominee most widely discussed (Saule Omarova) has written about giving the Federal Reserve broader account access and tightening commercial banks' activities, but she did not call for abolishing all private bank accounts; fact-checks and her own writings show regulatory reform proposals rather than a demand to eliminate private accounts.

claim: Georgia’s HOPE scholarship is "still the richest scholarship program in America."
rationale: Georgia’s HOPE scholarship was once unusually generous when first created, but its benefits have been reduced and capped over time. Numerous state and institutional programs and private full‑ride scholarships now provide equal or greater monetary value per recipient, so it is not objectively “the richest scholarship program in America” today.

claim: "Our children do not spend any time in school learning about our own U.S. Constitution."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as a blanket claim: U.S. K–12 curricula routinely include instruction on the U.S. Constitution in social studies, civics, U.S. history, and high-school government courses. While the amount and depth of instruction vary by state and district, it is not true that children universally receive no time learning about the Constitution.

claim: "President Obama has declared disasters in 48 of 50 states this year."
rationale: Presidential disaster declarations are made in response to specific events after state requests and historically do not cover 48 of 50 states in a single year. Even in very active disaster years, the number of states receiving declarations is far lower and such a sweeping claim is inconsistent with how FEMA/presidential disaster declarations are issued.

claim: "666,000 teachers have been laid off already since March."
rationale: There is no corroborating evidence from major news outlets, national education authorities, or labor statistics showing that 666,000 teachers were laid off 'since March.' A layoff of that magnitude in a single country would have produced widespread, verifiable reporting; available national education and employment data do not support such a large, sudden drop in teacher employment.

claim: Says Marilinda Garcia supports "$150 billion in new taxes."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that Marilinda Garcia publicly endorsed or proposed "$150 billion in new taxes." As a Republican candidate and officeholder she has generally campaigned against tax increases, so the claim appears to be a mischaracterization or taken out of context rather than a supported factual statement.

claim: "Hydroxychloroquine cures this ‘virus.’ It just so happens this is the treatment used for radiation sickness!!"
rationale: High-quality randomized trials and major health agencies found hydroxychloroquine does not cure COVID-19 and provides no mortality benefit, and it can cause harmful side effects. Hydroxychloroquine is not a recognized treatment for radiation sickness; management of radiation exposure uses measures such as potassium iodide, Prussian blue, chelators, growth factors and supportive care. The claim conflates unrelated conditions and is factually incorrect and potentially dangerous.

claim: "When the union says I want to eliminate tenure, that’s not true."
rationale: This is a denial of intent by an unnamed speaker and cannot be independently verified from the quoted sentence alone. Determining whether the person truly does not want to eliminate tenure requires examining concrete policy proposals, public statements, or voting records; absent that evidence the assertion should not be accepted as established fact.

claim: In Wisconsin, because a key provision of the Voting Rights Act was not in effect,  "somewhere between 40,000 and 80,000 people were turned away from the polls (in 2016) because of the color of their skin" and other factors.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 40,000–80,000 people in Wisconsin were turned away from the polls in 2016 'because of the color of their skin.' While Shelby County v. Holder (2013) ended preclearance and Wisconsin faced controversies over voter ID, purges, and long lines, documented instances of voters being denied ballots for race are far smaller or unproven. The 40k–80k figure appears to be a speculative or misattributed estimate of potentially affected registrations or voters, not a verified count of racially motivated turnaways.

claim: "Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, the average American family of four will receive a $1,182 tax cut."
rationale: The $1,182 number was an administration estimate (for 2018) based on a particular definition of a ‘family of four’ and the average (mean) tax change; independent analyses (Tax Policy Center, JCT) produced different estimates and showed distributional variation. The law’s benefits vary by income, filing status and year (many individual provisions sunset after 2025), so presenting a single $1,182 figure as a general outcome is misleading.

claim: Donald Trump’s "golf course on the island defaulted, like so many of his other failed business schemes. The failure left Puerto Rican taxpayers with a nearly $33 million bill."
rationale: Trump International Golf Club in Río Grande, Puerto Rico, was financed with public-bond-backed infrastructure deals that went into default when the developer failed, and Puerto Rican government entities were ultimately left on the hook for roughly $32–33 million. Reporting at the time described the shortfall as a near $33 million burden for Puerto Rican taxpayers tied to the failed project.

claim: Says "Cost of Mueller’s investigation: $3,200,000; Benghazi "investigation": $7,000,000; Trump’s golfing trips: $83,000,000; New debt from Republican tax bill: $1,500,000,000,000."
rationale: The figures are presented without context and at least one is clearly incorrect: DOJ reporting and news analyses show the Special Counsel Mueller office cost was on the order of tens of millions (commonly reported about $32 million total), not $3.2 million. The Benghazi and Trump-golf numbers are ambiguous and depend on timeframes and which expenses are counted, while the $1.5 trillion figure for the 2017 Republican tax bill is a commonly cited 10-year estimate but also depends on accounting assumptions.

claim: The U.S. has "over $62 trillion in unfunded liabilities."
rationale: The statement gives a single precise figure without defining the accounting method or timeframe; estimates of "unfunded liabilities" vary widely depending on which programs, time horizon, discount rate, and present-value method are used. Authoritative budget offices (CBO, Treasury/Trustees, GAO) publish different long‑term shortfalls that can be large but do not uniformly support a single definitive current number of "over $62 trillion."

claim: "A couple of debates ago, (Donald Trump) said if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless."
rationale: Donald Trump has historically opposed 'socialized' or government-run health care and there is no widely reported debate exchange where he said, 'if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless.' While he has used the word 'heartless' in political attacks, the specific claim that he urged support for socialized medicine and called opponents heartless is not supported by known debate transcripts or major news coverage.

claim: Will Hurd "tends to have a 96 percent straight Republican, straight party voting record."
rationale: Available public analyses and reporting characterize Will Hurd as more moderate and bipartisan than a near-perfect party-line voter; his scores on bipartisanship indexes and party-vote metrics are substantially lower than 96%. Saying he 'tends to have a 96 percent straight Republican...voting record' overstates his alignment with party votes.

claim: "While (women) represent 47 percent of the overall work force, we only make up 23 percent of STEM-related occupations."
rationale: The claim matches commonly reported U.S. statistics from the mid-2010s: women made up roughly 46–48% of the civilian labor force while their share of workers in STEM occupations was substantially lower, commonly reported in the low-to-mid 20s percent. Different surveys and definitions shift the STEM share by a few percentage points, but the statement is a reasonable summary of those data.

claim: "The Democrats are very sly. … (in New Hampshire) we have same day voter registration, and to be honest, when Massachusetts elections are not very close, they’re busing them in all over the place."
rationale: There is no credible evidence of a systematic scheme by Democrats to bus Massachusetts residents into New Hampshire to register and vote illegally. New Hampshire requires proof of residency for same‑day registration and state and local officials and independent fact‑checkers have found no proof of widespread busing or organized cross‑state voter fraud of the sort described.

claim: Says TikTok found Cassie Compton, who has been missing from Arkansas since 2014.
rationale: I find no credible reports or law-enforcement confirmations up to mid-2024 that TikTok 'found' Cassie Compton, a person said to have been missing from Arkansas since 2014. Claims that social media resolved a long-term missing-person case would have been reported by major news outlets and police, but I could not find such corroboration and the assertion appears to be unverified rumor.

claim: "For four years, we balanced the budget and paid off $405 billion in debt."
rationale: The U.S. recorded budget surpluses in several years in the late 1990s, but the specific claim that “for four years we balanced the budget and paid off $405 billion in debt” is inaccurate or misleading. While there were multi-year surpluses around 1998–2001, the federal debt was not reduced by $405 billion in a clear, verifiable way once one distinguishes gross debt versus debt held by the public and intragovernmental offsets. Publicly available historical budget and debt tables do not support a clean $405 billion payoff attributable to a four-year balanced-budget period.

claim: President Trump "hasn’t built any new (border) wall" during his time in office.
rationale: Official U.S. government and independent reporting document that the Trump administration constructed hundreds of miles of border barrier during his term. While a large portion consisted of replacement or reinforcement of existing fencing, there were also stretches of primary barrier built in locations where no barrier previously existed, so the blanket claim that he “hasn’t built any new wall” is incorrect.

claim: Atlanta has issued an increasing number of citations - and collected an increasing amount of revenue - since Mayor Kasim Reed took office in 2010.
rationale: The claim implies a continuous, citywide year-over-year rise in citations and revenue starting in 2010. Contemporary reporting and municipal budget summaries show increases in some early years of Mayor Kasim Reed's tenure, but the trends are not uniformly upward across all subsequent years and were affected by later reforms and fluctuations, so the broad blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "If you put the $47 billion in revenue (raised over 10 years by the Buffett rule) into infrastructure you could create 611,000 infrastructure jobs."
rationale: The $47 billion over 10 years is in the range of published Buffett-rule revenue estimates, but the claim that it would create 611,000 ‘infrastructure jobs’ is misleading because it omits crucial assumptions (whether these are job-years or permanent jobs and which spending-to-jobs multiplier is used). Different reasonable multipliers (e.g., $75k–$100k of spending per job-year) produce materially different totals, so the single 611,000 figure cannot be treated as a settled fact without the underlying methodology.

claim: "Children don’t seem to be getting this virus"
rationale: Blanket statement that "children don’t seem to be getting this virus" is inaccurate. Children are susceptible and have been infected in large numbers (often with milder or asymptomatic illness), and some have experienced severe outcomes such as multisystem inflammatory syndrome, so they do get and can transmit the virus.

claim: "Granite Staters who hold individual policies from Anthem...can indeed renew their policies and keep their current doctors and hospitals" in 2014.
rationale: The claim is overly broad. In late 2013 and early 2014 many individual policies nationwide — including plans sold by Anthem in various states — were cancelled because they did not meet Affordable Care Act standards; while federal and some state regulators allowed limited one-year 'transitional' renewals in some cases, renewals and network continuity were not guaranteed for all Anthem individual policyholders in New Hampshire in 2014.

claim: Says U.N. arms treaty will mandate a "new international gun registry."
rationale: No major U.N. arms treaty (including the Arms Trade Treaty) creates or mandates a centralized international registry of individual guns. These instruments require states to maintain national records, regulate transfers, and in some cases submit reports, but they do not establish a global database of civilian firearms.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "This country is doomed, not just because of African Americans, but because by 2040 this country is going to be minority white European."
rationale: There is no credible record of Joe Biden saying that quote. Public transcripts, recordings, and reputable fact-checking and news coverage do not show Biden stating that the country is “doomed” because of African Americans or using the specific phrasing attributed in the claim; it appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quotation. Biden's public comments on demographic change have been framed differently and not in this wording.

claim: "In my home state, nearly one in five Floridians live in poverty."
rationale: Recent U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey estimates put Florida's overall poverty rate in the low-to-mid teens (around 12–14% in recent years), which is substantially lower than 'nearly one in five' (≈20%). While some subgroups or specific counties in Florida have much higher poverty rates, the statewide overall rate is not close to 20%.

claim: "A 5 percent increase in domestic production would increase the world supply by less than 1 percent and do almost nothing to our dependence on foreign oil. This would also have virtually no effect on the price of gas at the pump."
rationale: If a country like the U.S. supplies roughly 10–13% of world crude, a 5% rise in its production increases world supply by only about 0.5–0.65%, i.e., under 1%. Such a small addition would only modestly reduce import dependence and would have limited effect on global crude prices and therefore little direct impact on retail gasoline prices, which also reflect taxes, refining, and distribution costs.

claim: Says 2010 video clip showing coffins in a field proves "COVID was planned."
rationale: A 2010 video cannot by itself prove that COVID-19 was planned because it predates the emergence of SARS-CoV-2 by about a decade; correlation in time or imagery does not establish causation. Coffins in a field can have many unrelated explanations (e.g., a past disaster, drill, film production, or burial practice), and claiming they prove a planned pandemic requires independent, direct evidence linking organizers to both the footage and a deliberate plan to create COVID-19.

claim: "Border agents discover body of 6-year-old girl: 'She was raped By 30 men'."
rationale: This appears to be a sensational social-media claim with no corroboration from reputable news outlets or official law-enforcement statements. A crime of this magnitude would be widely reported and would have official confirmation; no such verified reporting is available.

claim: "Under ‘Trumpcare,’" domestic violence and sexual assault "could be considered pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Proposed Republican replacement bills for the ACA (commonly called 'Trumpcare') rolled back or allowed waivers of key protections for pre-existing conditions and permitted insurers more discretion in pricing for people with prior conditions. While 'domestic violence' or 'sexual assault' are events rather than diagnoses, the physical and mental health consequences (injuries, PTSD, depression, pregnancy complications, etc.) can be treated as pre-existing conditions under those proposals, so survivors could have been charged more or faced exclusions.

claim: "8% of the votes cast" in Michigan’s Aug. 4 primary, 864 mailed ballots, came from dead voters. "NOTHING TO SEE HERE!!!"
rationale: This claim misinterprets the statistic. The cited 864 figure referred to mailings/returned envelopes or records flagged as associated with people later recorded as deceased, not 864 validated ballots counted as cast by dead people, and Michigan election officials and independent fact-checkers reported these were not equivalent to counted votes. Thus it does not represent 8% of votes cast in the Aug. 4 primary.

claim: "Moderna has been pulled in Iceland and pulled for everyone under age 30 in Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark due to heart issues."
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes Nordic vaccine policies. Several Nordic health authorities (Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark) issued recommendations favoring Pfizer over Moderna for younger age groups at certain times because rare myocarditis/pericarditis risks appeared higher with Moderna, but they did not uniformly or permanently "pull" Moderna for everyone under 30 across all these countries. Iceland likewise did not implement a blanket nationwide permanent withdrawal of Moderna for the entire population; policies and age cutoffs varied by country and changed over time.

claim: "This administration is slashing the Navy to pay for more Obamacare."
rationale: There is no evidence the administration directly ‘‘slashed the Navy’’ in order to fund expansions of the Affordable Care Act. Federal appropriations separate defense and health accounts, and past reductions (e.g., sequestration) were broad budget cuts or trade-offs, not a line‑item transfer of Navy money to pay for Obamacare.

claim: "There's only four senators senior to me ... there's still 44 older than me."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it lacks who is speaking and the date; both Senate seniority (by continuous service) and relative ages change over time. It is plausible in some circumstances for a senator to have only four colleagues with greater Senate tenure while 44 are older in age, but without identifying the senator and the time this cannot be checked and so the claim cannot be supported as stated.

claim: Says Joe Biden wants to "defund the police."
rationale: Joe Biden has publicly and repeatedly said he does not support the slogan 'defund the police' and campaigned on pursuing policing reforms and investments in community-based alternatives rather than eliminating police funding. His stated policies and federal proposals have focused on reform, oversight, and targeted program funding, not wholesale defunding of law enforcement.

claim: "Right now, in every major poll, national poll and statewide poll done in the last month, six weeks, we are defeating Trump, often by big numbers and always at a larger margin than Secretary Clinton is."
rationale: The claim is categorical but inconsistent with the polling record: major national and statewide polls in any recent 4–6 week window have shown mixed outcomes versus Trump, not universal defeats. Some polls show narrow leads or ties, and different pollsters produce different margins; Clinton in many periods had equal or larger margins against Trump in several polls. Therefore the assertion that every major poll in the last month–six weeks shows a consistent, larger-margin Sanders lead over Trump than Clinton is not supported.

claim: The U.S. military "is in 130 countries. We have 900 bases around the world."
rationale: The claim overstates and mixes figures that depend on definitions. Independent research and Defense Department data show U.S. forces or installations are present in far fewer countries (commonly cited estimates are roughly 70–90 countries) and counts of overseas bases vary by definition but are generally reported in the several-hundred range (around 600–800), not a clear 900 in 130 countries.
