Without verifiable context or evidence the assertion appears to be hearsay or a misrepresentation of an event. Given the lack of supporting documentation, the claim cannot be treated as true.

claim: Says "Senator Joe Manchin hit (an) all time low saying seniors and the disabled did not need the relief package $1000 on Fox News."
rationale: There is no verifiable record of Senator Joe Manchin saying on Fox News that "seniors and the disabled did not need the relief package $1000" in that exact phrasing. Manchin has publicly opposed broad flat stimulus checks at times and argued for more targeted aid, but major reports and transcripts do not show him explicitly saying seniors and disabled did not need the payment as quoted.

claim: "More people die from hands, fists, feet, than rifles."
rationale: National and global mortality data show deaths from firearms far exceed deaths from unarmed physical assaults (hands, fists, feet). Public health sources report that firearms, sharp instruments, and other weapons account for the majority of homicides, while deaths explicitly coded as 'assault by bodily force' are relatively rare.

claim: Kelly Ayotte "voted for a budget that had $90 billion of cuts to Pell Grants."
rationale: The $90 billion figure refers to proposed cuts in certain GOP House budget proposals (notably some Paul Ryan plans) and is not a straightforward description of a specific Senate vote by Kelly Ayotte. Ayotte did not cast a Senate vote that can be accurately described as "voting for a budget that had $90 billion of cuts to Pell Grants"; the claim conflates different budget proposals, scorekeeping conventions, and chamber actions.

claim: "Close to half of the folks in this country illegally entered legally (but) overstayed (their ) visas."
rationale: Multiple authoritative estimates indicate that a large share of people in the U.S. without legal status initially entered on valid visas and then overstayed; studies from Pew Research and DHS have put that share around 40–45%, which is reasonably described as "close to half." The exact percentage varies by year and methodology, but the general finding that visa overstays make up a plurality or near-half of the unauthorized population is supported by mainstream analyses.

claim: "449,000 Californians turned down jury duty because they were not citizens… but they were registered voters."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 449,000 Californians were excused from jury duty as noncitizens while being registered voters. Audits and fact-checks of California voter rolls have found only very small numbers (generally hundreds to low thousands) of noncitizen registrations, and jury pools are routinely screened and corrected; the 449,000 figure appears to be a misreading or conflation of unrelated administrative counts.

claim: The federal health care law tells "the American people precisely what type of coverage they have to have."
rationale: This is false. The Affordable Care Act sets minimum standards (minimum essential coverage and required categories of 'essential health benefits') and requires qualified plans for marketplaces, but it does not mandate one precise plan or exact set of benefits for every American; people choose among plan tiers and insurers and benefits can vary by state. Additionally, the federal individual mandate penalty was reduced to zero effective 2019, and some coverage rules apply differently to employer, Medicaid, and marketplace plans.

claim: "I'm the only front-line prosecutor in this race that's actually used the resources of the Wisconsin Crime Lab in the prosecution of cases."
rationale: The claim is a categorical, comparative statement of uniqueness (the only front-line prosecutor in the race to have used Wisconsin Crime Lab resources). I cannot verify that no other candidate has ever used the lab without reviewing case records, lab service logs, or detailed candidate prosecutorial histories. Because use of the state crime lab is common among prosecutors, asserting exclusivity is unlikely to be true without strong documentary evidence.

claim: Ketanji Brown Jackson "says she gave pedophiles lighter sentences (because) it’s different when they use computers vs mail to get volumes of child porn. This makes ‘total sense’ according to Jackson."
rationale: This claim misstates and quotes out of context. During her confirmation process Ketanji Brown Jackson explained judicial sentencing decisions and noted that possession/distribution via the internet can lead to larger volumes of images and therefore higher guideline ranges; she did not say she routinely 'gave pedophiles lighter sentences' for computer-based offenses, nor is there credible evidence she framed that distinction as a blanket reason to be more lenient. Her comments were descriptions of how sentencing guidelines and fact patterns differ, not admissions of an across‑the‑board policy of lighter sentences.

claim: A statewide poll showing 76 percent support and other surveys are a "strong indicator" of  broad public support in Milwaukee County for a $10.10 minimum wage
rationale: A statewide poll (76% support) cannot reliably be taken as a "strong indicator" of opinion in a specific county without a county-level breakdown or sufficiently large Milwaukee County subsample. Regional differences, sample sizes, weighting, and margins of error can cause county opinions to diverge from the statewide average, so county-specific polling is needed to support the claim.

claim: "Only sign outside Bucks County voting place. Democrats shown, republicans blurred out. … More scamming in Pennsylvania!"
rationale: There is no credible, corroborated evidence that a Bucks County polling place posted a sign showing only Democrats while blurring Republicans; local election officials and reputable news outlets did not document such an incident. The claim appears to rely on an unverified or manipulated image or social-media post rather than factual reporting.

claim: "Foreign companies in the United States have a significantly higher unionization rate than other companies overall."
rationale: There is no broad, consistent evidence that foreign-owned firms in the U.S. have a substantially higher unionization rate overall; unionization is strongly driven by industry, firm size, and location, and studies that control for those factors typically find mixed or no clear aggregate advantage for foreign firms. Some foreign-owned plants in heavily unionized industries may show higher unionization, but that does not support the blanket claim about all foreign companies.

claim: Says six eradicated diseases such as whooping cough and the bubonic plague are making a comeback "thanks to refugees and illegal immigrants."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on multiple counts: most of the diseases named (for example, whooping cough/pertussis and bubonic plague) were never globally eradicated and continue to occur at low or variable levels, and there is no robust evidence that refugees or undocumented immigrants are the primary cause of any broad resurgence. Public-health analyses attribute spikes in vaccine-preventable diseases to falling vaccination coverage, waning immunity, or local public-health breakdowns, while plague cases reflect zoonotic reservoirs and ecological factors. The blanket attribution to refugees/illegal immigrants is unsupported and misleading.

claim: "Covid-19 is now the leading cause of death in the United States."
rationale: Available U.S. mortality data through 2023 and provisional reports into 2024 show that heart disease and cancer remain the top two causes of death; COVID-19 caused many deaths during pandemic peaks but has not been the single leading cause in recent national annual counts. Without a specific date "now" is ambiguous, but based on the most recent public health data I was trained on, the claim is not correct.

claim: Alaska Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Mark Begich "vote as much as 80 percent of the time together."
rationale: Analyses of Senate roll-call voting during Mark Begich's tenure show that he and Lisa Murkowski voted together at rates near 70–85% in several years, and contemporary reports commonly cited roughly an 80% agreement. The exact share fluctuated year to year and depends on which votes are counted, but 'as much as 80 percent' is consistent with recorded agreement rates.

claim: "Crisis actor in Germany forgets he’s filming on TV."
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that a named incident in Germany involved a "crisis actor" who forgot he was on TV; such claims are a common meme that rely on short, out-of-context clips or misinterpreted rehearsal footage. Independent fact-checkers routinely debunk similar allegations as unproven or false, and ordinary broadcaster behavior (adjusting earpieces, rehearsals, candid moments) can be mistaken for staging.

claim: "The Family Research Council, according to some government agencies, is a terrorist group."
rationale: No government agency (U.S. federal, state, or international) has officially designated the Family Research Council (FRC) as a terrorist organization. The FRC has been labeled an anti-LGBT 'hate group' by a private civil-rights organization (the SPLC), which is sometimes conflated with formal government terror designations, but that is not a government determination of terrorism.

claim: The new health care law "will cut $500 billion from Medicare. That will hurt the quality of our care."
rationale: It is true that official estimates (CBO/JCT) projected roughly $500 billion in net reductions in Medicare spending over the first ten years of the ACA, but those were cuts to projected spending (mainly lower payments to Medicare Advantage plans and provider payment adjustments), not direct cuts to guaranteed Medicare benefits. The claim that these savings "will hurt the quality of our care" is a causal prediction that is not established; many analysts said the changes targeted overpayments and inefficiency and included protections for beneficiaries, so harm to quality is disputed rather than a proven outcome.

claim: In head-to-head polls for the general election, "I beat Hillary Clinton by more than anybody, by 11 points."
rationale: The broad claim that 'I beat Hillary Clinton by more than anybody, by 11 points' is not supported by national general-election polling or the final result. Most national polls in 2016 showed Clinton ahead or a close race, and she won the popular vote by about 2 points; while isolated or early polls at times showed Trump leading by varying margins, there was no sustained nationwide +11 advantage and other Republicans also led Clinton by large margins in some individual polls. The statement cherry-picks selective poll results and overstates a consistent 11-point edge or a unique biggest margin.

claim: "There's one (study) that came out of Pew in 2008 that showed 14 percent of people who voted were noncitizens."
rationale: Pew did not find that 14% of people who voted were noncitizens. The claim appears to misinterpret small numbers of survey respondents who self-identified inconsistently; later reanalysis and fact-checks concluded the apparent rate was due to survey error and misreporting, and corrected estimates of noncitizen voting are essentially zero or vanishingly small. Multiple independent fact-checks and Pew's own data cautions contradict the 14% assertion.

claim: "Russ Feingold got a memo in 2009 that outlined veteran harm" at a Wisconsin VA facility "and nothing was done."
rationale: I found no reliable documentation that former Senator Russ Feingold specifically received a 2009 memo describing veteran harm at a Wisconsin VA facility and that no action followed. Major reporting on the VA patient-harm scandals identifies different timelines and actors (including later disclosure by other officials) and does not corroborate this precise claim about Feingold. Given the lack of contemporaneous evidence tying Feingold to such a memo and the blanket assertion that "nothing was done," the claim is not supported.

claim: Potential Foxconn changes are due to "the wave of economic uncertainty" from Evers administration
rationale: There is no clear evidence that a ‘‘wave of economic uncertainty’’ created by the Evers administration was the cause of Foxconn’s announced changes. Public reporting and Foxconn statements attribute scaling-back and contract changes to broader factors such as shifting global market demand (notably for LCD panels and certain electronics), corporate strategy changes, and pandemic-era supply-chain and industry dynamics rather than actions by the state administration. The original agreement and incentives were negotiated under the prior administration, and multiple external economic factors better explain Foxconn’s adjustments.

claim: Says federal regulations adopted in 2011 increased the cost of each vehicle for his business by $10,000.
rationale: The claim is unsupported and implausible as stated because it gives no specifics about which 2011 federal rule, what vehicle models, or how costs were calculated. Regulatory impact analyses for the major 2010–2012 vehicle rules (fuel-economy and emissions standards) typically estimated per-vehicle compliance costs in the hundreds to low thousands of dollars range, not $10,000.

claim: "Pelosi’s $1.9 trillion bailout gives EVERY federal employee a $21,000 bonus check… they never lost their job!"
rationale: The $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan (passed in March 2021) did not include a universal $21,000 bonus payment to every federal employee. The law provided $1,400 direct payments to eligible individuals and funding for state and local aid, public health, schools, and unemployment benefits, but contains no provision authorizing $21,000 checks to all federal workers. Independent fact-checkers and the bill text show no basis for the claimed universal bonus.

claim: Says New Hampshire had the fourth-lowest unemployment rate in the country during Maggie Hassan’s time in the state Senate.
rationale: Maggie Hassan served in the New Hampshire State Senate from 2004–2010. State unemployment rankings fluctuate month-to-month and I find no clear, consistently supported evidence that New Hampshire was the fourth-lowest in the nation at any clearly specified point throughout her entire Senate tenure; without a specific month or year the claim is misleading and cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Says North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Thom Tillis "called Obamacare ‘a great idea.’ "
rationale: There is no reliable record of Thom Tillis saying the Affordable Care Act was outright 'a great idea.' Press accounts and fact-checkers note he has at times praised certain provisions (for example protections for preexisting conditions or dependent coverage) while criticizing the law overall; however the specific claim that he called Obamacare 'a great idea' is a misleading simplification of his nuanced comments.

claim: "Over 73% of all donations raised (from the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge) are going to fundraising, overhead, executive salaries, and external donations."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and the ALS Association's own financial disclosures show that the bulk of Ice Bucket Challenge donations were used for research, patient services and programmatic grants, not that over 73% went to fundraising, overhead, executive pay and external donations. The 73% figure appears to misinterpret or conflate categories and does not match published expense breakdowns for the main ALS charities receiving Challenge funds.

claim: The GOP’s health bill will protect people with pre-existing conditions "every bit as well as Obamacare did."
rationale: Major GOP replacement proposals (for example the 2017 American Health Care Act) included provisions—state waivers, looser community-rating, and alternatives like high-risk pools or continuous-coverage surcharges—that would allow higher premiums or limited access for people with pre-existing conditions. The ACA (Obamacare) barred denying coverage or charging higher premiums based on health status nationwide and required essential health benefits, protections that the GOP bills generally weakened or made optional. Independent analyses and the CBO concluded those proposals would leave many with pre-existing conditions less protected and facing higher costs than under the ACA.

claim: "In seven years that (nuclear) deal will have expired, and Iran is free to go ahead and create nuclear weapons."
rationale: The 2015 Iran nuclear agreement (JCPOA) included staggered, time-limited restrictions that expire at different times; not all key limits lapse after exactly seven years. Even if some provisions expire, Iran would remain a party to the NPT and subject to IAEA safeguards, and acquiring a nuclear weapon requires additional technical steps and would carry serious detection and political consequences—so expiration does not automatically make Iran "free" to build weapons.

claim: The presence of gorillas calls into question the concept of evolution.
rationale: The existence of gorillas is consistent with evolutionary theory: they are a distinct branch of the hominid family tree explained by common ancestry and speciation. Genetic, anatomical, and fossil evidence all support gorillas’ place in evolutionary relationships rather than undermining the concept of evolution.

claim: Says "Nicolás Maduro is carrying out a genocide on his people."
rationale: Labeling Nicolás Maduro as 'carrying out a genocide' is not supported by available legal findings: international bodies and major human rights organizations have documented widespread human rights abuses and concluded there are crimes against humanity, but there has been no authoritative legal determination of genocide. Genocide requires specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a protected group, a standard not met by the published fact-finding reports to date.

claim: "My mask will keep someone else safe and their mask will keep me safe."
rationale: Masks primarily act as source control by blocking respiratory droplets and aerosols, so when I wear a mask I reduce the likelihood of transmitting infection to others. Likewise, when others wear masks (especially well-fitting surgical masks or respirators) they reduce the amount of infectious material I inhale, providing reciprocal protection. Overall effectiveness depends on mask type, fit, and exposure context.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood is dead.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Clint Eastwood is dead; as of the last available, widely reported updates through mid-2024 he was alive and no credible obituaries or confirmations from family or major news outlets had been published. Claims of his death without such confirmations are therefore false based on those sources.

claim: Newt Gingrich "was fined $300,000 for ethics violations."
rationale: In 1997 the House Ethics Committee found Newt Gingrich had violated House ethics rules; he was formally reprimanded and agreed to pay a $300,000 penalty as part of a settlement. The payment was imposed by the House as disciplinary restitution rather than as a criminal fine.

claim: Says U.S. Senate opponent Eric Hovde "supported billions in stimulus for high-speed rail"  and "billions more to bail out banks."
rationale: Eric Hovde was a private businessman and Senate candidate, not a member of Congress who voted to approve multi‑billion federal packages; there is no documented record that he publicly endorsed specific multi‑billion stimulus bills for high‑speed rail or bank bailouts. Ads that assert he “supported billions” appear to misstate or conflate his candidacy with votes or positions for which there is no clear primary-source evidence.

claim: "In the last decade, the average income of the bottom 90 percent of all working Americans actually declined. The top 1 percent saw their income rise by an average of more than a quarter of a million dollars each."
rationale: Public data from agencies and researchers (Census, BLS, IRS/CBO analyses) show that over recent decades the incomes of lower- and middle-income workers generally did not undergo a uniform actual decline across an entire decade — instead they were flat or rose modestly in many commonly used windows — while the top 1% did see substantial gains. The specific blanket claim that the bottom 90% “actually declined” and the top 1% rose by “more than a quarter of a million dollars each” is misleading because results vary by exact decade, whether incomes are measured in nominal vs. real terms, and whether the unit is workers vs. households or tax units; using standard definitions the statement overstates and mischaracterizes the pattern.

claim: "President Obama pledged to go through the budget 'line by line,' but on his watch, non-defense spending has spiraled out of control, increasing by 67 percent in the last year alone."
rationale: While President Obama did say during the campaign and early presidency that he would go through the budget 'line by line', federal non-defense spending did not increase by 67 percent in a single year under his administration. Historical OMB/CBO budget tables show year‑to‑year changes in non‑defense spending that are much smaller; a 67% one‑year jump is not supported by mainstream budget data and typically reflects mischaracterized comparisons or mixing categories.

claim: "Donald Trump praises Colonel Sanders for his service in the Civil War."
rationale: This is false because Harland 'Colonel' Sanders was born in 1890, well after the American Civil War (1861–1865), so he could not have served in that war. There is no credible evidence that Donald Trump praised Sanders for Civil War service; any praise would have been about Sanders as a restaurateur, and the 'Colonel' title was honorary.

claim: There were no American flags at the first Democratic presidential debate.
rationale: The statement is presented as a universal fact but is ambiguous about which election cycle it refers to. Historically, many first Democratic presidential primary debates have displayed American flags on or near the stage, although a few more recent specific debates did not include them. Because the claim makes an absolute statement without a year and is not universally true, it is false as written.

claim: "More suicide deaths than coronavirus death past two months."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unsubstantiated as written — it gives no location or specific two-month period, so it cannot be verified. General data show global suicides are roughly 700,000 per year (~58,000 per month, ~116,000 in two months), while COVID-19 deaths have in many time windows and countries exceeded that number; a blanket claim that suicides outnumbered coronavirus deaths over the past two months is therefore misleading and likely false without strong, localized evidence.

claim: Says Texas routinely gets "a lot more federal spending" than it pays in taxes.
rationale: Most state-by-state analyses of federal taxes paid versus federal spending show Texas typically pays more in federal taxes than it receives in federal spending, making it a net contributor rather than a routine net recipient. While one-off events (large disaster relief or specific program allocations) can temporarily push federal spending to exceed taxes in a given year, the recurring pattern is that Texas does not 'routinely get a lot more' than it pays.

claim: "Our (Texas) graduation rate ranks 43rd out of 50 states."
rationale: The statement gives no year or data source and appears incorrect: in recent national data Texas’ high-school adjusted cohort graduation rate has generally been near or above the national median, not 43rd lowest. State rankings fluctuate by year and by the metric used, but Texas has not consistently placed as low as 43rd in modern NCES/DOE graduation-rate tables.

claim: "War for the soul of the TxDems: 57% of Dem incumbents for Tx House LOST their primary."
rationale: The claim that 57% of Texas House Democratic incumbents lost their primary is implausible and not supported by typical election records; incumbents rarely lose primaries at such high rates. Available reporting on recent Texas primaries shows only a small number of Democratic incumbents defeated, not a majority or 57% of the party’s incumbents.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan’s budget proposal "eliminates Medicare" in 10 years.
rationale: Paul Ryan's budget proposals called for converting Medicare’s financing for future beneficiaries to a premium‑support (voucher) model, not an immediate elimination of the program. The proposals preserved traditional Medicare for current beneficiaries and would phase in changes for younger Americans over time rather than terminating Medicare outright within ten years.

claim: Says Joe Biden tweeted, "the way white people talk leaving minorities confused."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Joe Biden posting a tweet with that wording from his verified accounts; major fact-checkers and news outlets have not reported such a statement. The phrasing is inflammatory and matches patterns of fabricated or parody social-media posts commonly misattributed to public figures.

claim: "Last week Joe Biden flashed the ‘white power’ sign. President Trump condemned white supremacists yesterday. Why hasn't Joe Biden?"
rationale: The allegation that Joe Biden “flashed the ‘white power’ sign” is unsubstantiated — the hand-shape commonly cited is an ordinary gesture (often the 'OK' sign) that has frequently been mischaracterized in viral posts, and credible fact-checking outlets have repeatedly found no evidence Biden intentionally made a white-supremacist signal. The follow-up about President Trump condemning white supremacists “yesterday” is time-dependent and unverified without a specific date, so the overall claim is misleading and unsupported as presented.

claim: "Collusion is not illegal."
rationale: The blanket statement is false: many forms of collusion — such as price-fixing, bid-rigging, and market allocation among competitors — are explicitly illegal under antitrust/competition laws in numerous countries and can lead to civil and criminal penalties. Whether a specific cooperative arrangement is lawful depends on the conduct and context, so some forms of coordination can be legal.

claim: "Actor Tom Hanks has passed away age 63."
rationale: Tom Hanks has not been reported deceased; credible sources and mainstream news have not announced his death at any point. He was born July 9, 1956, so being 'age 63' would have referred to 2019, and there were no reliable reports of his passing then or subsequently within available information.

claim: "We actually have this critical race theory moved into all our schools in Virginia."
rationale: The claim that Critical Race Theory has been moved into all Virginia schools is not supported by evidence. CRT is an academic legal framework usually taught at the college level, and Virginia has no statewide mandate requiring CRT in every K–12 classroom; state policy debates in recent years have focused on restricting so-called "divisive concepts," not imposing CRT universally. Individual districts may teach about race and history, but that is not equivalent to CRT being implemented across all schools.

claim: Says he can’t release his internal affairs record because there are Attorney General guidelines in place protecting it.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who 'he' is or which jurisdiction's Attorney General guidelines are being cited. In general, Attorney General opinions and guidelines vary by state and rarely provide a blanket prohibition against releasing internal affairs records; public-records laws and specific legal exemptions determine disclosure. Without specific evidence that a particular AG guideline legally prevents release in a named case, the claim cannot be accepted as true.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez took a "$10 million payout from Netflix."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez received a $10 million payout from Netflix. Major payments to members of Congress would appear on public financial disclosures and be widely reported; fact-checkers and news outlets have not substantiated any such $10M payment to AOC.

claim: A flight crew took a knee and stranded the New Orleans Saints on an airport runway.
rationale: There is no credible reporting that a flight crew 'took a knee' and left the New Orleans Saints stranded on a runway; such an incident would have been widely reported by major news outlets. Airline crews operate under FAA rules and standard procedures, and delays are normally attributed to mechanical issues, crew duty-time limits, or air traffic control, not a crew-wide protest action that immobilized passengers. The claim aligns with social-media rumor patterns rather than verified facts.

claim: Says Sens. Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins and Mitt Romney "are pro-pedophile."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Sens. Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins, or Mitt Romney have advocated for or supported pedophilia; their public records, statements, and votes do not endorse sexual abuse of children. The allegation appears to be a defamatory rhetorical attack rather than a factual characterization of their positions or actions.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton once "wanted a wall" on the Mexican border.
rationale: Hillary Clinton has previously expressed support for physical barriers along parts of the U.S.–Mexico border (she backed measures like the 2006 Secure Fence Act and spoke in favor of fencing/other barriers). She later clarified she did not support Donald Trump’s proposal for a continuous ``big, beautiful wall,'' so the claim is true but requires that nuance.

claim: Blinken, Austin trip to Kyiv may have been staged
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Blinken–Austin trip was staged. The visit was confirmed by U.S. and Ukrainian officials and documented with photos, video, and contemporaneous independent news reporting; staging such a high-profile diplomatic and security operation would require large-scale coordinated deception and thus is implausible without specific proof.

claim: Says that he’s responsible for Austin including Anderson Mill Road in the city's proposed transportation bond package.
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false as stated because it names no individual and provides no evidence that a single person was solely responsible for including Anderson Mill Road in Austin's proposed bond. Project lists for municipal transportation bonds are typically developed through staff proposals, council action, and public processes, so attributing inclusion to one unnamed person is unsubstantiated without explicit records or statements.

claim: ﻿Says JoAnne Kloppenburg’s side had a "3-to-1 money advantage" in the Wisconsin Supreme Court campaign.
rationale: The statement is not supported by campaign finance reporting for JoAnne Kloppenburg’s Wisconsin Supreme Court races; overall spending and outside independent expenditures did not show a clear 3-to-1 advantage for Kloppenburg’s side. In the contested races (notably the Prosser contests), independent conservative groups and opponent fundraising often matched or exceeded amounts supporting her, so a blanket 3:1 claim is inaccurate without specifying year and exact spending categories.

claim: Says Denmark’s suicide rate has been about twice as high as the United States’ over the past five decades.
rationale: International mortality data from WHO/OECD/CDC do not show Denmark’s suicide rate being about twice that of the United States over the past fifty years. Denmark’s suicide rate was higher than the U.S. in some earlier decades but declined substantially and in many recent years has been similar to or below the U.S. rate; it was not consistently ~2× higher across five decades.

claim: Says Chris Christie was the "first governor in America to endorse" Mitt Romney.
rationale: Chris Christie did endorse Mitt Romney during the 2012 campaign, but he was not the first sitting U.S. governor to do so. The 2012 endorsement timeline includes multiple governors who publicly supported Romney before Christie's widely noted endorsement, so the claim that Christie was the first governor to endorse Romney is incorrect.

claim: Says former NRA president Jim Porter said, "It’s only a matter of time before we can own colored people again."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that former NRA president Jim Porter said this. A statement this inflammatory would have been documented by major news outlets and archival sources, but reputable sources do not verify it and the phrasing mostly appears on unverified social media or partisan sites.

claim: "For the second quarter in a row, my campaign has raised more money than any other challenger in the nation and brought our fundraising total to over $800,000."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it omits the candidate's name and the exact reporting quarter; without those specifics one cannot confirm a national ranking. Public Federal Election Commission filings and independent trackers record quarterly and total fundraising and would be needed to substantiate a claim of 'more than any other challenger' and a total over $800,000. Given that many challengers raise large sums and rankings change by reporting period, the unqualified assertion is unsupported.

claim: In the 2012 election, there were more votes cast than registered voters in St. Lucie County, and Palm Beach County had 141 percent turnout.
rationale: Both parts of the claim are not supported by official election returns: counties publish certified 2012 canvass reports showing turnout well below 100% in both St. Lucie and Palm Beach. A 141% turnout figure is impossible as a percentage of registered voters and would reflect a miscalculation or misuse of a different denominator, and there is no evidence St. Lucie recorded more votes than registered voters in 2012.

claim: Says a group "estimates that the annual cost to Oregon taxpayers for government services to illegal aliens, after any income tax revenue from them, is $1 billion."
rationale: There is no robust, widely accepted evidence that the net annual cost to Oregon taxpayers for services to undocumented immigrants is exactly $1 billion; estimates vary widely by source and methodology and are often produced by advocacy groups with disputed assumptions. Claiming a precise $1 billion net cost without attribution or methodological detail is not supported by a consensus of independent analyses.

claim: Says Julie Parrish is "one of Sarah Palin’s mama grizzlies."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Sarah Palin officially labeled Oregon state representative Julie Parrish as one of her widely publicized 'mama grizzlies.' Palin's 'mama grizzlies' label was attached to a specific set of high-profile 2010 GOP female candidates, and commonly cited lists and news coverage do not include Julie Parrish. Without documentation of Palin using that label for Parrish, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says President Donald Trump "is still yet to say anything as the president of the United States about bounties on American troops."
rationale: President Trump publicly commented on the reports alleging bounties on U.S. troops after media accounts surfaced in late June 2020, calling the stories 'fake' or saying 'I don't think it was Russia' and later saying he had been briefed. Because he made public statements and answered questions in his capacity as president, the claim that he 'is still yet to say anything as the president' is inaccurate.

claim: MSNBC’s Mika Brzezinski said, "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That’s our job."
rationale: The specific quotation is not supported by reliable transcripts or reporting; fact-checkers have found the line is either fabricated or taken out of context from segments about media influence. Mika Brzezinski did not plainly state that controlling how people think is MSNBC’s job in the way the claim presents.

claim: Says police unions have it "written into a contract that (officers) are not going to be accountable" for misconduct.
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. While many police union contracts include due-process protections and provisions (mandatory arbitration, limits on disciplinary timelines, interview rules, or restrictions on use of complaints) that can make disciplining officers harder in practice, they do not universally and literally state that officers "are not going to be accountable." Contract language and effects vary widely by jurisdiction and employer practices.

claim: "This year, a majority of states are seeing premiums and costs double" under Obamacare.
rationale: Available data from CMS and state insurance filings do not support that a majority of U.S. states saw premiums and overall consumer costs double in a single year under the Affordable Care Act. While some insurers or specific plans in a handful of states have proposed or implemented very large increases, those are isolated cases and not a majority-state phenomenon.

claim: "Last year it was discovered that Rhode Island's public employees ranked 4th in average pay, while the private sector ranked 23rd."
rationale: I cannot corroborate a widely reported finding that Rhode Island public employees ranked 4th in average pay while the private sector ranked 23rd 'last year.' Rankings of state public vs. private pay vary substantially by the data source, year, and whether 'average pay' means mean wage, median wage, or total compensation, and no authoritative source consistently produces the 4th/23rd split as stated.

claim: "Moscow was engulfed in flames" after a giant explosion.
rationale: There are no credible contemporary reports from major international or Russian news organizations that Moscow as a whole was "engulfed in flames" after any single explosion; such an event would have produced widespread, corroborated coverage. Viral images and videos claiming this have previously been shown to be miscaptioned, from other incidents or localized fires rather than the entire city burning.

claim: Says David Perdue wants to abolish the U.S. Department of Education, which would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year and eliminate millions in student loans.
rationale: It is true David Perdue has publicly supported eliminating the U.S. Department of Education, but the downstream claims are misleading. Abolishing the department would risk loss of federal K–12 and higher-education funding to states and would end federal student loan programs going forward, but it would not automatically cancel existing student loan balances. The cited $1 billion figure for Georgia is a rough estimate and would vary by which programs were cut and how Congress replaced or redirected funds.

claim: Ed Gillespie’s "firm even lobbied for five foreign governments, including a dictator now awaiting trial for war crimes."
rationale: I could not verify the specific claim that Ed Gillespie’s firm lobbied for five foreign governments including “a dictator now awaiting trial for war crimes.” Public records of lobbying (FARA and congressional disclosure filings) and contemporary fact-checking reported some foreign-government clients for Gillespie’s firm but do not support the precise, dramatic wording that it represented five governments including a dictator currently awaiting trial for war crimes. The statement appears to be an exaggerated or misleading characterization rather than a strictly accurate summary of disclosed clients.

claim: States with voter ID laws have seen "zero decrease" in participation. "Most have seen an increase."
rationale: The claim is too categorical and not supported by the empirical literature. Peer-reviewed studies and nonpartisan analyses show mixed effects of voter ID laws: some find little overall change in turnout, while others find statistically significant decreases for specific groups (e.g., Black, Hispanic, low-income, or young voters). There is not consistent evidence that “zero decrease” occurred everywhere or that a majority of states experienced turnout increases after adopting ID laws.

claim: Sarah Palin "already has more executive experience" than Barack Obama and Joe Biden "combined."
rationale: This is false as stated. Sarah Palin's executive experience (Wasilla mayor 1996–2002 and Alaska governor 2006–2009, roughly 8–9 years total) is substantially less than the combined executive tenure of Barack Obama (eight years as U.S. president) and Joe Biden (multiple years as U.S. president, plus two terms as vice president), which together far exceed Palin's time in executive office. The claim would only be potentially defensible if tied to a specific earlier date or a narrow definition of "executive," but as a general present-tense assertion it is incorrect.

claim: "It was allowed," referring to her email practices.
rationale: The blanket claim that 'It was allowed' about her email practices is misleading. While State Department guidance allowed limited use of personal email if work records were preserved, investigations by the State Department Inspector General and the FBI found that her use of a private server violated record-keeping policies and resulted in the improper handling of classified information; the FBI called her handling 'extremely careless' even though prosecutors declined criminal charges.

claim: Says President Barack Obama told a room of students, "Children, every time I clap my hands together, a child in America dies from gun violence," and then a child told him he could solve the problem by not clapping any more.
rationale: There is no credible record, video, or contemporaneous news reporting of President Obama making that remark; the anecdote appears to be a fabricated or satirical quote that circulated on social media. A statement this provocative would have been documented and widely reported, but fact-checkers and archives show no evidence it was ever said.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine "will make the common cold/flu extremely lethal."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccines make common cold or seasonal flu infections more lethal. COVID-19 vaccines prime immune responses specific to SARS-CoV-2 and have not been shown in population surveillance or clinical studies to increase severity of unrelated respiratory viral infections. Theoretical mechanisms that might alter responses to other pathogens (e.g., transient immune modulation) have not resulted in observed increased lethality.

claim: "CA inmate pregnant after being forced to share prison with transgender ‘woman.’"
rationale: There are no credible news reports or official confirmations that a California inmate became pregnant after being forced to share housing with a transgender woman. While sexual assaults can and do occur in prisons, this specific claim appears to be a viral, unverified summary that mixes facts about housing policy with an anecdote without evidence. Pregnancy would also require a partner with functioning sperm, which the headline does not establish.

claim: Says Tallahassee mayor Andrew Gillum "wants to make Florida not a sanctuary city but a sanctuary state."
rationale: There is no clear, reliably documented statement in which then-Tallahassee mayor Andrew Gillum explicitly said he wanted to 'make Florida' a sanctuary state. Gillum did express support for local policies protecting undocumented immigrants and criticized federal immigration enforcement, but as mayor he did not have authority to declare statewide policy and his public comments are more typically framed as supporting sanctuary-style protections rather than a concrete plan to convert Florida into a 'sanctuary state.'

claim: Republican challenger Bill Flores "has never once voted in a general election in our district."
rationale: Bill Flores is a long-time resident and former U.S. Representative from the district and there is no credible evidence that he never voted in a general election there. As an active political actor who ran in and won multiple general elections in the district, it is implausible that he never cast a general-election ballot in the district. The claim appears to be a misleading attack that would require specific voter-roll checks to support.

claim: Says "John James supported Betsy DeVos’ agenda to cut public school funding and put it into wealthy private schools instead."
rationale: John James has publicly supported school-choice policies and said he would back Betsy DeVos' nomination as Education Secretary, but he has not explicitly framed his position as endorsing cuts to public-school budgets to funnel money specifically to wealthy private schools. The claim conflates his support for vouchers/choice with an asserted intention to cut public funding and benefit wealthy private institutions, which overstates the available public record.

claim: "Bill Gates calls for the withdrawal of all Covid-19 Vaccines; ‘The vaccines are far more dangerous than anyone imagined.’"
rationale: This quotation and claim are fabricated and contrary to Bill Gates' public record; he has consistently promoted COVID-19 vaccine development and distribution rather than calling for their withdrawal. No credible news outlets, his foundation, or his verified communications report him saying vaccines are 'far more dangerous than anyone imagined.' The claim appears to be a misattribution or hoax.

claim: Speedway is offering $500 fuel cards for $1.95 to help customers with rising fuel costs.
rationale: A legitimate retailer selling $500 fuel cards for $1.95 would represent a near-total loss and is implausible; no credible announcements from Speedway or major news outlets report such an offer. Similar viral claims are common phishing/scam tactics that ask for a small payment for a large reward. Consumers should treat such claims skeptically and verify promotions directly with the company.

claim: More than 500,000 mail in ballots in Virginia and 200,000 in Nevada were sent to dead people or pets
rationale: There is no credible evidence that hundreds of thousands of mail-in ballots were sent to dead people or pets in either Virginia or Nevada. State election officials, audits, and independent fact-checkers reviewed these claims and found they stem from misinterpreted voter-roll data or isolated, small-scale errors, not mass mailings of ballots to deceased individuals or animals. Actual confirmed instances of ballots sent to ineligible recipients have been limited and far smaller than the numbers claimed.

claim: Says no one has died from the coronavirus in the United States.
rationale: This is false. Since early 2020 U.S. public health authorities, hospitals, and news organizations have documented large numbers of deaths from COVID-19 — cumulatively far beyond zero — so the claim contradicts official mortality data and widespread reporting.

claim: "Bill Gates talked about using vaccines to control population growth" in an "unedited 2010 TED Talk video"
rationale: This claim is misleading. In his 2010 TED Talk Bill Gates argued that improving health (including vaccines) leads to lower child mortality and thereby slows population growth, not that vaccines would be used as a deliberate tool to 'control' populations in a coercive way; there is no credible unedited video showing him advocating vaccines as a population-control scheme.

claim: The Fair Tax proposal encourages innovation and investment "level the playing field" for American companies to compete globally.
rationale: This is a contested, normative claim promoted by FairTax supporters, not an established fact. While proponents argue replacing income and payroll taxes with a national retail sales tax would remove taxes on corporate income and exports and thus spur investment and innovation, economists do not reach a consensus and empirical evidence on dynamic effects is mixed and highly sensitive to model assumptions and transition details.

claim: U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has blamed the Republicans for the creation of Hamas."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz literally said Republicans 'created' Hamas. Hamas was founded in 1987 by Palestinian Islamists linked to the Muslim Brotherhood, long before contemporary U.S. party politics, and public statements from Wasserman Schultz criticize Republican policy or rhetoric but do not substantiate a claim that Republicans created the organization.

claim: "Seventy of Ohio's 88 counties now have more than 25 percent of their residents eligible for emergency food."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence that 70 of Ohio's 88 counties have over 25% of residents 'eligible for emergency food.' The claim is specific but lacks a cited source and the term 'eligible for emergency food' is ambiguous (eligibility standards differ between programs), and available county-level SNAP/food-insecurity data do not typically support such a uniformly high threshold across nearly 80% of counties.

claim: Says Mark Kelly wants to "defund the police."
rationale: This is false. Senator Mark Kelly has publicly stated multiple times that he does not support “defunding the police,” instead endorsing funding for public safety along with reforms and accountability measures. Media coverage and his campaign statements consistently report he opposes the slogan and supports law-enforcement funding with changes.

claim: "Coroner saying George Floyd died of drug overdose, not police brutality."
rationale: The official Hennepin County Medical Examiner concluded George Floyd's death was a homicide due to cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression. Although toxicology detected fentanyl and methamphetamine and defense parties argued drugs contributed, the coroner did not rule the death an overdose.

claim: "This year, Eric Cantor has received more money from oil companies than any other member of Congress."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because "this year" is unspecified and campaign contributions change annually; without a specific year and source, it cannot be confirmed. While Eric Cantor has historically been a major recipient of oil and gas industry contributions, public campaign finance databases show different members leading in different years, so the blanket statement is likely inaccurate.

claim: "74 percent of Republicans support the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: Contemporary national polling consistently shows a substantial majority of Republicans oppose the Affordable Care Act; a figure as high as 74% Republican support is inconsistent with major surveys. While certain individual provisions of the law (for example protection for pre-existing conditions) can poll well across parties, overall GOP support for 'the ACA' has typically been far lower than 74%.

claim: Delaware has the "eighth-largest black population in the country"
rationale: Interpreting the claim as an absolute count, Delaware—whose total population is under 1 million and whose Black population numbers in the low hundreds of thousands—ranks well below the eighth-largest Black populations, which are in much larger states (Texas, Florida, Georgia, New York, California, North Carolina, Illinois, etc.). If interpreted as a percent share of population the statement is still unlikely: Delaware has a relatively high Black share (around the low-20s percent) but most recent state-by-percent rankings place several states (Mississippi, Louisiana, Georgia, Maryland, Alabama, South Carolina, etc.) ahead of Delaware. Therefore the claim is not supported by typical Census-based rankings.

claim: Says "$1,100 of the tuition paid by every Oregon university student annually goes just to pay the costs of PERS."
rationale: The statement is misleading: PERS employer contribution costs are paid from university operating budgets (a mix of tuition, state appropriations and other revenues) and vary by institution and year, so you cannot say a fixed $1,100 of every student's tuition 'goes just to pay' PERS. Simple headlines that divide total PERS payments by student headcount or by tuition revenue produce different per‑student figures and ignore that many PERS costs are covered by state dollars or non‑tuition revenue. Independent analyses and budget documents show per‑student amounts vary and the claim overstates the direct tuition portion.

claim: Hillary Clinton in 2005 co-sponsored legislation that would jail flag burners.
rationale: There is no credible record that Senator Hillary Clinton formally co-sponsored a 2005 bill to criminalize flag burning. Sponsorship and co-sponsorship of federal bills are a matter of public congressional record, and claims that she "co-sponsored" such legislation in 2005 appear to conflate votes or later statements with actual co-sponsorship.

claim: "No Republicans voted for" recent hikes in the income tax, payroll tax, capital gains tax, dividend tax and estate tax. "These taxes were all passed under … Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did include specific tax provisions — notably the 0.9% additional Medicare payroll tax on high earners and the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax on investment income (capital gains, dividends) — and Republicans largely voted against the ACA. However, the claim is false because it overstates and misattributes: the ACA did not enact broad income-tax rate hikes or an estate-tax increase as described, and some other recent tax changes came from separate legislation. Saying "no Republicans voted for" all the listed "hikes" is misleading because not all those hikes were part of Obamacare and voting records vary by bill.

claim: "Constituents now face reality that all their personal issues will be made public" under Clean Missouri.
rationale: Clean Missouri (Amendment 1, 2018) increased transparency around redistricting, campaign finance, and certain disclosures for donors and officials, but it did not mandate that 'all their personal issues' of constituents be published. Privacy protections and public-record exemptions still limit what personal information becomes public; only specific categories (e.g., campaign donor names above thresholds, certain official disclosures) are made public.

claim: "The Clinton Foundation folded."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation did not cease to exist; it continued to operate programs, file tax returns, and make public statements about ongoing work after periods of downsizing. Although it reduced staff and funding at times and reorganized some activities, those changes do not equate to the organization having 'folded' entirely.

claim: Said Adolf Hitler and Donald Trump have both described deportations as "a military operation."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Adolf Hitler ever described deportations using the phrase "a military operation," and available records of Donald Trump's public statements about immigration and removals do not show him specifically calling deportations "a military operation." Both discussed enforcement and large-scale removals in different terms, but the specific shared phraseology is unsupported.

claim: "How is a misogynist bigot of epic proportions (like U.S. Rep. Steven Smith) allowed to serve?"
rationale: The claim asserts both that there is a U.S. Representative named Steven Smith and that he is "a misogynist bigot of epic proportions." Current rosters of the U.S. House do not list a member named Steven (or Steve) Smith, and the defamatory characterization is an opinion that would require specific documented evidence of sexist conduct or statements to be shown as fact.

claim: "Washington State Legislature votes to change its name because George Washington owned Slaves."
rationale: There is no record that the Washington State Legislature voted to change the state's name. While activists and some local bodies have discussed or proposed renaming institutions because George Washington owned enslaved people, the state legislature has not passed any law renaming Washington State. Changing a U.S. state's name would be a major legal process (legislative action plus likely voter or congressional approval) and has not occurred for Washington State.

claim: "We know that more than half of Hillary Clinton's meetings while she was secretary of state were given to major contributors to the Clinton Foundation."
rationale: Independent fact‑checks that compared State Department calendars with Clinton Foundation donor lists found far fewer than half of Clinton’s meetings as secretary of state involved major Foundation contributors; the claim is a substantial exaggeration. Many meetings were with foreign officials, NGOs or others not listed as major donors, and inclusion criteria (donor vs. associate, in‑person vs. group meetings) materially affect any count.

claim: Between 2008 and 2014, "criminal aliens accounted for 38 percent of all murder convictions in the five states of California, Texas, Arizona, Florida and New York."
rationale: The 38% figure is misleading and not supported as a general fact. It appears to come from selective counting for only five states and a specific period, uses an unclear definition of “criminal alien,” and has been flagged by independent fact-checkers as based on non-representative and opaque methods rather than a verified nationwide statistic.

claim: Dr. Phil and other celebrities are endorsing CBD gummies.
rationale: There is widespread, verifiable evidence that many celebrities have promoted or launched CBD products, but I am not aware of reliable, documented endorsements specifically by Dr. Phil for CBD gummies. Public reports and advertising archives do not show a clear, verifiable campaign tying Dr. Phil to a CBD-gummy endorsement. The claim therefore overstates or misattributes celebrity participation.

claim: "If there is a firearm available, it is 17 times more likely to be used either for suicide or for assaulting a friend, relative, an acquaintance than it is to be used in fending off an intruder."
rationale: While reputable epidemiological studies consistently find that firearms in the home are more often involved in suicide or domestic violence than in successful self-defense, the specific 17× figure is not a robust, widely supported estimate. Most peer-reviewed analyses report smaller and variable ratios (commonly cited figures around 4–5×) and results depend heavily on definitions and data sources. Therefore the precise "17 times" claim is misleading without a clear citation and context.

claim: "Today Russia holds many of our most precious national security satellites at risk before they ever get off the ground."
rationale: The statement is broad and asserts that Russia currently places many of the United States' most important national-security satellites at risk before launch; there is no public evidence that Russia systematically compromises or controls large numbers of U.S. pre‑launch military satellites. While Russia has anti‑satellite capabilities, electronic attack and cyber tools, these primarily threaten deployed space assets or represent general cyber espionage concerns rather than documented, widespread seizure or neutralization of U.S. satellites still on the ground. The claim overstates the publicly known threat posture and lacks corroborating public evidence.

claim: "This is the only state in the country that bypassed the General Assembly to authorize [in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants]."
rationale: The statement asserts a unique, nationwide occurrence, but multiple states have allowed in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants through non-legislative means (for example via boards of regents, administrative policies, executive actions, or court rulings) rather than by a state legislature. Therefore it is incorrect to claim only one state ever bypassed its legislature to authorize such tuition.

claim: Says in U.S. Congress, members "don’t even have to be on the floor for debates or votes."
rationale: As a general rule members of the House and Senate must be present on the floor (or at least in the chamber) to participate in debates and to cast floor votes. There have been limited exceptions—most notably temporary proxy voting in the House during the 2020 pandemic and some remote/virtual participation for committees—but these were not permanent, universal rules allowing members to entirely skip being on the floor for debates or votes.

claim: "I did not support the war in Iraq … The record shows that I’m right."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific individual's stance and claims the historical record confirms it, but no speaker or timeframe is provided, so the claim as presented cannot be verified. Verifying such a claim requires checking that person's votes, public statements, and other documented actions; without that context the assertion that "the record shows" is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Joe Biden’s great-grandfather Joseph J. Biden was a slave-owner and fought" for the Confederacy.
rationale: Contemporary fact-checking and genealogical records do not support that President Biden had a great-grandfather named Joseph J. Biden who owned slaves or served the Confederacy. Biden's ancestral records place his family in Northern states (Delaware/Pennsylvania) and researchers have found no evidence of a Confederate slaveholding ancestor with that name.

claim: "TSA WILL ACCEPT DRIVERS PRIV CARDS FOR ID AT THE AIRPORT"
rationale: TSA accepts only identity documents that meet federal requirements (Real ID-compliant state driver licenses/IDs or other federally acceptable IDs). Many "driver's privilege" or "driving privilege" cards are issued to undocumented residents and are explicitly marked as not valid for federal identification, so they are not accepted for TSA screening or to board commercial flights.

claim: Scott Walker "couldn’t get his own party" to back more than a 500-student increase in Milwaukee’s school choice program, but in Indiana, "Mitch Daniels’ voucher program is approaching 30,000 students two years after opening."
rationale: The claim mixes and misstates timelines and enrollment figures. In Wisconsin Walker did push expansions but the description that he “couldn’t get his own party” to back more than a 500‑student increase simplifies a legislative compromise and mischaracterizes GOP support; and Indiana’s voucher program under Mitch Daniels did grow quickly but did not reach or approach 30,000 students just two years after its launch according to enrollment reports from that period.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "voted for regime change with respect to Libya."
rationale: There is no record of Bernie Sanders casting a Senate vote explicitly authorizing or using the phrase 'regime change' with respect to Libya. While there were congressional debates and non-binding measures around the 2011 NATO intervention, no Senate roll-call vote directly authorized 'regime change' and Sanders has publicly criticized the Libya intervention afterward. Therefore the claim that he 'voted for regime change' is not supported by authoritative voting records.

claim: "Biden's plan is a 14% tax hike on middle class families."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated because no specific Biden proposal universally imposes a 14% tax increase on "middle class families." Major Biden tax proposals focused on raising taxes on high-income households, corporations, and capital gains, and independent distributional analyses (e.g., Tax Policy Center, CBO summaries) do not show a uniform 14% tax hike for middle-income households. The claim appears to conflate different metrics or selectively present numbers without context.

claim: "The United States imprisons more than any nation in the world."
rationale: The United States has one of the largest incarcerated populations and the highest incarceration rate per capita, but whether it imprisons more people than any other country depends on how prisoners are counted. China’s reported figures are opaque and may exclude large categories of detainees, and other countries’ counting practices vary, so the blanket claim is not reliably verifiable. Because of these data and definitional uncertainties the statement is not strictly supportable as an absolute fact.

claim: "California to teach kindergarteners there are 15 genders."
rationale: There is no California state mandate that kindergarteners be taught that there are '15 genders.' State guidance and some local curricula encourage age-appropriate, inclusive discussions of gender identity and family diversity, but do not prescribe a specific list of 15 genders to teach to kindergartners. Multiple fact-checks and the California Department of Education have not found any official policy matching the viral claim.

claim: "You're more likely to be the victim of a violent crime in Milwaukee than in 96 percent of the country."
rationale: Milwaukee does have a relatively high violent-crime rate compared with many U.S. cities, but the blanket claim that you are more likely to be a violent-crime victim there than in 96% of the country is unsupported. Whether Milwaukee ranks above the 96th percentile depends on the data source, year, and whether you compare cities, counties, or all jurisdictions; most public statistics place Milwaukee high among large cities but not unequivocally above 96% of all U.S. places across datasets and years.

claim: "If we keep the minimum wage at the current level, then single-parent families earning the minimum wage at a full-time job will live in poverty in New Jersey."
rationale: The claim is categorical but depends on key variables (number of children, exact minimum wage, and hours worked). For some single-parent households (for example a single parent with one child) earning a full-time wage at New Jersey's current minimum wage the annual income can be above the federal poverty line, while for larger households it can fall below. Because the statement asserts an unconditional outcome for all single-parent families without specifying family size or the exact wage level, it is not reliably true.

claim: "Forty-seven percent of (members of Congress) are millionaires."
rationale: The share of members of Congress who are millionaires fluctuates by congressional session and by how 'millionaire' is defined and estimated; there is no single, permanent 47% figure that is universally correct. Independent analyses of congressional financial disclosures have reported different percentages in different years (around roughly half in some recent sessions), so presenting '47%' as a general, timeless fact is misleading.

claim: "We now have more jobs in solar than we do in oil."
rationale: The claim is presented without a scope or time frame; globally the oil and gas sector supports millions of jobs across extraction, refining, transportation and petrochemicals, while solar employment—though fast-growing—is smaller worldwide. While solar jobs have surpassed oil-only jobs in some localities or in certain reporting definitions and years, the general unqualified statement is not correct without more context.

claim: "59 people die as pastor gives them dettol to drink in church to prevent coronavirus."
rationale: No credible reporting or independent fact-checking supports a verified incident in which a pastor gave congregants Dettol to drink that resulted in 59 deaths. The claim appears to be a viral misinformation item that conflates or invents events; while there were unrelated poisonings and many COVID-era disinformation stories about ingesting disinfectant, this specific mass-fatality account has not been corroborated by reputable news or health authorities.

claim: "North Carolina spends $855 less per student than it did before the Great Recession, and we have one of the lowest per pupil spending levels in the nation."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and therefore misleading: whether North Carolina spends $855 less per student depends on which year is called "before the Great Recession," whether figures are nominal or inflation-adjusted, and which spending measure (state-only, total current expenditures, or including federal/local). Public data show NC’s per-pupil spending fell during the recession but by some common measures and years had recovered to near or above pre-recession nominal levels, and rankings among states vary by year and data source so it is inaccurate to assert the single blanket figures in the claim without specifying the metric and year.

claim: The "state bureaucracy" Jane Norton managed "grew by $43 million in just three years."
rationale: The claim names a specific $43 million growth over three years for a 'state bureaucracy' Jane Norton managed but provides no named agency or timeframe; I cannot verify that specific increase. Jane Norton served as Colorado lieutenant governor and had various oversight roles, but attributing a precise $43 million growth to a bureaucracy she 'managed' is unsupported without a primary budget source. Given the ambiguity and lack of corroborating detail, the claim as stated is not verifiable and is likely misleading.

claim: "There is no reason to allocate 60 percent of bridge space to satisfy two percent of all travelers."
rationale: The statement is a normative opinion, not an empirically verifiable fact. Whether it makes sense to allocate 60% of a bridge to serve 2% of travelers depends on policy goals, safety, legal obligations (e.g., accessibility), and local context, so it cannot be categorically declared true.

claim: Photos show Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, Gretchen Whitmer and Cory Booker violating COVID-19 safety precautions.
rationale: The claim is too broad and unsubstantiated as written: no specific photos are cited, and whether an image shows a violation depends on context (date, location, local guidance, vaccination/testing status, and whether people momentarily removed masks). While isolated images of public figures unmasked or in close proximity circulated during the pandemic, many were taken under conditions that did not necessarily constitute a breach of prevailing safety rules or were miscaptioned. Without identified photos and contextual information, the blanket assertion that photos show these four individuals violating COVID-19 precautions is unsupported.

claim: "The unemployment rate for Wisconsin workers has reached historic lows. It’s never been this low before, ever, ever, ever."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim but is incorrect. While Wisconsin has seen very low unemployment in recent years, historical BLS state unemployment series show similar or lower lows in past periods (for example in the late 1990s/early 2000s and other earlier periods), so it is not true that it has 'never been this low' before.

claim: "A Gallup report recently said that nearly 50 percent of small business owners aren't hiring because of what they call ‘regulatory uncertainty.’"
rationale: I am not aware of a recent Gallup report showing that nearly half of small business owners are not hiring specifically because of 'regulatory uncertainty.' Gallup small‑business and employment polling typically finds reasons like inability to find qualified applicants, labor costs, or general economic uncertainty as the top hiring impediments, and surveys that ask about regulatory concerns (often from NFIB or other groups) generally report lower percentages. The claim appears to misattribute or exaggerate survey findings.

claim: Says a California surfer was "alone, in the ocean," when he was arrested for violating the state’s stay-at-home order.
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports, law-enforcement statements, and widely published photos of the arrest show other people on the beach and at least one other person in the water; the subject was not literally alone in the ocean when detained. Therefore the claim that he was "alone, in the ocean" is inaccurate for the widely circulated incident.

claim: "Wisconsin’s economy is in the best shape it’s been since 2000."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim but economic “shape” depends on which indicators and the exact date are used. Some measures (for example, unemployment rates in recent years) have been near or at multi‑decade lows, while other measures (real median income, labor force participation, and certain poverty metrics) have not uniformly surpassed levels since 2000. Because the claim lacks a defined metric and timepoint, it is not supportable as a blanket fact.

claim: The Senate seat won in a special election by a Democrat had been "held for more than thirty years by Republicans."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as a general fact because it refers to an unspecified special election and Senate seat. Whether a particular seat had been held by Republicans for more than thirty years is a concrete historical claim that requires the seat's state and timeframe; without that context the assertion is unsubstantiated. It may be true for some specific seats but is not provable as written.

claim: "In 2005, Dan Branch tried to expand third-trimester abortions in Texas."
rationale: Dan Branch is a Republican Texas legislator with a pro-life record and no reliable evidence shows he sought to expand third-trimester abortions in 2005. Contemporary reporting and his legislative history indicate he supported restrictions on abortion rather than expansions, so the claim misstates his actions and positions.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to get rid of the federal minimum wage."
rationale: There is no clear, on-record statement from Donald Trump explicitly saying he wants to abolish the federal minimum wage outright. His public remarks and policy positions have typically criticized federal increases, expressed support for state-level control or flexibility, or opposed raising the federal floor, but fact-checkers have found ads claiming he wants to 'get rid of' the federal minimum wage to be misleading without direct evidence of an intent to repeal the federal statute entirely.

claim: Old photograph shows a group of women in KKK attire holding a sign that reads "Women of the Democrat Party."
rationale: This claim is a documented example of a miscaptioned vintage photograph. Fact-checkers have found that viral versions of the image have been relabeled to read 'Women of the Democrat Party,' but the original photos and captions do not support that specific wording and the image has been used out of context for partisan messaging.

claim: Says Rick Scott has "teamed up with a felon convicted of running a Ponzi scheme to smear Charlie Crist."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or documented evidence that Rick Scott "teamed up" with a person convicted of running a Ponzi scheme to smear Charlie Crist. While Florida politics has involved donations and contacts with various controversial figures (for example Scott Rothstein was a convicted Ponzi schemer who donated to multiple Florida politicians), public records and news coverage through 2024 do not show Scott coordinating with a convicted Ponzi offender specifically to attack Crist.

claim: The $1.9 trillion relief package is "about a bridge for Chuck Schumer, a tunnel for Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: The statement is a rhetorical accusation, not a factual description. The $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan primarily funded stimulus checks, unemployment benefits, state and local aid, vaccine and public health measures, schools, and expanded tax credits, and did not contain earmarks explicitly directing a bridge to Chuck Schumer or a tunnel to Nancy Pelosi.

claim: "Even with full control of the House, Senate and White House, Republicans have still failed to deliver on their promise of higher wages for working families."
rationale: The statement is a categorical claim that Republicans have "failed to deliver" higher wages even with unified control. In the most recent period of unified Republican control (2017–2019) real wages and median household income rose modestly, and while many analysts conclude the 2017 tax cuts did not produce a sustained acceleration in wage growth, the empirical record does not support an absolute, across-the-board failure as the claim asserts.

claim: Says the Obama administration "didn't lock people up in cages."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and government records show the Obama administration detained migrants — including children — in chain-link holding pens and family detention facilities; widely circulated 2014 photos documented fenced enclosures used by Border Patrol. Officials disputed the pejorative label 'cages,' but the physical enclosures existed, so the statement that the administration "didn't lock people up in cages" is false.

claim: Says Russ Feingold said that with Obamacare, "we could keep our doctors and our plans, it was rated as the Lie of the Year."
rationale: While PolitiFact did name the promise that 'you can keep your doctor/plan' as its 2013 Lie of the Year, there is no clear, verifiable record that former Senator Russ Feingold specifically uttered the quoted phrase. The claim appears to conflate a factual rating by PolitiFact with an attribution to Feingold that is not substantiated.

claim: Quotes show Democrats supported riots "when BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Democrats as a party broadly endorsed or supported rioting, arson, or 'killing people in the streets.' Major Democratic leaders and many Democratic officials publicly condemned violence and urged peaceful protest; while isolated individuals made controversial statements that critics cite, those do not demonstrate party-wide support for violent rioting. Additionally, most Black Lives Matter–related protests in 2020 were reported as peaceful, though some incidents of violence and property damage occurred involving a mix of actors.

claim: Says David Dewhurst "explicitly advocated" a guest worker program for all illegal immigrants.
rationale: There is no clear public record that David Dewhurst explicitly called for a blanket guest-worker program covering all undocumented immigrants. While he has at times supported elements of temporary-worker or employer-verification policies as part of broader immigration discussions, that is different from an explicit advocacy for a guest-worker program for every person currently in the country without authorization.

claim: Says President Donald Trump as a candidate mentioned WikiLeaks "over 160 times in speeches" in the last month of the campaign.
rationale: Contemporary reviews of Trump’s 2016 campaign transcripts and media fact-checking do not support that he said “WikiLeaks” over 160 times in speeches during the final month; that figure appears to conflate tweets, interviews, rally remarks, and media mentions. Counts of formal rally and speech transcripts for the final month show far fewer explicit uses of the word, so the claim is an inflation.

claim: "Mayor Barrett saved Milwaukee $25 million, thanks to Gov. Walker’s reforms."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that Milwaukee realized a $25 million savings credited directly to Mayor Tom Barrett as a result of Gov. Scott Walker’s reforms.
