While Walker’s 2011 collective-bargaining and benefit changes (Act 10) changed municipal costs and some jurisdictions reported savings, the size and attribution of a $25 million ‘save’ for Milwaukee are disputed and not supported by independent city budget documents or contemporaneous reporting as a clean, attributable $25M benefit to Barrett’s administration.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi diverted "$2.4 billion from Social Security to cover impeachment costs."
rationale: This is false. Social Security benefits are paid from dedicated payroll-tax trust funds controlled by federal law and the Treasury; the House Speaker cannot unilaterally 'divert' $2.4 billion from Social Security to pay for impeachment. Impeachment-related expenses are covered by congressional appropriations and there is no credible record or official accounting showing a $2.4 billion transfer from Social Security for impeachment costs.

claim: Says "we know" Erika Harold would "discriminate against a loving gay couple who want to adopt a child, favoring an abusive straight couple instead."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that Erika Harold explicitly said she would favor an abusive straight couple over a loving gay couple in an adoption decision. Although she has held conservative views on marriage and LGBT issues, the specific categorical assertion that 'we know' she would discriminate in that exact manner is unsupported and speculative.

claim: Says under his leadership "Wisconsin median household income" is up 2.7%, while it is down 1.3% nationally under President Obama.
rationale: The statement is misleading. U.S. Census Bureau median household income data show that the national median did not fall by 1.3% over President Obama's entire time in office and in fact rose over much of his presidency; while Wisconsin may have seen a modest rise over some short windows, the claimed contrast (WI +2.7% vs US −1.3%) depends on a cherry-picked period and data source and is not an accurate summary of the full presidential term.

claim: Former Gov. Pat McCrory appointed liberals to the North Carolina Textbook Commission, which "mandated textbooks" pushing critical race theory.
rationale: While Governor Pat McCrory did make appointments to North Carolina education bodies, there is no credible evidence that a state Textbook Commission he appointed 'mandated' K–12 textbooks that push critical race theory. Critical race theory is an advanced academic legal framework not typically taught as doctrine in K–12 textbooks, and reviews/adoptions of textbooks in North Carolina follow a formal review process rather than a unilateral mandate to teach CRT. Claims that a McCrory-appointed commission imposed CRT in textbooks conflate partisan disagreement over content with an official mandate.

claim: "Did you know that in 2013 over 50 percent of all babies born in Oregon were Hispanic?"
rationale: Statewide vital statistics for Oregon do not show that a majority of births in 2013 were to Hispanic mothers; Hispanics are a minority of Oregon's population and their share of births was well under 50% that year. The claim likely confuses the statewide figure with certain cities or counties with large Hispanic populations where births to Hispanic mothers can exceed half.

claim: "Senator Obama has, in fact, never had a serious Republican challenger."
rationale: This is false: in the 2004 Illinois Senate race Republican Jack Ryan was a credible GOP front‑runner and nominal challenger to Obama before withdrawing amid scandal, and the GOP later ran Alan Keyes in the general election. The existence of Ryan’s initial candidacy (and Keyes as the replacement) contradicts the absolute claim that Obama "never" had a serious Republican challenger.

claim: Says his plan to end the toll on Ga. 400 fulfills his campaign promise to commuters.
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and cannot be verified as presented: it asserts that 'he' says his plan fulfills a campaign promise but gives no identity, timeline, or evidence that the toll has actually been ended. Announcing a plan or saying it will fulfill a promise is not the same as having fulfilled it; toll removal on GA‑400 would require concrete actions (funding, approvals or buyout) that are not documented here. Without proof the toll has been discontinued or that the promise was legally or administratively completed, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "We have a 40 to 50 percent dropout rate in our inner-city schools."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. National and most urban district high-school dropout measures are well below 40–50%, although some specific inner-city schools or districts at particular times have experienced very high dropout rates. Without a specified city, time period, or definition of “dropout,” the claim is not supportable as stated.

claim: "Under the federal Controlled Substance Act, marijuana is listed in the same Schedule I as heroin," even though "marijuana is not a killer drug like heroin."
rationale: Under the federal Controlled Substances Act both marijuana (cannabis) and heroin (diacetylmorphine) are listed in Schedule I. Empirically marijuana has a very low acute lethality and far fewer documented overdose deaths compared with heroin, which is an opioid that commonly causes fatal overdoses.

claim: The largest number of gamblers are "from the poorest segments of the population."
rationale: The assertion conflates higher prevalence of problem gambling among low‑income people with the absolute number of gamblers. Empirical surveys typically show that while lower‑income groups often have higher rates of problem gambling, overall gambling participation is widespread and many gamblers come from middle‑income and other segments; which group has the largest absolute number depends on country, type of gambling, and how ‘gamblers’ are defined.

claim: "We paid down the debt for four years -- paid down $600 billion on the national debt."
rationale: Treasury and CBO historical data do not show any recent four-year period in which the federal debt was reduced by $600 billion. The only notable multi-year decline was in the late 1990s and it amounted to a few hundred billion at most; in most administrations the nominal federal debt rose, not fell. Without specifying which four years or whether this refers to gross debt vs. debt held by the public, the $600 billion paid-down claim is not supported by the standard federal debt series.

claim: "Obama certificate a fake."
rationale: Official records and multiple independent reviews have confirmed that Barack Obama was born in Hawaii and that the long-form birth certificate released by the White House in 2011 is authentic. The Hawaii Department of Health has repeatedly stated its records show his birth in Honolulu, and fact-checking organizations have found no credible evidence of forgery.

claim: Says the Wisconsin Republican Party tweeted "Happy International Women's Day! You ladies should get paid less and not be able to make health care decisions."
rationale: There is no credible record or reporting that the official Wisconsin Republican Party account posted that blatant, derogatory message; such an inflammatory tweet would have been widely documented and archived. The claim matches a common pattern of fabricated or screenshot-altered social media posts intended to go viral.

claim: Says 12 restaurants and food companies are "supporting Trump’s re-election."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as presented: no list, timeframe, or evidence is provided to show 12 specific restaurants/food companies have officially or materially "supported" Trump's re-election. Corporate endorsements of presidential candidates are relatively rare and political spending is publicly reported, so a specific, verifiable list would be required. Without that evidence, the assertion is not verifiable and therefore treated as false.

claim: "He's the only candidate who's balanced budgets and brought jobs to Providence."
rationale: The statement asserts a unique achievement but gives no named person, timeframe, or metrics. Multiple Providence officeholders and candidates have presided over balanced budgets or job-creation initiatives, so the exclusivity claim cannot be substantiated without comprehensive, verifiable comparisons.

claim: "KXL Radio in Portland reported today that Firefighters are now being shot at by suspected Antifa and BLM members."
rationale: This specific allegation is unverified and appears to be misinformation. A claim that firefighters are being shot at by 'suspected Antifa and BLM members' would be a major, widely corroborated news event; there are no widely reported or corroborated accounts attributing such a report to KXL. The phrasing is also vague about timing and sourcing, which reduces credibility.

claim: At this point in 2012, "Rick Perry was ahead at 29.9 percent, and we had seven more leads before it finally settled on Mitt Romney."
rationale: The statement as framed is misleading and unsupported: while Rick Perry did surge in some 2011–2012 GOP polls, there is no clear authoritative snapshot showing him at exactly 29.9% “at this point in 2012,” nor evidence that there were precisely seven additional polling/leads before the race "finally settled" on Mitt Romney. The 2012 Republican nomination featured multiple shifts (Perry, Gingrich, Santorum, Romney among leaders) but the claim's precise numbers and sequence are not borne out by contemporaneous poll archives and primary results.

claim: "Since President (Donald Trump’s) election, 36,000 jobs have been created in WI."
rationale: The statement is misleading as presented. Official sources (BLS state payroll and Wisconsin workforce reports) do not support a definitive figure of exactly 36,000 jobs 'since the election' without specifying an end date and whether payroll or household jobs are counted; published series for Wisconsin show different cumulative gains or losses depending on the exact timeframe and dataset, so the flat claim of 36,000 is not reliably true.

claim: "Wikileaks also shows how John Podesta rigged the polls by oversampling Democrats, a voter suppression technique."
rationale: There is no credible evidence in the Podesta emails released by WikiLeaks that John Podesta instructed pollsters to 'rig' polls by oversampling Democrats. Discussions in those emails focus on campaign messaging, targeting, and turnout strategy, while oversampling is a common legitimate polling technique used to ensure adequate subgroup sample sizes, not a proven method of rigging or voter suppression. The claim conflates routine polling practices and campaign targeting with intentional fraud.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood called Joe Biden an "incompetent, lying, flip-flopping, insincere, double-talking, radical socialist."
rationale: There is no contemporaneous, reputable reporting or recorded speech attributing that exact string of insults to Clint Eastwood about Joe Biden. Eastwood has made occasional public remarks about politicians, but fact‑checking and media archives do not show him using this specific list of descriptors. The claim appears to be a misattribution or a fabricated quote spread on social media.

claim: "Unvaccinated, you can get COVID and have over 99% chance of survival. Get vaccinated and you can still get COVID and will still have over 99% chance of survival."
rationale: The statement is misleading and inaccurate as a blanket claim. While many younger, healthy people have a high probability of survival from COVID-19, infection fatality rates vary substantially by age, health status, and variant—older adults and people with comorbidities face much higher mortality than implied. Vaccination does not only affect infection risk; it substantially reduces the risk of severe disease and death, so vaccinated people generally have a lower chance of dying from COVID-19 than otherwise similar unvaccinated people.

claim: "Illegal immigration costs state taxpayers over $3 billion every year."
rationale: The claim presents a precise annual dollar figure without providing methodology or source. Estimates of the fiscal impact of undocumented immigrants vary widely by study and depend on how "costs" are defined (state vs. federal, gross vs. net, which programs included), so there is no consensus supporting a single, reliably measured figure of "over $3 billion every year." Many reputable analyses produce very different totals or emphasize substantial uncertainty.

claim: It is a myth that Florida's education legislation was "negotiated in secret."
rationale: The statement is overbroad and cannot be affirmed as a general myth: Florida education bills have gone through public committee hearings and floor debates, but reporters and advocates have also documented private negotiations and closed-door meetings around particular provisions. Whether a given piece of education legislation was "negotiated in secret" depends on the specific bill and timeframe, so labeling the entire claim a myth is misleading.

claim: "Less than 500 people a year killed by all rifles combined" and "4,000 a year killed by illegals."
rationale: The two-part claim mixes a mostly accurate statement about rifle deaths with a false and unsupported claim about killings by undocumented immigrants. U.S. homicide statistics (FBI/CDC) show deaths caused by rifles are relatively low and typically under 500 per year, but there is no credible evidence that 4,000 people per year are killed by undocumented immigrants; reputable analyses and official data do not support such a high figure.

claim: "BREAKING: Queen Elizabeth II Dead At 94"
rationale: While Queen Elizabeth II has indeed died, the claim's stated age is incorrect. Official announcements and major news outlets reported she died on 8 September 2022 at age 96, not 94.

claim: "If you look at the jobs lost in the private sector as opposed to the job gains in the public sector, it's out of whack. The government's growing and the private economy's shrinking."
rationale: The statement is a broad, context-free claim that is frequently misleading. In the U.S. and many other advanced economies, private-sector employment is much larger than public employment and over long periods has generally grown more than government payrolls; temporary periods (recessions, COVID) can see private losses and relative public-sector stability or small increases, but that does not support a general claim that the government is steadily growing while the private economy is shrinking.

claim: "Autopsy results from Vince Foster’s exhumed body — Cause of death to be changed!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Vince Foster’s body was exhumed and that his official cause of death was changed. Multiple official investigations and the District of Columbia medical examiner concluded in 1993 and subsequent reviews that his death was a suicide; no reputable news outlets or government reports have reported a reversal. Claims of a new autopsy changing the cause appear to be unsubstantiated rumors circulated by conspiracy sites.

claim: "The average age of the minimum wage worker is 35 years old."
rationale: Official labor statistics and demographic analyses show that workers paid at or near the minimum wage are disproportionately young, with average/median ages generally in the mid-to-late 20s rather than 35. Saying the average is 35 contradicts common findings from U.S. labor data and scholarly analyses.

claim: "If you’re a single mom, and you’ve two kids in the city of Richmond, you can almost make $50,000 a year on the public dole."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Typical cash welfare (TANF) payments to a single mother with two children are modest (usually a few hundred dollars a month), and while additional in-kind benefits (SNAP, Medicaid, housing subsidies, tax credits) provide significant support, they do not equate to nearly $50,000 in cash income from government assistance alone in most U.S. cities. Many of these programs have strict eligibility limits and are non‑cash benefits, so saying someone can “make” nearly $50,000 on the public dole is inaccurate.

claim: Says Allen West violated federal law by scuba diving with U.S. flag.
rationale: The claim is incorrect: the U.S. Flag Code's provisions about not using the flag as apparel or for advertising are advisory guidance, not criminal prohibitions, and federal statutes criminalizing flag desecration have been curtailed by Supreme Court rulings. There is no evidence Allen West was federally charged for scuba diving with a U.S. flag.

claim: "Germany owes ... vast sums of money to NATO & the United States must be paid more for the powerful, and very expensive, defense it provides to Germany!"
rationale: There is no factual basis that Germany "owes" vast sums to NATO as if to a creditor; NATO is an alliance with small common budgets funded by member contributions, and defence is primarily financed by each member. The United States does host forces in Germany and has urged Germany to increase its national defence spending (the 2% NATO guideline), but there is no formal requirement that Germany pay the U.S. for the U.S. providing NATO collective defense beyond normal bilateral and alliance cost-sharing arrangements.

claim: "Hillary Clinton leaves the country as Mueller indictment is announced."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that Hillary Clinton left the country at the time any Robert Mueller indictment was announced. Major Mueller indictments were widely covered and Clinton's public appearances and travel were documented; this claim appears to be an unfounded rumor or social-media fabrication.

claim: "Sen. Mark Begich cast the deciding vote in favor of President Obama’s authority to issue executive amnesty to illegal aliens."
rationale: No single Senate vote — and certainly not a single senator — “gave” President Obama authority to issue executive actions on immigration. Obama’s 2014 administrative actions (expanded DACA and DAPA) were taken by the executive branch, not granted by a senator’s decisive vote. Mark Begich did vote for the 2013 bipartisan Senate immigration bill (S.744) and supported cloture, but that bill and his votes were not the source of legal authority for the 2014 executive actions.

claim: "Embalmers finding ‘strange clots’ in jabbed people"
rationale: The claim rests on isolated anecdotal reports but there is no credible evidence that embalmers are routinely finding novel or vaccine-specific "strange clots." Forensic pathologists and fact-checkers have explained that post-mortem coagulation, decomposition, and embalming artifacts can produce unusual-looking clots, and no systematic autopsy or toxicology data link routine COVID-19 vaccination to such findings.

claim: In the federal government, "there’s $16 billion in duplicate programs" that can be cut.
rationale: The statement gives a specific $16 billion figure with no source or timeframe; there is no single, authoritative, current federal estimate that universally labels exactly $16 billion as ‘duplicate programs’ available to cut. Government audits (GAO, OMB) have repeatedly identified duplicative, overlapping, or inefficient spending and have produced varying estimates and lists of potential savings, but the totals depend on definitions and assumptions and are not a settled $16 billion.

claim: "Republicans would give seniors a (Medicare) voucher that limits what's covered, costing seniors as much as $6,400 more a year."
rationale: The claim mixes a broad political claim with a specific dollar figure and is misleading. While some Republican proposals (notably premium‑support or “voucher” plans advanced by some GOP lawmakers) would shift more costs to seniors and independent analyses including CBO and advocacy groups have projected higher out‑of‑pocket costs for many beneficiaries, the effects vary by specific plan, year, and cohort; the $6,400 figure is a high‑end estimate cited for particular scenarios, not a universal guarantee that "Republicans would give seniors" that exact voucher and cost increase.

claim: "In 2017, we had more marijuana possession arrests in our country than all other violent crimes combined."
rationale: For the United States in 2017 this statement is not correct: FBI Uniform Crime Reports indicate marijuana possession arrests numbered in the several-hundred-thousand range, while arrests for violent offenses (murder, rape, robbery, aggravated assault) combined were larger. Thus marijuana possession arrests did not exceed all violent-crime arrests combined that year.

claim: Says Virginia Gov. Ralph Northam said, ‘You will give up your guns, if you don’t I’ll have the National Guard cut your power, your phone lines, and your internet. Then, if you still refuse to comply I’ll have you killed.’"
rationale: There is no credible record—no transcript, video, or reputable news report—showing Virginia Gov. Ralph Northam made this threat. The quote has circulated on social media and mirrors fabricated or misattributed statements that have been debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: The average Atlanta resident "spends an extra $924 each year in additional gasoline and wasted time."
rationale: The precise figure of $924 cannot be verified without a cited year or study. Estimates of Atlanta’s per-person congestion costs vary substantially by source and methodology (some studies report higher or lower amounts and often report per-driver rather than per-resident values), so the blanket statement that the average Atlanta resident spends exactly $924 extra annually is unsubstantiated as stated.

claim: "Iowa's Republican caucus stopped mattering years ago. It in no way determines the party nominee."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. While Iowa has not reliably produced the eventual Republican nominee in recent cycles (for example Rick Santorum in 2012 and Ted Cruz in 2016 won Iowa but did not become the nominee), the Iowa caucus still shapes media narratives, fundraising, organization and early delegate allocation and therefore can materially affect the trajectory of candidates. It does not on its own 'determine' the nominee, but it clearly still matters in practice.

claim: "2008 was the deadliest year of the war (in Afghanistan) for American forces."
rationale: Official U.S. Department of Defense casualty data and contemporary news reporting indicate that U.S. military fatalities in Afghanistan peaked after 2008, with 2010 widely reported as the deadliest year for American forces. Thus the claim that 2008 was the deadliest year for American forces in the Afghanistan war is incorrect.

claim: Says Jennifer Aniston said, "Me and all the Trump supporter celebrities decide to make a company named ‘celebrities for Trump’"
rationale: There is no credible record of Jennifer Aniston saying this; she has not publicly endorsed Donald Trump and is widely reported to have avoided supporting him. The phrasing and lack of sourcing are characteristic of fabricated or misattributed celebrity quotes.

claim: What Republicans call the "death tax" is the estate tax "on the ultra wealthy" which, in 2016, was paid by only "two out of every 1,000 people."
rationale: Republicans commonly refer to the federal estate tax as the "death tax," and the tax applies only to estates above a high exemption. IRS data and contemporary analyses show that in 2016 only about 0.2% of decedents' estates — roughly two out of every 1,000 — owed federal estate tax, so the numerical claim is accurate in that context.

claim: "Last year, 36 million Americans didn’t have a prescription filled because they couldn’t afford it."
rationale: I cannot verify the exact claim that 36 million Americans went without a prescription last year because of cost. Multiple national surveys and reports do show that tens of millions skip or delay medications for financial reasons, but estimates differ by survey year, question wording, and whether they count adults only; I am not aware of an authoritative source that gives precisely 36 million for 'last year.'

claim: The budget for the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau "is only about 1 percent of the amount banks generate just from late fees and overdraft fees."
rationale: The CFPB’s annual budget is on the order of several hundred million dollars (roughly $500–700 million in recent years), while U.S. banks collect tens of billions annually from late fees and overdraft/NSF charges. Comparing those magnitudes shows the CFPB budget is roughly 1% (order-of-magnitude) of the total fees banks generate each year. The statement is a reasonable characterization of the scale difference.

claim: Officials "recommend that women who get one of these (COVID-19) shots should absolutely not get pregnant for at least the first two months after they’ve been injected."
rationale: Major public-health agencies and professional bodies (CDC, WHO, ACOG, EMA) did not issue a blanket recommendation that women avoid pregnancy for two months after COVID-19 vaccination. Early clinical trials excluded pregnant people, which led to caution and evolving guidance, but subsequent guidance and data have stated there is no need to delay pregnancy after receiving approved COVID-19 vaccines.

claim: In 2010, uninsured voters made up "about 5 percent of the electorate."
rationale: The national uninsured rate in 2010 was roughly 14–16%, and although uninsured people vote at lower rates than the insured, exit-poll and survey analyses from that period put the share of voters who were uninsured closer to the high single digits rather than as low as 5%. Saying uninsured voters made up "about 5 percent of the electorate" understates their presence and is misleading.

claim: "Eighty-five percent of every dollar donated to the Clinton Foundation ended up either with the Clintons or with their staff to pay for travel, salaries, and benefits. Fifteen cents of every dollar actually went to some charitable beneficiary."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Audited financial statements and IRS Form 990s for the Clinton Foundation across multiple years show the majority of expenses were programmatic (grants, program services and partner payments), not payments 'to the Clintons' or to staff for travel/salaries; program expense ratios reported were far higher than 15% in most years. Independent fact-checkers and charity evaluators have debunked the 85% assertion as a misreading/misallocation of line items.

claim: "In fact, there’s more state funding for education today than any other time."
rationale: The statement is too broad and misleading. While total nominal state education appropriations are larger than in earlier decades because of inflation and population growth, inflation-adjusted and per‑pupil funding levels are not universally higher today than at any prior time and vary substantially by state and year. National data show funding has fluctuated and in many cases peaked in different periods (for example around the late 2000s/early 2010s) rather than being at an all‑time high today.

claim: "Congresswoman Frederica Wilson successfully postpones closure of the North Perry airport tower."
rationale: I am not aware of reliable reporting that Rep. Frederica Wilson personally succeeded in postponing the closure of the North Perry airport control tower. FAA tower closures or postponements are federal operational decisions typically attributed to the FAA or broader congressional delegations, and coverage of North Perry’s tower does not credit Wilson with a successful sole intervention.

claim: "News report accidentally reveals doctors giving ‘banned’ COVID treatment to the Queen."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official royal statement indicating doctors administered a ‘banned’ COVID treatment to the Queen; such claims have circulated on social media but were not substantiated by mainstream news outlets or official sources. The allegation appears to be a misinterpretation or misinformation rather than a documented factual event.

claim: Says "over 1 million signatures" were submitted in attempt to recall Gov. Scott Walker.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and state records from the 2011–2012 Wisconsin recall drive show organizers turned in roughly 930–940 thousand signatures (commonly reported as about 931,000), not over 1 million. The Government Accountability Board later certified that petitioners had exceeded the required threshold of valid signatures, but the submitted total was under one million.

claim: "We saw the president of the United States engage American troops in a fourth conflict in a foreign land. This is historic."
rationale: The claim is vague and not verifiable as stated: it does not specify which president, which four conflicts, or what counts as 'engaging' troops. Historically, multiple U.S. presidents have committed American forces to several foreign conflicts, so a blanket statement that this instance is uniquely a "fourth conflict" and therefore "historic" cannot be confirmed. Without specific, checkable details the assertion is not supported.

claim: The 2018 Academy Awards show was the "lowest rated Oscars in HISTORY."
rationale: The 2018 (90th) Academy Awards drew about 26.5 million viewers, a roughly 19% decline from 2017, and was widely reported based on Nielsen metrics as the lowest-rated Oscars telecast in history up to that point. News organizations and ratings data characterized it as the lowest-rated ceremony since Nielsen began tracking Oscars viewership.

claim: Says "99 percent of the time police officers aren't charged when they kill young people of color."
rationale: The claim that officers are not charged 99% of the time when they kill young people of color is an unsupported and overly precise statistic. Reliable databases and academic studies show criminal charges in only a minority of police killings, but rates vary by dataset, time period, and definitions and do not uniformly support a 99% non-charging figure.

claim: Says when Republicans took over the state legislature in 2010, New Hampshire’s tax rate for employers was 50th in the nation, and unemployment had more than doubled under Democrats.
rationale: The claim mixes two different, imprecise assertions and lacks supporting evidence. While New Hampshire unemployment did rise during the 2008–2010 Great Recession under a Democratic governor, whether it “more than doubled” depends on the chosen baseline month and is not a clear-cut, reliably supported statement; similarly, there is no clear, authoritative basis to say a single “tax rate for employers” in New Hampshire was ranked exactly 50th in 2010 because employers face multiple taxes (unemployment insurance, business taxes, etc.) and rankings vary by tax and methodology.

claim: Says Sen. Thad Cochran "voted to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on ... the Bridge to Nowhere in Alaska instead of shifting the money to repair a bridge damaged by Hurricane Katrina."
rationale: The claim oversimplifies and misrepresents a complex set of votes. Thad Cochran was Mississippi’s senator and broadly supported Katrina relief measures; while some transportation bills that included long-disputed Alaska earmarks passed, attributing a single vote by Cochran as choosing the Alaska “Bridge to Nowhere” over repairing a Katrina-damaged bridge is misleading. The relevant funding and amendment votes were multiple and procedural, and Cochran’s record shows he worked to secure disaster aid for Mississippi rather than explicitly voting to deny it in favor of the Alaska project.

claim: Says opponent Ted Cruz has not led businesses.
rationale: The claim that Ted Cruz has not led businesses is misleading. Cruz served as Texas Solicitor General and spent years in private legal practice, including partner-level roles at law firms and running his own legal work and campaign organizations, which involve leadership and management responsibilities. Therefore saying he has "not led businesses" is inaccurate without a narrow definition of "business."

claim: Says Sidney Blumenthal wrote that the Benghazi attack was "almost certainly preventable. Clinton was in charge of the State Department, and it failed to protect U.S. personnel and an American consulate in Libya."
rationale: There is no reliable, attributable source showing Sidney Blumenthal wrote that exact sentence. Blumenthal did circulate memos and commentary criticizing U.S. policy in Libya and Hillary Clinton's role, but the specific quoted phrasing has not been documented as his in public records; therefore the claim as stated is unverified.

claim: "When the wind stops blowing, that’s the end of your electric."
rationale: Wind turbines produce variable power and will reduce output when winds die, but that does not mean electricity ceases. Modern grids use a mix of dispatchable generation (natural gas, hydro, coal, nuclear), energy storage (batteries, pumped hydro), interconnections, and demand response to maintain supply when wind is low.

claim: "The Democrats want you American taxpayers to shell out $3 billion for ‘non-racist’ trees."
rationale: There is no evidence that Democratic lawmakers proposed a $3 billion program to buy or produce so‑called ‘non‑racist’ trees. The claim conflates or exaggerates unrelated proposals (such as funding for urban forestry, tree‑planting for climate resilience, or small renaming efforts) and uses a mocking label not found in any serious legislative text.

claim: Says Section 1325 of U.S. immigration law was "put into place in 1929, by a segregationist."
rationale: The modern 8 U.S.C. §1325 (criminalizing unlawful entry) traces its roots to early 20th-century immigration statutes and a 1929 law did introduce criminal penalties for unlawful entry, but the claim that Section 1325 was explicitly "put into place in 1929, by a segregationist" is misleading. The current section number is a later codification and there is no clear, widely accepted attribution to a single sponsor described as "a segregationist."

claim: Says Texas unemployment is dire in various ways such as a doubling in the jobless rate during Rick Perry's governorship. Also, the Texas rate has increased faster than the national rate during Barack Obama's presidency.
rationale: The claim mixes time periods and cherry-picks peaks. Texas unemployment did rise sharply during the Great Recession (peaking around ~8% in 2009–2010 from roughly ~4% in the early 2000s), which is approximately a doubling from an early-2000s low; but over Rick Perry’s full 2000–2015 governorship the rate did not remain doubled and fell back to pre-recession levels by the mid-2010s. Likewise, during Barack Obama’s presidency the national unemployment rate rose sharply in 2008–2009 and then declined; Texas’s unemployment did not uniformly increase faster than the national rate across the entire Obama term and in many months rose less and recovered faster, so the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: Says the U.S. Postal Service has taken no taxpayer aid since 1971, funds operations entirely from the sale of stamps and related products and makes an "operational profit year after year."
rationale: While the 1970 Postal Reorganization Act created a self-funding model, the USPS has at times received federal support and appropriations for specific programs and emergencies, and it has reported operating losses for many years rather than an uninterrupted operational profit. The claim that it has taken no taxpayer aid since 1971 and makes an operational profit year after year is inconsistent with public financial reports and known congressional actions.

claim: "Justice Kennedy quit because he and his son helped Trump launder illegal Russian money through Deutsche Bank."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy or his son helped President Trump launder Russian money through Deutsche Bank; Kennedy announced his retirement in 2018 for personal and institutional reasons. Such a serious criminal allegation would have been investigated and widely reported, but no substantiation exists.

claim: Quotes Winston Churchill as saying "Diplomacy is the art of telling people to go to hell in such a way that they ask for directions."
rationale: There is no reliable primary-source evidence that Winston Churchill ever said or wrote this line. It is widely and repeatedly attributed to him in popular sources, but quote-researchers have found no contemporary record in Churchill's speeches, writings, or reported remarks and it appears to be apocryphal or originated elsewhere.

claim: The health care law was "a 2,733-page bill! . . . No amendments!"
rationale: The statement is inaccurate. The Affordable Care Act's page count varies by how versions are printed and whether related reconciliation text is included, but the signed main law is commonly reported as roughly 2,400–2,500 pages in many formats (and the reconciliation bill added more), not a definitive 2,733 pages; furthermore the law was changed through the reconciliation process and has been amended and interpreted by subsequent legislation and regulations, so it was not enacted with “no amendments.”

claim: Poll results from the past 35 years show that State of the Union speeches "do not move" presidential approval numbers.
rationale: Multiple polling analyses covering recent decades find State of the Union addresses typically produce only very small, short-lived changes in presidential approval—usually within poll margins of error—and rarely produce sustained shifts. While individual speeches have occasionally produced brief upticks or downturns, the average effect across roughly the past 35 years is negligible.

claim: Says Texas has more than 80,000 abortions each year.
rationale: Recent reliable estimates from state reports, the CDC and the Guttmacher Institute show Texas had roughly 50,000–60,000 abortions per year in the late 2010s and that totals fell further after 2021 due to new restrictions; recent annual totals do not exceed 80,000. Therefore the blanket claim that Texas has more than 80,000 abortions each year is not supported by available data for current years.

claim: Fewer Democrats were on the Georgia general election ballot in 2012 than in more than 100 years.
rationale: The claim is not supported without a precise definition of which offices are being counted; Democrats fielded candidates in major 2012 Georgia races (president, U.S. Senate/House, and several state offices). Reliable historical comparisons require specifying whether the count is for every office on the statewide ballot, partisan contests only, or number of Democratic nominees, and available evidence does not clearly show 2012 was the lowest in over a century.

claim: Says North Carolina’s "Democratic Secretary of State" controls the state's elections.
rationale: In North Carolina, elections are administered by the State Board of Elections and local county boards, not the Secretary of State. The NC Secretary of State's office primarily handles business registrations and related administrative functions, so it does not "control" statewide elections.

claim: "The biggest contribution" behind a decrease in U.S. unemployment "was 1.2 million people leaving the workforce"
rationale: The statement is unverified as written because it gives no time period; whether 1.2 million people leaving the workforce was the "biggest contribution" to a decline in unemployment depends entirely on the specific monthly BLS household survey data. In most recent months of decline, reductions in unemployment were often driven by employment gains rather than a single 1.2 million drop in the labor force, so the absolutist phrasing is misleading without a clear date and source. Therefore the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "Before Leaving, Obama Enacts Rules to Take $3,000 From EVERY American."
rationale: No credible evidence exists that President Obama enacted a rule taking $3,000 from every American before leaving office. A universal levy of that magnitude would require legislation or clear administrative authority and would have been widely reported, but no such action occurred.

claim: "Under @BarackObama illegal immigration dropped to a 50-year low."
rationale: Obama-era policies coincided with declines in illegal border crossings and a gradual fall in the estimated unauthorized immigrant population from its peak, but the assertion that illegal immigration dropped to a 50-year low is not supported. Most authoritative sources show declines to multi-decade lows by some measures (often cited as ~40-year lows in border apprehensions) or smaller drops in the unauthorized population, not a clear 50-year nadir across standard metrics.

claim: Hank Aaron’s death was caused by a COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hank Aaron's death was caused by a COVID-19 vaccine. Contemporary fact-checking and reporting stated he died after a brief illness, and neither his family nor medical authorities attributed his death to vaccination; no public autopsy or medical report linked a vaccine to his death.

claim: Says Bill White is refusing to debate.
rationale: The claim is presented without any source, date, or indication of which Bill White is meant, so it cannot be confirmed as stated. Without contemporaneous reporting or a direct campaign statement showing he refused to debate, the assertion is unsupported; historically Bill White (the Texas politician) has participated in debates in past campaigns, so a blanket refusal is not established.

claim: The Paul Ryan budget proposal would "privatize Medicare."
rationale: Paul Ryan's budget proposals did not immediately abolish Medicare; they proposed converting Medicare for future beneficiaries into a 'premium-support' or voucher-like system that would subsidize private plans while leaving traditional Medicare as an option and protecting current beneficiaries. Critics called this 'privatization' because it shifts future enrollees toward private insurance, but the proposals stop short of an immediate, complete privatization of the program.

claim: Emails show Democrats, Hillary Clinton and George Soros instigated and orchestrated racial protests in Charlottesville by trying to "control" and keep people "desperate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence in leaked emails showing Democrats, Hillary Clinton, or George Soros instigated or orchestrated the Charlottesville racial protests. Investigations and mainstream reporting attribute planning and violence to white supremacist organizers, and fact-checkers have debunked claims tying Clinton or Soros to directing the events. References to emails are typically misinterpretations or out-of-context excerpts that do not demonstrate orchestration or intent to 'control' and keep people 'desperate.'

claim: The federal government "now tells us which light bulbs to buy."
rationale: The federal government has enacted energy-efficiency standards (notably the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 and subsequent DOE rules) that phase out many low-efficiency incandescent bulbs, but it does not direct consumers to purchase specific brands or exact bulb models. Those standards set minimum efficiency/lumen-per-watt requirements, and manufacturers sell bulbs (LEDs, CFLs, or compliant incandescents) that meet them, so consumers still choose among compliant options.

claim: "(Brendan) Doherty wants to raise the eligibility age for Social Security benefits for anyone born after 1960, with no regard for the challenges it would cause for people working in physically demanding occupations."
rationale: There is no verifiable public record that Brendan Doherty has proposed a policy to raise Social Security eligibility for everyone born after 1960; mainstream retirement-age proposals vary and typically target future cohorts with phased changes rather than a single cutoff year. The claim’s phrase 'with no regard for the challenges...' is a subjective judgment about motives that cannot be independently verified from policy statements.

claim: It is a "myth" that "per-student funding only rose by 47 cents this year."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify and cannot be accepted as true without specifying the jurisdiction, fiscal year, and whether amounts are nominal or inflation-adjusted. Claims about per-student funding changes rely on detailed budget data (state vs. district, formula vs. total spending, one-time vs. recurring items), so labeling the “47 cents” figure a myth without that context is unsupported. Therefore I judge the blanket assertion that it is a myth to be false given the missing specifics.

claim: Says Donald Trump "cashed in" on Sept. 11,  "collecting $150,000 in federal funds intended to help small businesses recover — even though days after the attack Trump said his properties were not affected."
rationale: Contemporary news reports and later fact-checks document that Trump-owned entities received about $150,000 in Small Business Administration disaster-relief funds after the Sept. 11 attacks. Those payments were federal small-business recovery loans, and Trump had publicly said in the days after the attacks that his properties were not affected. Therefore the claim that he collected about $150,000 in federal small-business recovery funds despite saying his properties were unaffected is supported by reporting.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers "wants to force residents to fund Planned Parenthood abortion business."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Gov. Tony Evers has supported restoring funding access and allowing Planned Parenthood to receive public reimbursement for reproductive health services, but he has not proposed a policy that 'forces' individual residents to directly pay Planned Parenthood for abortions; public funding for abortions is tightly restricted by law and Planned Parenthood also provides many non‑abortion services.

claim: "When I was Mayor of South Pasadena, we actually reduced the property taxes we collected."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated and is implausible on its face: in California (where South Pasadena is located) property tax rates and assessments are governed largely by state law and the county assessor under Proposition 13, not unilaterally by a city mayor or council. A mayor might influence local parcel taxes or city fee policy, or the city’s share of property tax revenue could decline for budgetary/allocation reasons, but the blanket statement that “we actually reduced the property taxes we collected” is unsubstantiated without specific measures or budget records showing an intentional, enacted reduction.

claim: Says the man who rushed the stage at him in Dayton, Ohio, "had chatter about ISIS, or with ISIS" in his social media posts.
rationale: I am not aware of credible reporting or official statements confirming that the person who rushed the stage in Dayton posted 'chatter about ISIS' on social media. Major news coverage and law enforcement updates available through mid-2024 did not identify ISIS ties for that incident; claims of such extremist ties appear unsupported by verified sources.

claim: "We spend less than 2 percent more every year. That is the lowest increase in spending since they have been keeping numbers."
rationale: The claim is vague and almost certainly incorrect as stated: it does not specify who "we" are, what spending is measured (federal, state, household), or whether increases are nominal or inflation-adjusted. Historical budget/outlay data for the U.S. and many governments show year-to-year nominal spending increases frequently above 2%, and there have been periods in earlier records with lower or comparable growth, so the absolute statement that spending increases have been under 2% every year and are the lowest on record is not supported.

claim: Of six Rhode Island tax-credit programs worth about $35 million, "three companies got 90 percent of that -- CVS and two companies not even located in the state of Rhode Island."
rationale: The claim lacks a verifiable timeframe, source, or identification of the six tax-credit programs, and distribution of tax credits across multiple programs is normally public and dispersed. Additionally, CVS is headquartered in Woonsocket, Rhode Island, which undercuts any implication that CVS was an out-of-state beneficiary; without specific data showing three firms received 90% of ~$35M across those programs the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says President Donald Trump’s hold on Ukraine aid was like when "the Obama administration withheld $585 million of promised aid to Egypt in 2013 ... (and within the  fiscal year) they didn't have to disclose the halt to anyone."
rationale: The claim is misleading. In 2013 the Obama administration announced a public suspension/review of certain security and military assistance to Egypt after the ouster of President Morsi and imposed restrictions on transfers; it was not a secret freeze of exactly $585 million with no required disclosure. Trump's 2019 hold on congressionally approved Ukraine aid involved a different legal and political posture (a delayed release of appropriated funds and limited immediate notification to Congress), so equating the two actions and the specific $585 million/non-disclosure assertion is inaccurate.

claim: Georgia has the highest flu activity in the country.
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or source and therefore cannot be verified; flu activity changes week-to-week and season-to-season. U.S. CDC and state health surveillance data show different states (and countries) lead in activity at different times, so there is no basis to assert Georgia consistently has the highest flu activity nationwide.

claim: Republicans are now "taking credit" for provisions of the health care bill "that they had tried to derail."
rationale: The claim is a broad, universal assertion that cannot be verified without naming the specific health‑care bill, provisions, time period, and which Republicans. While individual Republican politicians have in some cases praised or embraced popular provisions they previously opposed, that does not substantiate the sweeping claim that Republicans as a group are "now taking credit" for items they tried to derail. The statement is vague and overgeneralizes isolated instances into a universal behavior.

claim: ICE está en Uvalde, Texas, "entonces los padres indocumentados tienen que temer la deportación antes de verificar si sus hijos están vivos".
rationale: No hay evidencia pública creíble de que ICE estuviera realizando operaciones de deportación en Uvalde que obligaran a padres indocumentados a temer la deportación antes de verificar si sus hijos estaban vivos. Funcionarios y reportes periodísticos indicaron que no se estaban realizando redadas en hospitales y no se documentaron deportaciones masivas en el lugar; aunque es comprensible que inmigrantes teman la deportación, la afirmación categórica no está respaldada por la evidencia disponible.

claim: "NAVY SEALs raid cargo ship full of smuggled children."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official confirmation of a U.S. Navy SEAL raid that rescued a cargo ship “full of smuggled children.” Claims like this have circulated on social media before and were debunked by fact-checkers; such a large, dramatic operation would have been widely reported by mainstream and official sources. Without specific details (date, ship name, location) the assertion appears to be a viral, unsubstantiated rumor.

claim: "Democrats oppose any effort to secure our border."
rationale: The claim is an absolute blanket statement that is inaccurate. Many Democrats support securing the border but favor different methods (e.g., technology, staffing, ports-of-entry improvements, and targeted enforcement) and have voted for border security funding and bipartisan bills, even while opposing some proposals like a large border wall or family separation policies.

claim: Obama "voted for ... $3-million for an overhead projector at a planetarium in Chicago."
rationale: This claim mischaracterizes an appropriation. As an Illinois state senator Obama voted for a capital bill that included funds for planetarium-related projects, but there is no record that $3 million was earmarked for a single 'overhead projector' or that he specifically voted for such an item; fact-checkers have called the wording misleading.

claim: Says Florida Gov. Rick Scott "subtracted $1.3 billion from public schools."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Florida K–12 funding was reduced around the 2011 budget cycle and some analyses point to roughly $1.3 billion fewer state dollars compared with prior years, those changes were the result of broader legislative budget decisions, shifts in federal stimulus aid, and accounting choices over multiple years; it is inaccurate to state simply that Gov. Rick Scott personally "subtracted $1.3 billion from public schools."

claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics "supports banning guns."
rationale: The American Academy of Pediatrics advocates for strong gun-safety policies (safe storage, universal background checks, child access prevention) and has supported restrictions on certain weapons like military-style assault rifles and high-capacity magazines, but it does not call for a blanket ban on all civilian firearms. Saying the AAP “supports banning guns” without qualification misrepresents its published policy positions.

claim: "Hundreds of illegal immigrants subject to detainers were released in the last week since the new sanctuary policy was adopted by the Travis County Sheriff's Office."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence in public reporting or from the Travis County Sheriff's Office or ICE up to mid‑2024 that 'hundreds' of immigrants subject to detainers were released within a single week following a new sanctuary policy. Large-scale, short‑term releases of that magnitude would typically be documented by local officials or media; absent such documentation the specific numeric claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Your chances of throwing it are actually a little bit better in that situation."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify; it gives no definition of what 'throwing it' means or what 'that situation' entails, so its truth cannot be established. Probabilistic claims require concrete conditions and data, which are missing here.

claim: Says four Republican representatives "voted to impeach President Donald Trump."
rationale: The number four is incorrect for the major House impeachments: in the December 2019 House impeachment votes only three members who were then associated with the GOP voted for at least one article, and in the January 2021 House impeachment ten House Republicans voted to impeach. There is no House impeachment vote in which exactly four Republican representatives voted to impeach Donald Trump.

claim: Says there is a 4,250% increase in fetal death from the flu shot.
rationale: High-quality evidence and public-health agencies do not support a 4,250% increase in fetal deaths from flu vaccination in pregnancy. Large cohort studies and systematic reviews find no increased risk (and some find reduced stillbirth risk), and the dramatic percentage likely stems from misinterpreted or small-number VAERS reports rather than controlled research.

claim: Says "Karen Handel’s office budget increased a whopping 42 percent."
rationale: I could not find authoritative evidence that Karen Handel’s office budget rose by 42%; the claim is ambiguous about which “office” and time period it refers to and appears to be a cherry-picked or misleading figure. Congressional member office funding (the Members' Representational Allowance) is set by House formulas and annual appropriations and does not typically change by such a large percentage absent a clear reclassification or one-time adjustment.

claim: "It costs nearly five times as much in California to build and maintain a mile of road as it does in the rest of the nation."
rationale: California does have higher road construction and maintenance costs than many other states because of factors like labor, environmental regulations, right-of-way and seismic requirements, but reputable data and state audits show typical multipliers more in the roughly 1.5–3× range for many projects rather than 'nearly five times.' The blanket claim of ~5× appears to rely on selective examples and does not match broader federal and state cost-comparison data.

claim: Says he has "a fiduciary responsibility to his business, his family and his employees to pay no more tax than legally required."
rationale: The claim presents a quoted statement but gives no speaker, date, or source to verify. Without attribution or corroborating evidence (audio, transcript, or reputable report), the assertion that "he says" this cannot be confirmed and thus is treated as false for lack of verification.

claim: The Iran deal says that "if any other country tries to undermine (Iran's) nuclear program, we have to help them defend themselves against Israel, Egypt, Saudis, our own allies."
rationale: The 2015 JCPOA (the Iran nuclear deal) contains nuclear restrictions, verification measures, sanctions relief, and dispute-resolution procedures, but it does not include any clause obligating signatories to help Iran defend its nuclear program or to provide military assistance against Israel, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, or other states. No provision in the agreement creates a mutual-defense or military-assistance requirement for parties to intervene on Iran's behalf.

claim: Gov. McDonnell's proposed budget "is cutting" public education.
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as true: Gov. McDonnell proposed multiple budgets over his term with differing effects on education funding. Some proposals reduced certain state appropriations or shifted costs to localities while other measures maintained or increased base K–12 funding, so saying simply that his proposed budget "is cutting" public education is unsupported without a specific year and definition of "cutting."

claim: Quotes incoming U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "under capitalism, man oppresses man. Under socialism, it’s the other way around."
rationale: There is no authoritative record or credible sourcing showing Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez uttered that quip; it is a longstanding satirical one-liner that has been repeatedly misattributed to various public figures. Searches of her speeches, official statements, and verified social media do not support the attribution.

claim: "The stock market has hit record numbers, as you know. And there has been a tremendous surge of optimism in the business world."
rationale: The claim is too vague and therefore not verifiable as stated: whether the market has hit 'record numbers' depends on which index and what date, and business optimism varies by sector, country, and survey. Historical data show that some indices occasionally hit records while others do not, and sentiment indicators frequently move in both directions, so the blanket assertion cannot be confirmed without a specific timeframe and market.

claim: "This election marks the largest Senate gains for a president's party in a first midterm election since at least President Kennedy's in 1962."
rationale: The claim is unverified as written because it does not specify which election is meant, and historical Senate net changes in first midterms vary. Generally presidents' parties typically lose seats in first midterms, and I cannot confirm that any recent first-midterm gain exceeded whatever Democratic gains occurred in 1962 without year-by-year seat-change data. Given the ambiguity and the unusual nature of the assertion, it should not be accepted as fact without specific election-year evidence.

claim: Says Vice President Kamala Harris called the unvaccinated "dirty Trump people."
rationale: There is no credible record or transcript showing Vice President Kamala Harris used the phrase "dirty Trump people." Her public remarks have included urging vaccination and criticizing misinformation, but reputable fact-checkers and news transcripts do not support this exact derogatory quote, indicating it was misattributed or fabricated on social media.

claim: There were "63 murders this weekend" in Chicago and Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s legacy is "more murders in his city than ever before."
rationale: Contemporary Chicago Police and media reporting do not support a claim of 63 murders in a single weekend; typical weekend homicide counts are in the low single digits to low teens, and such a spike would have been widely documented. Likewise, Rahm Emanuel’s mayoralty did not produce the highest murder totals in Chicago history—earlier periods (notably in the late 20th century) recorded higher annual homicide counts than during his tenure.

claim: "Our state economic development agency under Walker, WEDC, actually isn’t even using the funds that are appropriated to it."
rationale: WEDC (Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation) under Governor Scott Walker did receive and spend appropriated funds on grants, loans, tax credits and agency operations. While state audits and news reports criticized WEDC for poor controls, transparency and some unspent balances, the organization clearly expended appropriated monies rather than 'not even using' them.

claim: Tim Tebow used to "kneel in prayer and the NFL complained."
rationale: Tim Tebow did frequently kneel in prayer on the field (popularly called 'Tebowing'), but there is no clear record that the NFL as an organization formally complained or punished him specifically for those prayers. The league discussed celebration rules broadly, but it did not launch a targeted complaint or ban aimed at Tebow's on-field prayers.

claim: Says he "never supported" federal health care individual mandate.
rationale: The claim as presented lacks an identified speaker or source and therefore cannot be verified. Statements about what someone 'says' require a named individual, time, and citation; without those details the assertion is not a provable fact. If a specific person and quote were provided, it could be evaluated against public statements and records.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on abortion.
rationale: Mitt Romney has publicly changed his position on abortion: during his 1994 U.S. Senate campaign he described himself as pro-choice and supporting Roe v. Wade, whereas by the 2000s and during his 2008 and 2012 presidential campaigns he identified as pro-life and opposed Roe in many statements. Multiple contemporaneous reports and Romney's own statements document these shifts in stance.

claim: Says he was the first person to call for invoking the Defense Production Act.
rationale: The claim as written is unverified because it does not identify who 'he' is, and historically multiple officials publicly urged use of the Defense Production Act in close succession (notably during early 2020). Absent a specific name and timestamp proving that this person was demonstrably the first, the assertion is not supported and is likely incorrect.

claim: Military spending cuts, known as the sequester, were President Barack Obama’s idea.
rationale: The sequester mechanism predates Obama and the specific automatic military cuts resulted from the 2011 Budget Control Act, a congressional compromise reached during debt‑ceiling negotiations. While the Obama administration agreed to the backstop as part of the deal, it was not uniquely his idea or initiative.

claim: The CDC said it "made a mistake" and reduced its count of Florida COVID-19 cases from 90,000 to 11,000.
rationale: There is no credible record of the CDC publicly saying it cut Florida’s total COVID-19 case count from 90,000 to 11,000. What did occur during the pandemic were occasional CDC data-table adjustments, de-duplication, or reporting-format errors that changed counts at the county or provisional level and were sometimes misreported or misunderstood. The specific claim about a reduction from 90,000 to 11,000 is a misrepresentation of those routine corrections.

claim: A video shows "massive explosion as Ukraine destroyed 280 Russian tanks to pieces using U.S. Javelin missiles."
rationale: The claim that a single video shows Ukraine destroying 280 Russian tanks with U.S. Javelins is implausible and uncorroborated. Javelins are individual anti-tank missiles with limited stocks and are used against single vehicles; destroying 280 tanks in one event would require extraordinary evidence and wide independent reporting, which is absent. Viral videos are frequently misattributed, edited, or show explosions of depots/vehicles rather than the mass destruction claimed.

claim: Says his budget provides "the highest state funding level in history" for education.
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated — it does not specify which state, which fiscal year, or whether ‘highest’ refers to nominal dollars, inflation‑adjusted dollars, total education spending, state share, or per‑pupil funding. Frequently such claims are technically true in nominal terms or when one‑time federal aid is included but false when spending is adjusted for inflation or measured per pupil. Without those details the blanket assertion is not reliably true.

claim: Under President Barack Obama’s leadership, "since June 2009, (the auto) industry has added a quarter of a million jobs."
rationale: The claim overstates what can be reliably supported by official employment data. BLS series for motor vehicles and parts manufacturing and for broader auto-related employment show a substantial but smaller recovery after the 2008–2009 recession, and wording is ambiguous about which categories and end date are counted; available public data do not clearly support a clean +250,000 figure 'since June 2009' attributable solely to the auto industry under President Obama.

claim: Says Sen. Kamala  Harris "introduced a bill today to forbid a police officers from drawing his/her gun without permission from their supervisor."
rationale: There is no record that Sen. Kamala Harris introduced a federal bill that would bar police from drawing firearms without prior supervisor permission. Her known federal policing proposals (for example, co-sponsoring the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act) addressed use-of-force standards and accountability but did not impose a blanket supervisor-authorization requirement to draw a weapon. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or conflation of broader policing reform proposals.

claim: "(Sen. Robert) Gordon cost us money, exempting the Newark sports arena from paying property taxes and sticking us with the bill."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that a single state senator unilaterally 'exempted' the Newark arena from property taxes and thereby directly 'stuck us with the bill.' Property‑tax relief or exemptions for large redevelopment projects are typically created through negotiated PILOT (payment-in-lieu-of-taxes) agreements and legislation involving multiple local and state actors, not the sole act of one senator. The claim oversimplifies responsibility and misattributes a complex financing and tax arrangement to a single individual.

claim: "In every single country, she had a majority of the vote -- or more of those who'd already made up their minds."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable and highly implausible as stated because it provides no identification of who “she” is, which countries or time period are meant, or whether this refers to actual election results or opinion polls. No political figure or candidate plausibly achieves a majority (or plurality among decided voters) in every single country — outcomes and polling vary widely and many countries lack comparable polls. Given the missing context and the global variability of political support, the claim is false as a general statement.

claim: Says the estate tax is a threat to family farms.
rationale: The claim is overbroad: federal estate tax only applies to estates above a relatively high exemption threshold, so the vast majority of family farms are not liable for it. In addition, farms commonly use legal planning tools (life insurance, valuation discounts, trusts, installment payments) that mitigate estate-tax-driven forced sales, though very large farms could still be affected in specific cases.

claim: "All schools in Canada are closed for the rest of the school year, each family will receive $950 every two weeks for the next 15 weeks, banks were notif(ied) to suspend mortgage payments for at least 6 months, and student loans deferred."
rationale: The claim bundles several nationwide mandates that did not uniformly occur. School closure decisions were made provincially and not all jurisdictions announced closure for the entire school year; federal income supports were different (e.g., CERB provided about $2,000/month, not $950 every two weeks); banks offered voluntary mortgage-deferral options rather than a single mandated suspension, and student loan relief (a federal six-month pause for Canada Student Loans) applied to federal loans but details varied by province and lender.

claim: Hillary Clinton advocates "a freeze on foreclosures. Barack Obama said no."
rationale: The claim oversimplifies and misstates positions. While Hillary Clinton supported stronger protections and homeowner relief measures during the 2008–2009 crisis, she did not successfully enact or universally call for a nationwide blanket foreclosure ‘freeze’ as a clear, implemented policy; Barack Obama and his campaign likewise opposed a blanket moratorium and instead promoted targeted mortgage modification programs. Presenting it as a simple binary (‘Clinton: freeze; Obama: no’) omits timing, scope, and nuance.

claim: "Facts have now come out to show conclusively" that the 2020 presidential election wasn’t legitimate.
rationale: Extensive post‑election reviews, recounts, and dozens of court rulings found no credible evidence of widespread fraud that would change the 2020 result; state election officials certified results and the Department of Justice and election security officials reported no evidence of fraud affecting the outcome. Claims to the contrary have been litigated and investigated and were not substantiated. Therefore the statement that facts have now come out showing conclusively the election wasn’t legitimate is false.

claim: "Inspections of abortion centers around Virginia have found multiple violations of parental consent laws … but Gov. Terry McAuliffe and his administration have done nothing."
rationale: There is no clear, credible record showing that state inspections around Virginia uncovered widespread, multiple violations of parental consent laws by abortion centers and that Gov. McAuliffe simply did nothing. Reporting from the period does not substantiate a pattern of documented parental-consent violations combined with an administration-wide refusal to act; enforcement of parental-consent issues typically involves courts and local prosecutors as well as health agencies. Because the claim bundles two strong assertions (multiple violations + deliberate inaction), and reliable public records do not support both, the combined claim is not supported.

claim: "These are radical Islamic terrorists, and (Hillary Clinton) won't even mention the word."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions but lacks context about who “these” refers to, making the first part unverifiable as stated. The second part — that Hillary Clinton “won’t even mention the word” — is misleading: during the 2016 campaign she often criticized or avoided the specific phrase “radical Islamic terrorism,” but she did discuss Islamist extremism and used related terms at times rather than never mentioning it. Framing it as an absolute categorical refusal is therefore false.

claim: "MSNBC announced Trump won 2020 election."
rationale: MSNBC, along with other major U.S. news networks, projected Joe Biden as the winner of the 2020 presidential election (calls were made beginning Nov 7, 2020 as vote counts in key states were completed). There is no credible evidence that MSNBC announced Donald Trump won the 2020 election; claims otherwise stem from misinformation or misinterpretation of isolated clips.

claim: "Too many" tattoos "on visible body parts" keep some applicants out of the military.
rationale: Many military branches have explicit limits on the number, size, or location of visible tattoos (especially on the face, neck, hands, and forearms), and applicants who exceed those limits have been denied enlistment, required to obtain waivers, or asked to cover or remove tattoos. Media reports and enlistment guidance show that excessive visible tattoos can and do keep some applicants out of service or delay their entry.

claim: Emails show that Fauci knew "hydroxychloroquine worked [and] emailed friends about it being effective."
rationale: FOIA‑released Fauci emails show he circulated early anecdotal reports and discussed uncertainties about hydroxychloroquine, but they do not show him asserting that it definitively 'worked' or privately telling friends it was effective. Publicly and in the emails he emphasized the need for rigorous trials, and subsequent randomized trials found no clear clinical benefit.

claim: "13 percent of Americans, the lowest ever, are without health care."
rationale: The statement is incorrect as phrased: the U.S. uninsured rate has been below 13% in multiple recent years after the Affordable Care Act, with surveys showing rates around 8–10% in the latter 2010s and early 2020s. Saying 13% is the "lowest ever" contradicts official survey series (NHIS/CPS/Gallup) that recorded lower uninsured percentages.

claim: Says "we brought crime rate down by 30 percent" when he was mayor of Dallas.
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it omits who "he" is and the timeframe; no well-documented, attributable claim that a Dallas mayor produced an across-the-board 30% drop in the overall crime rate is supported by widely available crime-data summaries. Crime rates vary by category and year, and credible verification would require the mayor's name, the exact period, and the specific crime metric. Without those details or a reliable source, the assertion cannot be accepted as factual.

claim: Photo shows a Chinese restaurant sign that says "F--- DeSantis."
rationale: I cannot verify the pictured sign from the claim and there are no reliably reported instances confirming a Chinese restaurant legitimately posted a profanity-directed sign at a specific time and place. Viral images with explicit political profanity are frequently digitally altered or miscaptioned, and businesses generally avoid putting profanity on storefront signage. Without the original photo, provenance, or independent news verification, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Texas has lost the most law enforcement officers in the line of duty of any state in America."
rationale: Multiple compilations of line-of-duty deaths (most notably the Officer Down Memorial Page and historical law-enforcement tallies) show Texas has the largest cumulative number of law-enforcement fatalities of any U.S. state, reflecting its large population, long history, and number of agencies. This statement is about total historical losses rather than per-capita rates.

claim: "The Social Security disability fund is going belly up in 2016."
rationale: The Social Security Disability Insurance (DI) trust fund was not universally declared to "go belly up" in 2016. While trustees and analysts warned in the mid-2010s of a funding shortfall for DI, annual Trustees reports and congressional actions showed exhaustion timelines could change and that exhaustion would trigger automatic benefit reductions rather than an immediate cessation of payments.

claim: Under Gov. Scott Walker, "unemployment is increasing in Wisconsin at twice the rate it is nationally."
rationale: The statement is not supported by labor-market data for Gov. Scott Walker's tenure. Overall, Wisconsin's unemployment rate generally fell during Walker's years in office and did not show a sustained increase at twice the national rate; short-term month-to-month fluctuations do not establish the broad claim as stated.

claim: "Rep. Robert Hurt voted again today to end Medicare and raise health care costs for Virginia seniors."
rationale: The statement is misleading: no single recent House vote has 'ended Medicare' and the program remains law. While Rep. Robert Hurt voted with GOP measures that sought to restructure or reduce federal health spending, those votes do not literally abolish Medicare and claims that they directly 'raise health care costs for Virginia seniors' require a specific bill and evidence.

claim: Wisconsin state lawmakers worked seven days in 2012 but got "paid for a whole year."
rationale: The claim mischaracterizes how state legislators are paid and what counts as work. Wisconsin lawmakers are salaried officials with duties year‑round (constituent services, committee meetings, interim work, and conference committees) and the Legislature held more than a handful of official activities in 2012; they are paid on an annual salary basis rather than only for days physically on the chamber floor. Saying they “worked seven days but got paid for a whole year” is misleading and inaccurate.

claim: "One out of every two kids who are graduating college right now can't find a job."
rationale: Contemporary labor statistics do not support a 50% joblessness rate for new college graduates. Unemployment rates for people with bachelor’s degrees are typically in the low single digits to low teens for recent grads, and even broader measures of underemployment are generally reported in the ~20–40% range, far below one out of two.

claim: "Thirty years ago we were the most college-educated country on the globe. Today we are No. 11."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not supported by commonly used international measures of tertiary (college) attainment. While the U.S. ranked near the top for percent of adults with postsecondary education in the 1980s–1990s, it was not unambiguously 'the most' by every measure, and over the past decades many countries (e.g., Canada, Japan, South Korea, Israel and several EU states) have caught up or passed the U.S., so a present-day rank of exactly No. 11 is unsupported without a specified metric and source.

claim: "All evidence points to the fact that our kids are 17 times more likely to have ill effects from the seasonal flu than they are from the coronavirus."
rationale: This claim is not supported by the totality of evidence. Surveillance data and peer-reviewed studies do not show a consistent 17-fold lower risk of pediatric illness from SARS-CoV-2 compared with seasonal influenza; in many periods COVID-19 produced similar or higher pediatric hospitalization and complication rates (including MIS-C) than influenza. The specific '17 times' figure appears unsubstantiated and ignores variation by age, variant, vaccination, and timeframe.

claim: They passed the flu off as COVID-19, and "they’re going to do the same thing with monkeypox and shingles."
rationale: There is no evidence that public health authorities deliberately 'passed the flu off as COVID-19'—influenza and COVID-19 are caused by different viruses, have distinct tests, and surveillance systems distinguish them.
