claim: "If Joe Manchin had his way, Judge Gorsuch never would have been able to get a vote."
rationale: This is false: Senator Joe Manchin did not want to prevent a vote on Neil Gorsuch and ultimately voted to confirm him. Also, a single senator could not have unilaterally stopped the Senate majority from changing rules or holding a confirmation vote in 2017.

claim: Obamacare has led to fewer health insurance options for millions of Americans.
rationale: Implementation of the Affordable Care Act coincided with large-scale insurer market changes: many insurers exited or reduced offerings in some counties and millions of individual-market plans that did not meet ACA rules were cancelled, resulting in fewer choices for sizable numbers of consumers. While the ACA also created new options (exchange plans, Medicaid expansion) for others, the net effect in multiple local markets was a reduction in insurers or plan choices for millions.

claim: "Suntrust Bank cancels account because company sells guns."
rationale: The statement presents a specific causal claim but provides no named company, date, or verifiable evidence. There is no widely reported, documented instance showing SunTrust (now merged into Truist) cancelled an account solely because a customer sold guns; banks do sometimes close merchant accounts for compliance or risk reasons, but that is not the same as the asserted categorical action.

claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written because it refers to ‘this election’ without identifying which election or providing any metrics (vote margin, turnout, recounts, seat changes) to determine closeness. Without specifying the election and comparing its margin to historical norms or statistical measures of competitiveness, the claim cannot be verified. Therefore I treat the blanket assertion as false due to lack of evidence.

claim: Quotes actor Will Smith as saying: "I’m not afraid to say that Trump and his supporters are ba…"
rationale: There is no record in reputable news outlets, interview transcripts, or verified social media accounts attributing this quote to Will Smith; the snippet appears to circulate on unverified platforms and is likely a fabrication or misattribution. Public figures' explicit political statements are typically documented, and this exact phrasing cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says Andrew Gillum is running "from the FBI."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Andrew Gillum is literally "running from the FBI." While he has been the subject of federal scrutiny reported in news coverage, public records and major reporting up to mid‑2024 do not show he has been charged with federal crimes or documented as evading investigators; the phrase appears to be partisan rhetoric rather than a factual account.

claim: The Chamber of Commerce says new carbon regulations will kill "244,000 jobs a year" and cost average families "$1,200 a year."
rationale: I cannot confirm the U.S. Chamber of Commerce made that precise standalone claim; similar headline figures (hundreds of thousands of jobs lost and roughly $1,000+ per household) have appeared in media but typically originate from model-based studies the Chamber cited and depend on specific scenarios and assumptions. Presenting the two numbers as an unqualified Chamber statement omits caveats about timeframes, policy scope, and modeling methodology, so the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: "Alabama’s Crimson Tide was disqualified from national championship."
rationale: There is no record that the University of Alabama's 'Crimson Tide' was broadly disqualified from a national championship; the football program has won multiple recognized national titles and has not been barred from championship competition in recent history. The claim provides no year or sport, and no major governing body has announced such a disqualification.

claim: Says the Obama administration plans to ban all weapons for U.S. citizens through international treaties.
rationale: There is no credible evidence the Obama administration had a plan to ban all weapons for U.S. citizens via international treaties. The administration participated in UN negotiations on an Arms Trade Treaty aimed at regulating international arms transfers, not confiscating private firearms, and any treaty affecting U.S. law would require Senate ratification and would face constitutional limits.

claim: "When Nancy Nusbaum was Brown County executive, spending went up nearly 50 percent."
rationale: Public budget records and contemporary reporting do not support a nearly 50% rise in county spending during Nancy Nusbaum's tenure. While Brown County's budgets grew in some years, the increase is substantially smaller when using consistent measures (operating budget, adjusted for inflation, and excluding one‑time capital or pass‑through funds); the 50% figure appears to overstate or cherry‑pick categories or timeframes.

claim: Text from someone "connected" to Raleigh police: "antifa may be heading into the wealthy neighborhoods tonight to take what should be theirs."
rationale: There is no reliable public evidence that an authenticated text from someone officially connected to Raleigh police said that "antifa may be heading into the wealthy neighborhoods tonight to take what should be theirs." Such messages have circulated on social media as unverified claims and lack corroboration from Raleigh police press releases or credible news reporting. Given the absence of sourcing and the common pattern of rumor-spreading in these cases, the claim is best treated as false until verified.

claim: Says the CEO of Camping World told Trump supporters "Frankly, don’t shop at my business."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record of the CEO of Camping World making the exact statement "Frankly, don’t shop at my business." While Marcus Lemonis (CEO of Camping World) has publicly criticized Donald Trump and expressed opposition to Trump supporters on social media at times, reputable contemporaneous sources do not substantiate that exact quoted line as an attributable direct quote.

claim: Says Texas voters are being asked to act this November on a proposed constitutional amendment affecting property taxes.
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and provides no year or specific measure; I cannot confirm that a proposed constitutional amendment affecting property taxes is on the ballot 'this November.' Texas constitutional amendments appear only if the Legislature approved a joint resolution and the measure was placed on a specific election ballot, so the claim cannot be verified as stated.

claim: The United States paid for a 274-mile wall between Jordan and Syria, "approved by the Dems in the house and senate," in order "to keep ISIS out."
rationale: There is no evidence the United States wholly paid for a continuous 274-mile wall between Jordan and Syria that was explicitly "approved by the Dems in the house and senate." Jordan constructed border barriers and fortifications along parts of the Syrian frontier beginning in the mid-2010s, and the U.S. provided limited security assistance, equipment, and training to Jordan and to coalition partners, but did not fund or build a single 274-mile U.S.-paid wall solely to "keep ISIS out." The claim conflates Jordanian construction, partial U.S. assistance, and partisan approval language inaccurately.

claim: Says the U.S. Department of Justice has "seen in the past" that police department "consent decrees don’t work, that there’s very little change, that oftentimes immediately after a consent decree goes into effect, crime actually goes up."
rationale: The Department of Justice has not issued a blanket finding that police consent decrees “don’t work” or that crime regularly rises immediately after they take effect. DOJ’s Civil Rights Division has overseen many consent decrees and in multiple cases reported measurable reforms in practices and training; empirical studies of crime trends after decrees are mixed and show no consistent, uniform increase caused by decrees. The claim overstates and generalizes outcomes that in practice vary by jurisdiction and context.

claim: Says "47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’ in Antrim County (that switched 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden in that county)" and votes in the state are "potentially fraudulent."
rationale: This is false. Michigan state and county election officials and independent fact‑checks concluded the Antrim problem was an isolated reporting/configuration and human‑error issue in that county’s tabulation process, not a malicious software swap of 6,000 votes, and statewide audits/recounts found no evidence of widespread fraud. The statement that 47 additional counties “used the same software” conflates different vendor products and uses; those counties did not experience the same error or altered results.

claim: Sarah Palin was repeating "Abraham Lincoln's words" in discussing the war in Iraq.
rationale: There is no clear record or reliable fact‑check showing Sarah Palin verbatim repeating a known Abraham Lincoln quote while discussing the Iraq war. Palin has used familiar patriotic language and occasional historical references, but claims that she was "repeating Abraham Lincoln's words" in that context appear to be unsubstantiated or based on loose paraphrase rather than a direct Lincoln quotation.

claim: After merging with Tim Hortons of Canada, Burger King is "not moving. … Our headquarters will remain in Miami" and "(we) will continue to pay all of our federal, state and local U.S. taxes."
rationale: While Burger King executives publicly said the company was "not moving" and that its operational headquarters would remain in Miami and that it would continue to pay U.S. taxes, the merger created Restaurant Brands International, legally domiciled in Canada. That corporate inversion changed the legal headquarters and tax domicile, reducing the parent company's U.S. tax exposure even though U.S. subsidiaries continued to pay taxes on U.S. income.

claim: "Human meat found in McDonald’s meat factory"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that human meat was found in a McDonald’s meat factory. McDonald’s uses regulated suppliers subject to inspections and testing, and any discovery of human remains in the food supply would have prompted major official investigations and widespread coverage, which did not occur. The claim matches common hoax patterns and has been debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: "Even today part of Romney’s fortune is invested in China."
rationale: Romney's wealth historically has been held in diversified private equity funds and mutual funds (notably Bain-related vehicles) that have had international exposure, including holdings or stakes in companies with operations in China. Public disclosures and reporting over multiple election cycles have noted that parts of his portfolio are invested in firms that do business in or have subsidiaries in China, so it is plausible that some of his fortune remains exposed to China.

claim: "99 percent of all new income today (is) going to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. While researchers (e.g., Saez and Zucman) have documented short periods in which the top 1% captured the vast majority of income gains in the U.S. recovery years, the share of 'new income' going to the top 1% varies by time window, country, and whether one measures pre-tax, post-tax, or household income, and is not universally 99% 'today.'

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott is "spending a quarter of a million of our tax dollars to robocall people."
rationale: The claim asserts Gov. Rick Scott is spending $250,000 of tax dollars on robocalls, but there is no clear, corroborated evidence tying a specific $250,000 taxpayer-funded robocall program to Scott for political purposes. Public records and prior fact-checking show state offices sometimes pay for constituent outreach calls for official business, while campaign robocalls are paid from campaign funds; conflating the two would be misleading. Without a specific time, contract, or spending record showing a quarter-million in taxpayer-funded political robocalls, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Due to the recent downturn in steel production, more than 13,600 Americans have been laid off and the steel industry is facing billions in losses."
rationale: The claim bundles two specific quantitative assertions without a cited source or timeframe. Public reporting on recent U.S. steel layoffs shows company- and plant-level reductions but does not support a documented, aggregated total of 'more than 13,600 Americans' laid off tied to a single recent downturn, and while the industry can incur multi‑billion dollar impacts, that broad statement is unverified as presented.

claim: Says the government has "gotten the TARP money back plus a profit."
rationale: On a cash/official Treasury accounting basis the government ultimately recovered the bulk of TARP disbursements and reported a modest net gain once repayments, interest, dividends and asset sales were counted. However, independent analyses using fair‑value accounting (such as CBO estimates) have treated market valuation changes differently and concluded the program showed a small net cost, so the accuracy of the plain claim depends on the accounting method used.

claim: "One of the most troubling aspects of the Rubio-Schumer Gang of Eight bill was that it gave President Obama blanket authority to admit refugees, including Syrian refugees, without mandating any background checks whatsoever."
rationale: The 2013 'Gang of Eight' immigration bill (S.744) addressed immigration reform and legalization pathways but did not grant President Obama blanket authority to admit refugees without checks. Refugee admissions are governed by the Refugee Act of 1980 and existing interagency procedures (State, DHS, FBI, intelligence) require security and background vetting. The bill did not eliminate those statutory vetting requirements.

claim: "The EPA has tried to define a puddle or a drainage ditch on your farm to be navigable waters and thus subject to massive environmental regulations."
rationale: This claim is an exaggeration. EPA and the Army Corps have at times proposed WOTUS definitions that could bring some ephemeral streams, ditches, or puddle-like features under federal jurisdiction if they have a demonstrable connection or "significant nexus" to traditional navigable waters, but they have not sought to categorically treat every puddle or every farm drainage ditch as navigable waters subject to broad federal regulation. Court decisions (e.g., Rapanos) and subsequent rules and guidance have limited and clarified jurisdiction, and many ordinary, isolated puddles and ditches are excluded or require site-specific analysis.

claim: "The state's unemployment rate is fifth-highest in the country, a full point above the nationwide rate and higher than all of our...neighboring states."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it omits which state and the time period; state unemployment rankings and the national rate change monthly. Without a specific state and date, the assertion that it is fifth-highest, exactly one percentage point above the national rate, and higher than all neighboring states cannot be confirmed. Because key contextual details are missing, the claim should be treated as unsubstantiated.

claim: "You didn't see Republicans when we had control of the Senate try to rig the game."
rationale: This claim is false because Senate Republicans enacted high-profile procedural actions while in control of the Senate that critics described as changing the rules to their advantage. Notable examples include refusing in 2016 to hold hearings or a vote on President Obama's Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland and using the 2017 'nuclear option' to eliminate the filibuster for Supreme Court and other nominations to facilitate confirmation of Neil Gorsuch and other judges.

claim: Says Mitt Romney’s investments created zero jobs.
rationale: The absolute claim that Mitt Romney’s investments created zero jobs is inaccurate. Romney co‑founded and led Bain Capital, whose portfolio included companies that both expanded and hired workers as well as firms that cut jobs; independent reporting and analyses document instances of job creation in some Bain investments. Therefore it is incorrect to assert uniformly that his investments created no jobs.

claim: "Yesterday afternoon the Republicans in the General Assembly used the nuclear option to pass North Carolina's over $20 billion budget."
rationale: I cannot verify that "yesterday" Republicans in the North Carolina General Assembly used a "nuclear option" to pass a >$20 billion budget. My training data through June 2024 contains no record of such a time-specific action, and the phrase "nuclear option" normally refers to changing Senate filibuster rules at the federal level rather than a routine state budget vote. Without contemporaneous local reporting or documentation, the claim is unverified and likely false.

claim: "Phony" ballots "were printed without my name on it."
rationale: The statement is presented without any supporting specifics (who, which election, where, or when) and cannot be independently verified as true. Allegations that ballots were printed without a particular person's name require concrete evidence such as audited ballot inventories, chain-of-custody records, or credible investigative reporting; none is provided here, so the claim is not substantiated.

claim: Amanda Murphy has "two vacation homes around the world."
rationale: There is no reliable public reporting, property record evidence, or official financial disclosure documentation indicating that Amanda Murphy owns two vacation homes 'around the world.' In the absence of verifiable sources linking her to multiple international vacation properties, the specific claim is unsubstantiated and should be treated as false.

claim: Says it was "a crime for Nixon to wiretap the Democrats at Watergate but OK for Obama to wiretap Republicans at Trump Tower."
rationale: Nixon's administration carried out illegal wiretaps and related crimes at Watergate, which led to investigations and convictions. There is no credible evidence that President Obama ordered a wiretap of Trump Tower or that such an order was legally authorized as a blanket surveillance of Trump Tower; DOJ Inspector General and other reviews found no proof Obama directed such wiretapping and any surveillance that occurred was conducted under FISA targeting specified individuals. Thus the claim that Nixon's wiretaps were criminal but Obama's were 'OK' is unsupported.

claim: Says Democrats "have issued more subpoenas than they’ve passed bills."
rationale: The statement is a broad, context-free claim that is unlikely to be true: across recent Congresses Democrats (as a party) have sponsored and passed dozens to hundreds of bills in chambers they controlled, while the number of subpoenas issued by Democratic committees in any comparable period is typically smaller. The claim also conflates different measures (bills passed vs. subpoenas issued) and lacks a defined timeframe or chamber, making it misleading as a general assertion.

claim: The transportation sales tax would cost the average consumer an estimated $112 a year.
rationale: The statement is presented without any jurisdiction, time period, tax rate, or source; cost to an 'average consumer' depends on the specific tax rate and the region's average taxable spending. Such a precise figure ($112/year) could be accurate for a particular local proposal and set of assumptions, but cannot be verified as a general fact without the supporting analysis. Because the claim lacks context and sourcing, it cannot be affirmed.

claim: "30,000 Arizonans may have no choice" on Affordable Care Act coverage.
rationale: The claim is presented without a date, source, or context and cannot be verified as a current, factual figure. Enrollment and insurer participation on ACA exchanges fluctuate year to year, and while some Arizonans have limited insurer choices at times, an unsupported precise number like 30,000 cannot be confirmed from general knowledge alone. Without a cited official estimate (state insurance filings or CMS data) this specific claim is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: The health care bill "cuts the deficit by over $1 trillion dollars."
rationale: The statement is misleading without specifying which bill and time frame. Major recent U.S. health‑care legislation (notably the Affordable Care Act) was scored by the Congressional Budget Office and Joint Committee on Taxation as reducing the federal deficit by a few hundred billion dollars over a ten‑year window, not by over $1 trillion. No widely cited official score supports a >$1 trillion deficit reduction on standard 10‑year CBO scoring for those bills.

claim: "2 million rounds of ammo that ‘went missing’ under Obama turns up in enemy hands"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that exactly “2 million rounds” that went missing under President Obama were later recovered in enemy hands. Reporting and fact-checking around the period documented isolated incidents of diverted weapons and munitions in Libya, Afghanistan and other theaters, but not a verified single transfer of 2 million rounds from U.S. stocks to hostile forces.

claim: Says she couldn't take stimulus money because it required "universal building codes."
rationale: There is no evidence that federal stimulus programs broadly required jurisdictions to adopt a single "universal building code" as a condition of receiving funds. While some targeted federal grants (especially disaster-mitigation programs) set minimum standards or favor jurisdictions with codes in place, that is not the same as a blanket requirement that recipients adopt a specific universal code.

claim: Since Sept. 11, 2001, "270,000 Americans were killed by gunfire at home."
rationale: There is no authoritative source that confirms the precise figure of 270,000 'killed by gunfire at home' since Sept. 11, 2001. CDC mortality data show total firearm deaths in the U.S. since 2001 are substantially higher than 270,000, while the subset that occurred at home depends on location coding and inclusion of suicides, so the claim as stated is unsupported and misleading without a clear definition or source.

claim: "Attorney General McCollum, Speaker-Designate Cannon, Senate President-Designate Haridopolos and I stood up to Governor Crist and worked to remove Jim Greer as Chairman because of his mismanagement of the party."
rationale: Jim Greer was forced out as Florida Republican Party chairman amid allegations of financial mismanagement and internal disputes, and senior Florida Republicans including Attorney General Bill McCollum, House Speaker-designate Dean Cannon and Senate President-designate Mike Haridopolos publicly pushed for his removal and backed legal/organizational steps to remove him. Contemporary news coverage and party statements show these leaders broke with or pressured other state officials, including Governor Charlie Crist, in the dispute over Greer’s leadership.

claim: Says a photo shows a white man smiling while holding a black man with a bloody face.
rationale: I cannot verify the described photo because no image, source, or corroborating context is provided; without seeing the photo and its provenance the claim is unverified. Viral images are frequently miscaptioned, doctored, or presented out of context, so asserting the description as fact is unsupported. To substantiate it would require the original image, metadata, and independent verification from reliable sources.

claim: Says a photo shows a memorial vandalized by Black Lives Matter protesters.
rationale: A standalone photo cannot by itself establish who committed an act; it only shows damage, not the perpetrators. Numerous prior cases have shown images of vandalized memorials misattributed to Black Lives Matter without corroborating evidence such as timestamps, geolocation, video, or credible witness/official reports. Absent independent verification tying the vandalism to BLM, the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Texas ranks 49th nationally in "what we are doing to support our per-pupil investment in education in the state."
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated national dataset that consistently places Texas 49th in overall per‑pupil investment; major sources (U.S. Census, NCES, Education Week analyses) typically put Texas in the lower tier but not usually as low as 49th. Rankings vary by year and by metric (total per‑pupil spending, state share, or inflation‑adjusted spending), so a blanket claim of 49th is unsupported without a specific source and measure.

claim: "The stock market does better when you have a Democratic president in the White House."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While some historical analyses show that major indexes (like the S&P 500) have on average posted higher returns during Democratic presidencies over certain multi-decade periods, results depend strongly on the chosen time window, index, start/end dates and are driven by many economic and global factors—so there is no robust causal rule that the market 'does better' simply because a Democrat is president.

claim: Says Tammy Baldwin supports a law "in which government will take over your decisions on medicine, on doctors and on hospitals."
rationale: This is a partisan exaggeration. Tammy Baldwin has supported expanding public health coverage (and has at times backed single‑payer or stronger federal roles in financing), but she has not advocated for a law that literally hands the government control of individual medical decisions, doctors, and hospitals. Opponents commonly describe public insurance proposals as a 'government takeover,' which is rhetorical rather than an accurate statement of policy mechanics.

claim: Say video "shows massive alligator strolling across Florida golf course."
rationale: There is no provided video, source, metadata, or independent reporting to confirm that the clip actually shows a massive alligator on a Florida golf course. While large alligators do occasionally appear on Florida golf courses, viral clips are frequently miscaptioned or taken elsewhere, so the claim cannot be verified as presented.

claim: "The number of people who just got their voting rights restored in Florida is greater than the populations of Wyoming, Vermont, Alaska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Delaware, Rhode Island, Montana, Maine and New Hampshire."
rationale: The widely reported estimate of people whose voting rights were restored by Florida's Amendment 4 is roughly 1.4 million. Each of the listed states (Wyoming, Vermont, Alaska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Delaware, Rhode Island, Montana, Maine, and New Hampshire) has a population under about 1.4 million, so the restored-rights total exceeds each state's population individually.

claim: The planned expansion of Savannah’s port is a "jobs creating project."
rationale: Port expansion projects like Savannah’s (dredging, added berths and terminal improvements) are routinely projected and designed to create construction jobs during building and additional long‑term jobs through increased cargo throughput, logistics, and related business activity. Official plans and economic studies for Savannah’s expansions have explicitly cited job creation as a principal benefit, though the exact number and permanence of jobs can be debated.

claim: "In the last several months, the Biden administration has released over 7,000 illegal aliens who were COVID positive just in one Texas city." Biden's border policies are "endangering not just the people of Texas, but people all across the country."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public-health data showing that the Biden administration released over 7,000 COVID-positive migrants into a single Texas city in the last several months. Independent fact-checkers and available DHS/HHS/local health records do not support the specific numeric claim, and officials have denied any policy of mass release of known COVID-positive individuals. The follow-up statement that the policy is "endangering" people is a political judgment not established as an empirically proven consequence by the cited numeric claim.

claim: As a senator, Hillary Clinton "has her name on three laws in eight years."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated: independent fact-checkers and congressional records indicate Senator Clinton had her name on more than three laws during her eight years in the Senate when one counts measures she sponsored or cosponsored that became law. The exact tally depends on whether one counts only bills where she was the primary sponsor or also includes cosponsored bills and amendments, but in any common counting method the number exceeds three.

claim: "California has more kids in poverty ... than virtually any other state."
rationale: Interpreted as the absolute number of children living in poverty, California typically has the largest count because it is the nation's most populous state and Census/ACS data show California leads other states in number of children below the poverty threshold. This does not mean California has the highest child poverty rate, which is higher in several smaller states.

claim: Says the WIC program was created by the Black Panthers to help feed single mothers and children in their communities.
rationale: The WIC program (Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children) was established by the U.S. federal government via legislation and federal agencies in the early 1970s, not created by the Black Panther Party. While the Black Panthers ran community food and free breakfast programs that highlighted hunger and pressured policymakers, they did not found or officially create the federal WIC program.

claim: "There's no such thing as a lone wolf. ... That was a phrase invented by the last administration to make Americans stupid."
rationale: The phrase "lone wolf" long predates any recent U.S. administration and has been used for decades in criminology, journalism, and counterterrorism to describe individuals who act independently. There is no evidence that a recent administration "invented" the term or that it was coined as a deliberate tactic to "make Americans stupid," which is a conspiratorial claim without supporting documentation.

claim: "In America, there is a father who is holding down two jobs and paying more taxes than the richest 400 families in America."
rationale: No credible data supports that a single father working two jobs pays more in taxes than the richest 400 families in the U.S.; the 400 wealthiest families together (and typically individually) pay very large amounts of federal taxes according to IRS and public analyses, far exceeding what a single low- or middle-income earner could owe. The claim is implausible on its face given the scale of incomes and tax payments at the very top of the distribution.

claim: Ron Johnson didn’t "show up" for a day of impeachment hearings.
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated — it gives no date, which impeachment, or what is meant by "show up." Attendance at congressional hearings is a matter of public record (roll calls, video, and transcripts), so a blanket assertion that Ron Johnson skipped "a day of impeachment hearings" cannot be confirmed without those specifics and is therefore unsupported as presented.

claim: Vaccines "will remove parts of your DNA and replace it with GENETIC CODING (TECHNOLOGY)" that will "cause people to HAVE to cooperate with the New World Order."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that approved vaccines remove parts of human DNA or insert 'genetic coding' that would control behavior. mRNA vaccines deliver transient RNA that does not enter the cell nucleus or integrate into the genome, and common vaccine platforms are designed to stimulate immune responses, not alter genes. The claim that vaccines would compel political obedience (e.g., 'cooperate with the New World Order') is a conspiracy theory with no biological mechanism or evidence.

claim: Says Baltimore police are "trained by Mossad and Shin Bet."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Baltimore Police Department is trained by Israel’s foreign intelligence service (Mossad) or its internal security agency (Shin Bet). While some U.S. law-enforcement agencies have at times participated in exchanges or received training from Israeli police or private contractors, intelligence services like Mossad and Shin Bet do not run routine training programs for local U.S. police departments.

claim: "This Is Real: Biden Waves To An Empty Field."
rationale: The statement asserts as fact that Biden waved to an empty field but provides no date, location, or verifiable source. Without the original footage or corroborating reporting it is not possible to confirm the scene was truly empty — camera angle, cropping, timing, or misleading captions can make crowds invisible. Because the claim is unverified and easily misrepresentable, it should not be treated as established fact.

claim: "When the president's spokesman was asked about (Anwar) al-Awlaki's son, … he said he should have chosen a more responsible father."
rationale: I cannot find reliable evidence that a "president's spokesman" said the quoted line; contemporary White House press statements about Anwar al-Awlaki and his son expressed concern or called the deaths tragic rather than using the flippant phrase attributed here. The reported quote appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase that exaggerates or invents the spokesman's wording.

claim: "6,400 Ohioans ... lost manufacturing jobs in the month of September."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not specify which September or cite a source; monthly manufacturing employment figures are published by the BLS and Ohio labor agencies and vary by year. Without a specific month/year and supporting official data, the claim cannot be confirmed and should be treated as false.

claim: "Without a shred of clinical data to support its decision, the Biden Administration has revoked the emergency use authorization for lifesaving monoclonal antibody treatments."
rationale: The FDA did limit or revoke EUAs for certain monoclonal antibody treatments when they were found to be ineffective against dominant SARS‑CoV‑2 variants, but the actions were explicitly based on laboratory neutralization data and variant surveillance showing loss of activity, not made with no supporting data. Regulators cited in vitro studies and genomic surveillance indicating the treatments would not work against Omicron and similar variants when making EUA changes.

claim: "Biden took down Dr. Seuss and Mr. Potato Head."
rationale: The withdrawals were corporate decisions, not actions taken by President Biden. Dr. Seuss Enterprises chose in 2021 to cease publication of six titles for racist imagery, and Hasbro announced a 2020 rebrand around Mr. Potato Head; there is no evidence the Biden administration ordered or carried out these removals.

claim: Newt Gingrich "has suggested" building "a mirror system in space" could improve the Earth’s habitability.
rationale: Newt Gingrich publicly proposed space-based geoengineering ideas during his political commentary and 2012–2016-era remarks, including suggesting a system of mirrors or reflectors in space as a way to alter sunlight and thereby affect conditions on Earth. Media reports and transcripts of interviews record him raising the concept as one of possible technological options to change or improve habitability.

claim: President Obama has "the worst ratings of any president at the end of his first year."
rationale: This claim is not true as stated. Historical presidential approval data (e.g., Gallup tracking since 1938) show that several presidents had lower approval ratings at the end of their first year in office than Barack Obama did, so Obama did not have the worst first‑year ratings of any president.

claim: "Chick-fil-A now open Sunday (Blacks only)."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Chick-fil-A implemented a policy of opening on Sundays only for Black customers. Chick-fil-A historically kept most restaurants closed on Sundays and any race‑exclusive policy would be illegal under U.S. civil rights laws and would have generated major national news, which it has not.

claim: Says the Obama Administration has fulfilled all of Texas’ requests for fire management assisting grants.
rationale: Federal fire-management grants (such as FEMA’s Fire Management Assistance Grants) are reviewed and approved case-by-case rather than automatically fulfilled. Public practice during the Obama years shows approvals, denials, or modifications depending on incident eligibility and documentation, so it is unlikely the administration fulfilled every single Texas request. The absolute claim that all requests were fulfilled is therefore false.

claim: Says Judge Gonzalo Curiel "is a member of a club or society, very strongly pro-Mexican."
rationale: Donald Trump publicly made statements in 2016 criticizing Judge Gonzalo Curiel and said essentially that Curiel "is a member of a club or society, very strongly pro-Mexican," arguing the judge would be biased in the Trump University litigation. Major news outlets and fact-checkers reported and quoted this phrasing or close paraphrases at the time.

claim: Says "11 straight years of no major hurricanes striking land" in the United States "bores a hole right through the whole climate change argument."
rationale: While the U.S. did experience a noted stretch (roughly 2006–2016) without a Category 3+ hurricane making U.S. landfall, that single regional, short-term observation does not invalidate the scientific evidence for anthropogenic climate change. Climate change concerns long-term, global trends (temperature, ocean heat content, and changing storm intensity/precipitation patterns), and landfall frequency in one country over a decade is subject to natural variability and chance.

claim: The infant mortality rate is 15 percent higher in states with right-to-work laws.
rationale: The statement gives a precise 15% higher infant mortality in right-to-work states but there is no consensus or authoritative source establishing that exact effect. Research on right-to-work laws and health outcomes is mixed and effect sizes vary by study period, controls, and methodology, so the specific 15% claim is unsupported as a general fact.

claim: A map shows "all the cargo ships backed up by the Suez Canal. Get ready for shortages and prices to skyrocket."
rationale: A ship‑tracking map can show many vessels waiting near the Suez Canal but cannot reliably display 'all' cargo ships (AIS coverage gaps, different tracking services, and vessels that turned back or rerouted are omitted). While Suez blockages cause delays, higher freight rates, and sector‑specific supply problems, broad claims that shortages and prices will universally 'skyrocket' are speculative and not supported by evidence—economists expected some disruptions and cost increases but not guaranteed immediate, economy‑wide price spikes.

claim: "In the last five years only one out of 60 -- one out of 60 -- appropriations bills has been passed on time before the end of the fiscal year."
rationale: The claim is presented as an exact statistic but lacks a clear timeframe and is not supported by the public record: Congress frequently fails to enact all 12 regular appropriations bills by the fiscal-year deadline and instead uses continuing resolutions or omnibus packages, but specific five-year tallies vary and are not uniformly '1 out of 60.' Without a defined five‑year period and a consistent way of counting bundled omnibus bills, the precise 'one out of 60' figure is not reliable.

claim: "Not only is there no scientific evidence that CO2 is a pollutant, higher CO2 concentrations actually help ecosystems support more plant and animal life."
rationale: This claim is false because there is extensive scientific evidence that rising CO2 is a greenhouse gas driver of global warming and causes many harmful impacts (heat extremes, sea-level rise, ocean acidification, ecosystem disruption). Although higher CO2 can stimulate plant growth in some controlled or nutrient‑rich settings (the CO2 fertilization effect), those benefits are limited by nutrients, water, temperature stress, pests, and reduced crop nutritional quality and do not outweigh the broad ecological and societal harms of climate change.

claim: "The vast majority of our public school students are receiving less state support than their private voucher peers."
rationale: The claim lacks jurisdiction and a clear definition of “state support,” but as a general statement it is incorrect: in most U.S. states overall per‑pupil public funding (state + local + federal) is equal to or higher than typical voucher payments, and vouchers usually cover only a subset of students. Voucher programs tend to provide smaller, capped payments and serve limited numbers, so it is unlikely that a ‘vast majority’ of public school students receive less state support than private voucher recipients.

claim: "BIDEN: 'I'm not gonna take any questions because I think it's inappropriate.'"
rationale: I cannot verify that President Biden actually said that exact sentence. While Biden has frequently declined to take reporters' questions and has used similar language in various instances, there is no clear, sourced record provided here of this precise quotation, so the claim as stated is unverified and likely a paraphrase or misattribution.

claim: When Mitt Romney was governor of Massachusetts, "we didn’t just slow the rate of growth of our government, we actually cut it."
rationale: Romney did impose hiring freezes and some program cuts and slowed the growth of state government, but independent fact-checks and state budget data show the reductions were modest and dependent on accounting choices. Measured across common metrics (total state spending, overall employment adjusted for transfers and federal funds, or inflation), Massachusetts government did not show a clear, sustained net cut during his full tenure; the claim overstates the case.

claim: "What I have done -- and this is unprecedented ... is I've said to each agency ... 'look at regulations that are already on the books and if they don't make sense, let's get rid of them.'"
rationale: The speaker likely did direct agencies to review and remove regulations that 'don't make sense,' which is plausible, but the claim that this is 'unprecedented' is false. Prior presidents and administrations have routinely ordered regulatory reviews and deregulatory initiatives (via statutes and executive orders), so telling agencies to reexamine existing rules is not without precedent.

claim: Says new Medicare billing guidelines "have nine codes for (injuries by) turkeys."
rationale: There is no evidence that Medicare or the ICD‑10‑CM updates added exactly nine new, distinct billing codes specifically for 'injuries by turkeys.' While ICD‑10 includes external‑cause codes for animal encounters and encounter-type extensions (initial, subsequent, sequela), social posts exaggerate counts by counting repetitive encounter suffixes or conflating broader bird/animal codes. Official code sets and CMS/CDC guidance do not list nine unique turkey injury categories as a new standalone addendum.

claim: Says Obama replaced the American flag on the tail of his plane with his campaign logo.
rationale: Official presidential aircraft (Air Force One) retain U.S. national markings and the presidential seal; they were not rebranded with a campaign logo. Pictures circulating showing Obama’s campaign logo on the tail were digitally altered or depicted non-official campaign planes, not a replacement of the American flag on the presidential aircraft.

claim: "The State of Texas is funding … women’s health services at historically high levels; they just increased their level another $50 million for the next two years."
rationale: The claim mixes a vague, subjective assertion (“historically high levels”) with a specific $50 million increase over two years but gives no program name or date. Based on public Texas budget processes and summaries available through mid-2024, there is no clear, verifiable appropriation that matches this precise $50 million two‑year increase earmarked generically for “women’s health services.” Without a named program, bill, or budget line, the claim cannot be substantiated as stated.

claim: Says an NBC producer at the Olympics was caught on a hot mic saying "60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days."
rationale: No credible news organizations or reputable fact-checkers reported an NBC producer making that claim on a hot mic at the Olympics, and the quote circulated only on social media without verifiable sourcing. Such an inflammatory statement would have generated widespread mainstream coverage and official responses but none exists, indicating the claim is false or misattributed.

claim: A provision of the Senate immigration bill would require you to have government permission to get a second job.
rationale: No major Senate immigration proposal has imposed a blanket requirement that U.S. citizens obtain government permission before taking a second job. Immigration bills commonly address work authorization for noncitizens, employer verification (e.g., E-Verify), or conditions on specific visa or benefit recipients, but they do not generally require government approval for citizens to take additional employment. The claim misstates typical provisions and conflates rules for noncitizens or program participants with a universal requirement for everyone.

claim: "98 percent of small businesses make less than $250,000" and would not see a tax increase under Barack Obama's plan.
rationale: The "98%" figure was based on a narrow White House framing that counted pass‑through business owners whose individual taxable income was under $250,000, not all firms or gross receipts. That framing excludes many C corporations and depends on how "small business" and "make" are defined, and some owners under $250k could still be affected by other tax changes. Because the claim collapses distinct concepts (business receipts/profits vs. owner taxable income) and overstates the guarantee of "no tax increase," it is misleading.

claim: "They found 60 votes in the Senate in 2006 and 2013" for immigration legislation, and "each time the House Republican majority refused to take it up."
rationale: The 2013 Senate bipartisan immigration bill (S.744) did exceed 60 votes (it passed 68-32), and the Republican House leadership declined to take it up. However, there was not a separate Senate tally in 2006 showing a 60-vote majority for comprehensive immigration reform—efforts in 2006 failed to reach cloture and no definitive 60‑vote Senate passage of a comprehensive bill occurred then. Because the 2006 part of the claim is incorrect, the overall statement is false.

claim: "(Obama's) entire national security team, including his secretary of state, said we want to arm and train and equip (Syrian rebel forces), and he made the unilateral decision to turn them down."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate and overly absolute. Public reporting and declassified material show Obama’s national security team was divided over arming Syrian opposition—some officials advocated limited support while others cautioned against it—and Obama did not simply 'unilaterally' reject a unanimous recommendation; the administration later authorized covert assistance and vetted training programs rather than an outright, one-time rejection of arming all rebels.

claim: "Bernie Sanders wants free health care for all and was asked how he would pay for it. His answer was raise taxes to 52% on anybody making over $29,000 per year."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has advocated for Medicare-for-All, but he did not propose a blanket 52% tax on anyone earning over $29,000. The specific '52% on incomes over $29k' figure arose from misinterpretations and modeling choices that combined existing payroll/employer health costs with new taxes and counted employer health contributions as taxable income; it is not a statement Sanders made as a policy. Independent fact-checkers and analyses have characterized that claim as misleading.

claim: "Yet, for all that spending, health outcomes today on Medicaid are mediocre and many patients have difficulty accessing care."
rationale: Empirical studies and health system data show Medicaid enrollees often have worse outcomes and lower access than the privately insured, and many patients report difficulty finding providers due to low reimbursement and limited provider participation. While Medicaid improves access and mortality compared with being uninsured, outcomes and access remain uneven and frequently described as suboptimal given the program's large spending.

claim: "Half of all CEOs say that the shutdown and the threat of shutdown set back their plans to hire over the next six months."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it gives no source and purports a precise majority of 'all CEOs.' I am not aware of a reputable, representative national poll showing half of all CEOs said a shutdown and its threat set back their hiring plans over the next six months; CEO survey findings on shutdown impacts have varied by sample, timing, and question wording.

claim: "Roy Cooper won't say how he will pay for ‘free’ college tuition."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad claim of refusal. Roy Cooper and his administration have put forward budget proposals and discussed funding approaches for higher-education initiatives; without a specific program, time, or quote, it is incorrect to assert categorically that he 'won't say' how he would pay for free tuition. Specific press moments may show limited detail, but the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: Says a "Clorox bottle claimed it could kill (the 2019 coronavirus)... before it was developed."
rationale: Claims that a Clorox bottle label explicitly stated it could kill the '2019 coronavirus' before the virus existed are false. The SARS‑CoV‑2 virus was identified in late 2019 and companies updated or clarified product claims in 2020; circulating images claiming an earlier date were altered or misinterpreted and were debunked by fact‑checking.

claim: Says Paul Manafort "played a very limited role" in the Trump presidential campaign.
rationale: Public reporting and campaign records show Paul Manafort served as a senior Trump campaign official in 2016 — he was elevated to campaign chairman and briefly campaign manager and oversaw strategy and delegate operations for several months before resigning in August 2016. Describing his role as "very limited" contradicts contemporary accounts that portray him as a central figure in campaign operations during that period.

claim: The House passed "cut, cap and balance" with "bipartisan support."
rationale: The 'Cut, Cap and Balance' legislation was passed by the House in 2011 largely along party lines and did not enjoy broad bipartisan backing. While a very small number of Democrats may have supported it, the measure was driven by Republican votes and is not accurately described as having bipartisan support.

claim: The Republican election platform "was actually written with the help of a former lobbyist for AIG and a former lobbyist for Exxon-Mobil."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that a Republican national election platform was expressly written with the assistance of a former AIG lobbyist and a former ExxonMobil lobbyist as a general fact. Platform drafts are created by party platform committees and many advisers and delegates, and while individuals with industry ties sometimes serve as advisers, the specific blanket claim is unverified and likely misleading without naming the year or individuals.

claim: George Soros was an SS officer.
rationale: This claim is false. George Soros was born in 1930 in Hungary and was a Jewish teenager during World War II who survived by using forged identity papers and living under assumed identities; he was not an SS officer. Biographies and Soros's own memoirs document his wartime experience and do not support any service in the Nazi SS.

claim: The number of people who have died in the U.S. in 2020 is on par with years prior to COVID-19.
rationale: Total U.S. deaths in 2020 were substantially higher than in the immediately preceding years due to the COVID-19 pandemic; CDC provisional and final mortality data and excess-death analyses show several hundred thousand more deaths in 2020 than in 2018–2019. Thus the statement that 2020 deaths were "on par" with prior years is incorrect.

claim: "The federal government spent over $500k trying to force fish to exercise on treadmills, an additional $150k to see if gingerbread houses are earthquake proof."
rationale: The claim states precise dollar amounts and frames two research or outreach projects as wasteful spending, but this is a misleading compression of disparate, often small or context-specific research grants. Federal agencies do fund studies using swim tunnels to study fish physiology and outreach/teaching demonstrations that have used model houses, but there is no clear, verifiable record that the federal government spent exactly over $500,000 to "force fish to exercise on treadmills" and an additional $150,000 specifically to test gingerbread houses for earthquake resistance as described. The amounts and characterizations appear exaggerated or taken out of context.

claim: There are about 120,000 solar energy jobs in the United States, but only 1,700 of them are in Georgia.
rationale: Recent industry counts (e.g., the Solar Jobs Census and SEIA reports) put U.S. solar employment well above 120,000 — typically in the ~200,000–255,000 range in recent years — so the national figure of about 120,000 is incorrect. Likewise, state-level data show Georgia employing several thousand solar workers, not just 1,700, so that state figure is also misleading or out of date.

claim: Says James Clapper "and virtually everyone else" said "there is no collusion" in the Russia investigation findings.
rationale: The Special Counsel's report said it did not establish criminal conspiracy or coordination, which is not the same as an absolute finding that 'there is no collusion.' While many commentators and officials (and likely James Clapper in public remarks) framed the report as showing 'no collusion,' the precise language and legal nuance in the report contradict a blanket assertion that everyone said there was no collusion. Therefore the claim as stated overgeneralizes and misstates the investigation's findings and how they were characterized.

claim: Oregon concealed gun applications include "home phone numbers, home address, Social Security numbers, what kinds of guns you have in the house … whether you were dishonorably discharged from the military, what controlled substances you are taking and  were you ever accused of -- accused, mind you -- of stalking."
rationale: Oregon concealed-handgun license applications do request personal identifying information (name, address, phone, and Social Security number) and ask about disqualifying factors such as dishonorable military discharge, unlawful use of controlled substances, and certain convictions or restraining orders. However, the form does not ask applicants to list what kinds of guns they have in the house, nor does it ask only about being "accused" of stalking — it asks about convictions or active prohibiting orders rather than mere accusations. Therefore the quoted claim mixes accurate items with incorrect or misleading items.

claim: Sen. Sherrod Brown "has chosen to side with Washington bureaucrats and fringe extremists in the attacks on our natural resources."
rationale: The statement is a broad, pejorative claim that Sherrod Brown has sided with 'Washington bureaucrats and fringe extremists' in attacks on natural resources, but it provides no specific incidents or evidence. Brown's public record as an Ohio Democratic senator shows long-standing support for environmental protections and conservation efforts rather than supporting attacks on natural resources. Without concrete examples tying him to such actors or actions, the claim is unsubstantiated and misleading.

claim: "In the past two years in Congress, I’ve written more bills, passed more amendments on the floor of the House and enacted more of my bills into law than any other member of the House."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as framed because it names no speaker or exact two‑year window and it is highly unlikely one member led all 435 members simultaneously on bills introduced, floor amendments passed, and bills enacted. Legislative records show these metrics are tracked separately and tend to be led by different members (e.g., committee chairs or leaders for floor amendments, senior/majority members for enacted laws). Without a specific identity and dates, the broad comparative claim cannot be verified and is implausible.

claim: Zoo animals were released during protests in Chicago.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that zoo animals were released during protests in Chicago. Lincoln Park Zoo and city officials publicly stated animals were secured and social-media claims that animals were freed were debunked by news outlets.

claim: "They talk about this problem with binding arbitration. It doesn’t make a lot of sense to me to have somebody from Los Angeles fly into Zanesville and impose a wage settlement on you ... and then they’re on the plane back to Los Angeles."
rationale: This is a subjective opinion about the wisdom of out‑of‑area arbitrators rather than an objectively verifiable factual claim. In practice binding arbitration routinely uses neutral arbitrators from outside the local area (and increasingly remote hearings), and their geographic origin alone does not invalidate or objectively make outcomes nonsensical.

claim: Says Mark Kirk "called for the mass arrest of 18,000 African Americans" and "was apparently fine with Trump’s #StillTooRacist call for mass deportation."
rationale: There is no credible record or mainstream reporting showing Senator Mark Kirk publicly called for the "mass arrest of 18,000 African Americans," nor evidence he explicitly endorsed a Trump call for mass deportation under the #StillTooRacist label. The allegation appears to be a misattribution or social‑media distortion rather than a documented quote or policy position by Kirk.

claim: Says 15,000 IRS employees "have to be added to administer ‘ObamaCare’ and look at the tax implications."
rationale: This overstates the IRS staffing requirement for the Affordable Care Act. The IRS did request additional resources to implement ACA provisions (such as premium tax credit administration and reporting), but public budget requests and independent analyses indicated staffing needs in the hundreds to low thousands for ACA tasks, not 15,000 hires explicitly to 'administer Obamacare.' The 15,000 number appears to be a mischaracterization or conflation with other IRS hiring plans.

claim: "Texas law enforcement officer fatally shot upon arriving for work by 3 Muslim refugee."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or official law-enforcement statements documenting a Texas officer being fatally shot upon arriving for work by three Muslim refugees. An event of that nature would be widely reported and verified by major outlets and police agencies; the absence of such coverage indicates the claim is fabricated or a misleading conflation of incidents.

claim: Says the U.S. government caused the coronavirus pandemic because it sent mRNA coronavirus vaccine candidates to university researchers weeks before the COVID-19 outbreak.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the U.S. government 'caused' the COVID‑19 pandemic by sending mRNA vaccine candidates to university researchers weeks before the outbreak. SARS‑CoV‑2 was first identified in late 2019 and its genome became publicly available in December 2019/January 2020; mRNA vaccine designs were made after the virus sequence was known and routine preexisting coronavirus research does not constitute a cause of the pandemic. The allegation conflates legitimate, long‑standing coronavirus research and material sharing with a causal action that is not supported by documented facts.

claim: Florida’s coastal and stormwater infrastructure are "two of the most critical areas during a storm, and received D-plus and D ratings, respectively, by the American Society of Civil Engineers in 2016."
rationale: I cannot confirm that the American Society of Civil Engineers assigned a D-plus to coastal infrastructure and a D to stormwater in 2016; ASCE issues report cards at national and state levels in different years and my available knowledge does not corroborate those exact 2016 grades. The phrase that they are “two of the most critical areas during a storm” is subjective and not a verifiable ASCE designation. Because the specific grade-year pairing is unverified, the claim as stated is likely incorrect or at least misleading.

claim: "Reporters rehearse questions with White House press (secretary)."
rationale: It is not standard practice for reporters to rehearse their questions with the White House press secretary; press briefings are meant to be unscripted Q&A and reporters maintain editorial independence. While White House staff may distribute written talking points, hold background briefings, or informally preview topics with some outlets, that is not the same as reporters rehearsing questions with the press secretary.

claim: Between 40 and 50 percent of tax filers do not owe any income tax.
rationale: Reputable analyses (e.g., Tax Policy Center and similar IRS/CBO summaries) show that in recent years roughly 40–50% of U.S. tax units or filers had zero federal income tax liability after accounting for deductions and refundable credits. The exact share varies by year and definition, but the central estimate frequently cited is about mid-40 percent, which falls in the 40–50% range.

claim: "More than 3 million young adults ... have gained insurance under (the Affordable Care Act) by staying on their family’s plan."
rationale: The ACA provision allowing dependents to remain on parental insurance until age 26 led to documented gains in coverage for young adults, with government and public-health analyses reporting that more than 3 million people in that age group obtained insurance through staying on a family plan in the early years after implementation. Multiple analyses (HHS, CDC summaries and CBO estimates) from 2010–2013 reported gains on the order of about 3.1 million young adults covered due to the policy.

claim: Kasim Reed has kept every promise he made as a candidate.
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that Kasim Reed kept every single campaign promise, which is extremely unlikely and contradicted by general reporting and oversight of his tenure. Reviews of Reed's mayoralty and subsequent ethics controversies indicate some promises and goals were not fully achieved or were undermined by scandals, so the universal claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says photo shows that Chick-fil-A distributed "Back the Blue" T-shirts to employees in response to recent protests over police brutality.
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checks and the lack of any corporate confirmation indicate the photo has been misattributed; it does not show a verified, company-wide Chick-fil-A distribution of 'Back the Blue' T-shirts in response to recent protests. Available reporting ties the image to a different event or an independently owned location rather than a corporate action.

claim: "Most of your serial killers, most of your people who commit domestic violence, they start off by abusing animals."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes. Research does show a correlation between childhood animal cruelty and later violent offending and many high-profile offenders have histories of animal abuse, but evidence does not support that a majority of all serial killers or a majority of all domestic violence perpetrators universally "start off" by abusing animals. Studies are often small, retrospective, or biased toward criminal samples, so the claim is too strong.

claim: Miami-Dade County is the "No. 1 donor county in the state."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as written because “donor county” can mean different things (net fiscal contributor to the state budget, donor of political contributions, per‑capita vs total dollars) and rankings change by metric and year. While Miami‑Dade, as the state's largest and wealthiest county, is often a major net contributor in many measures, there is no single, consistently maintained ranking that proves it is universally the “No. 1 donor county in the state.” Without a specified metric and timeframe the claim is not reliably supportable.

claim: In annual surveys of Rhode Island communities that receive Drug Free community grants, many report that more than 50 percent of youth surveyed do not think daily marijuana use poses any serious risk of harm.
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence that multiple Rhode Island Drug Free Communities grantees report annual survey results where a majority (>50%) of youth say daily marijuana use poses no serious risk. National and state youth surveys do show rising perceptions of lower risk for marijuana, but published data do not support the specific claim about many Rhode Island DFC communities having over 50% of youth endorsing ‘no serious risk.’

claim: "Wisconsin took a break, and when they returned, Biden coincidentally came back ahead by 100k."
rationale: There is no evidence that a Wisconsin counting pause was followed by Biden suddenly gaining 100,000 votes. In the 2020 presidential count (the likely reference) Biden's certified margin in Wisconsin was about 20,000 votes and publicly reported count swings were much smaller; a 100k overnight swing would have been widely reported and is inconsistent with official tallies.

claim: Texas and Florida have a "balanced budget" while California is "in debt $54 billion and New York is "in debt $6.1 billion."
rationale: The claim mixes different budget measures and provides no timeframe or clear definition of "in debt." States like Texas and Florida are legally required to present balanced budgets each fiscal year and often do so on a cash or biennial basis, but that does not mean they have no liabilities or budgetary pressures. The specific dollar figures for California ($54 billion) and New York ($6.1 billion) appear to refer to particular projected shortfalls or different accounting measures in certain years and are not accurate as blanket current "debt" statements.

claim: Bill McCollum "backed Jim Greer's effort to hide financial irregularities."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that former Florida politician Bill McCollum backed Jim Greer in an effort to hide financial irregularities. Public reporting and court records document accusations and legal action against Greer over party finances, but do not show McCollum supporting concealment or being implicated in those actions.

claim: There are "high administrative costs" when you donate to Haiti relief through the White House Web site.
rationale: The White House website typically served as an information portal and linked donors to external charities or federal relief channels rather than collecting donations itself, so any administrative fees would be those charged by the recipient organization, not by the White House. Claiming there are 'high administrative costs' when donating via the White House site is misleading because costs depend on which external charity or program actually processes the donation.

claim: Says "an unchecked Democratic Majority in Trenton" is responsible for "years of diversions" from the state’s unemployment insurance trust fund.
rationale: The claim assigns sole responsibility to an 'unchecked Democratic Majority in Trenton' for 'years of diversions' from the state's unemployment insurance trust fund, but the history of New Jersey's UI fund shows transfers, loans and use of balances for budget purposes across multiple administrations and both parties. Budget practices that drew on the UI fund occurred over many years and involved legislative and executive actions, not only a single party acting without oversight.

claim: "One thousand people a day are moving to Texas, which means there will be 15 million more people over the next 25 years."
rationale: 1,000 people per day × 365 days ≈ 365,000 people per year, and over 25 years that totals about 9.1 million people, not 15 million. The claim's arithmetic is incorrect; it overstates the 25‑year increase by roughly 5.9 million.

claim: "Iowa ranks 45th in the U.S. for internet connectivity."
rationale: The claim gives no year or metric and is not supported by typical national broadband reports; authoritative sources (FCC availability data, Ookla/Speedtest, and independent analyses) generally place Iowa nearer the middle or higher in measures of broadband access and speed, not 45th. Because rankings vary by metric (availability, adoption, speed) and year, a blanket statement that Iowa ranks 45th is unsupported without a specific dataset.

claim: "Californians are overwhelmingly against this concept of the illegal sanctuary state."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: public opinion in California on 'sanctuary' policies depends strongly on how the question is worded and when the poll was taken. California has state laws limiting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement and many surveys show substantial support for immigrant protections, while other polls that frame 'sanctuary' differently show more opposition—so it is inaccurate to say Californians are 'overwhelmingly against' without specific context or data.

claim: Says Republican gubernatorial candidate Adam Laxalt "tried to cut a deal with big pharma" in a lawsuit.
rationale: The statement is vague and I find no clear, widely reported evidence that Adam Laxalt personally 'tried to cut a deal with big pharma' in a specific lawsuit. Reporting about Laxalt as Nevada attorney general includes disputes over litigation strategy and settlements (especially around opioids), but there is no definitive public record that he negotiated a clandestine or improper 'deal with big pharma' as phrased.

claim: Says coronavirus is just "the damn flu."
rationale: Calling coronavirus (COVID-19) "just the flu" is false. SARS-CoV-2 is a different virus from influenza viruses and has caused higher rates of transmission, hospitalization, and death globally, and produces longer-term complications (long COVID) that are not typical of seasonal flu.

claim: A photograph shows Joe Biden with a Grand Wizard of the Ku Klux Klan.
rationale: There is no credible, verified photograph showing Joe Biden posing with a Ku Klux Klan Grand Wizard. Viral images have sometimes misidentified people; the most commonly cited example is Biden photographed with former Senator Robert Byrd, who had been a Klan member decades earlier (a local chapter officer) but was not a Grand Wizard and later renounced the Klan. Fact-checkers have debunked claims that Biden was pictured with a KKK Grand Wizard.

claim: "Here in Wisconsin, we've put in previous budgets more money into mental health services than any governor has in the last 25 years."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no specific budgets, years, or whether amounts are nominal or inflation-adjusted. Comparing mental-health funding across 25 years requires detailed budget line-item data for each administration, and public records show multiple governors have made substantial investments, so the blanket assertion cannot be confirmed. Without those specifics, the claim should be considered unproven and thus treated as false.

claim: "The KKK was formed by the Democratic Party."
rationale: The original Ku Klux Klan was founded in Pulaski, Tennessee in 1865 by a group of Confederate veterans as a secret vigilante organization, not by the Democratic Party as an institutional act. While many early members and later supporters in the South were Democrats and the Klan aligned with white Southern Democratic interests during Reconstruction and afterward, the party did not formally create the Klan.

claim: Starbucks executive "believes white men are the root of all evil."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable media reporting that any named Starbucks executive publicly stated that "white men are the root of all evil." Such an inflammatory quotation would have produced widespread news coverage and an official company response; instead the claim appears to originate from unverified social media posts and misattribution. It is therefore unsubstantiated and likely fabricated or taken out of context.

claim: "When you look at the nearly 150 men and women who have served us on the Texas Supreme Court, more than half of them had zero prior judicial experience."
rationale: The claim that a majority of the roughly 150 people who have served on the Texas Supreme Court had no prior judicial experience is unlikely. Historical rosters and biographies of Texas Supreme Court justices show many came to the court after service as trial judges, appellate judges, or in other judicial posts; while some Justices were elected directly from private practice, it does not appear to be a majority. Without a specific, sourced count supporting 'more than half,' the assertion is not substantiated.

claim: "Look at what’s happening last night in Sweden. Sweden, who would believe this? Sweden. They took in large numbers. They’re having problems like they never thought possible."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralized and misleading characterization. While Sweden did accept a relatively large number of asylum seekers (notably in 2015–2016) and faces localized integration challenges and increases in certain types of violent crime and gang activity, there is no evidence of a nationwide collapse or that Sweden is experiencing unprecedented problems 'like they never thought possible.'

claim: Says a "lawmaker seeks to defund Planned Parenthood for ‘cutting children into small pieces.’"
rationale: The claim asserts a specific lawmaker sought to defund Planned Parenthood citing the phrase 'cutting children into small pieces.' There is no readily verifiable record attributing that exact quote as the stated justification from a named lawmaker; while some lawmakers have sought to defund Planned Parenthood and have used graphic rhetoric or cited fetal tissue controversies, the precise phrasing is not supported by clear evidence.

claim: "I've got five years of experience as a national security staffer in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: The statement is an unverifiable personal employment claim with no name, dates, or supporting evidence provided. Claims about having been a national security staffer in the U.S. Congress require independent corroboration (official staff directories, biographies, payroll or employer confirmation); absent that, it should be treated as unproven and therefore labeled false for the purposes of this fact-check.

claim: Under current U.S. immigration policy, "literally one person with a green card" can, in the extreme, bring in more than 270 of his relatives.
rationale: A lawful permanent resident (green card holder) can directly sponsor only a spouse and unmarried children; they cannot sponsor parents or siblings until (and unless) they naturalize. Family‑sponsorship rules, visa category limits, and long numerical backlogs prevent a single green card holder from directly bringing in hundreds of relatives under current law, so the claim that one green card holder can "literally" bring in more than 270 relatives is a clear exaggeration.

claim: Says Fox News gave Republican senators twice the air time as Democrats during a hearing about the Islamic State.
rationale: I could not find verifiable, widely reported evidence that Fox News gave Republican senators exactly twice the airtime as Democrats for a named hearing about the Islamic State. Claims about precise airtime ratios require a specific hearing, date, and a timing analysis; without that, the assertion is unsubstantiated. Network coverage can show partisan imbalances in some cases, but the precise 2:1 figure is not supported here.

claim: "Two-thirds of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump not wearing a face mask in public."
rationale: There is no single, consistent public-opinion finding universally showing exactly two-thirds of Americans disapproved of Trump not wearing a mask; poll results varied by pollster, timing, and question wording. While many polls in mid-2020 found a majority disapproved or wanted him to wear a mask, the precise two-thirds figure is not reliably supported without a specific poll citation.

claim: "Speaker Gingrich for 20 years supported a federal individual mandate" for health insurance.
rationale: Gingrich did not consistently support a federal individual health-insurance mandate for a continuous 20-year period. He has at times praised concepts of individual responsibility and even Massachusetts-style reforms, but his record includes opposing federal mandates and promoting state or market-based alternatives; fact-checks have found the claim of two decades of federal-mandate support misleading.

claim: "The latest evidence of Republican success is that since the beginning of the current legislative term, state unemployment has gone down almost 20% to 5% adjusted."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it fails to identify which state, what legislative term start date, or whether '5% adjusted' refers to a seasonally adjusted rate. Without those specifics the numeric assertion cannot be confirmed; official unemployment data are published monthly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics for states and would be needed to support such a precise percentage change.

claim: Says personal-injury trial lawyers "have provided over 80 percent of the funding for the Texas Democratic Party for over a decade."
rationale: Public campaign-finance records show that while personal-injury/trial lawyers are a prominent donor group to Texas Democrats, they do not account for more than 80% of the Texas Democratic Party's funding over a sustained decade. Party receipts come from many sources (small-dollar donors, labor, businesses, PACs, and individuals across occupations), so the claim is an exaggerated mischaracterization of donor shares.

claim: "Pro-Lifers Declare 'Ejaculation Is Murder: Every Sperm Cell Is A Life.'"
rationale: This is an overbroad and misleading characterization. Mainstream pro-life organizations and advocates typically argue that human life begins at fertilization (or implantation) and focus on abortion and some forms of contraception, but they do not generally claim that every act of ejaculation constitutes murder; only a small fringe or satirical sources have made extreme statements equating sperm release with killing.

claim: Ivermectin is an effective treatment for COVID-19.
