rationale: The claim is false because several 20th- and 21st-century U.S. presidents did not initiate new wars; for example, Gerald Ford (1974–1977) and Jimmy Carter (1977–1981) did not start new large-scale wars. While Trump carried out military strikes and targeted actions, he is not uniquely the first modern president to avoid launching a new full-scale war.

claim: "Remember that developers are forced to use the ‘195 land union’ contractors, so tap an extra $10 million into any construction project."
rationale: There is no general legal rule that developers are universally forced to use a specific entity called the “195 land union”; which contractors are required depends on local project labor agreements, procurement rules, and contract terms. The recommendation to automatically add an extra $10 million is arbitrary and unsupported without project-specific cost estimates or a documented legal requirement.

claim: Says "we are overcharging students . . . to help pay for the health care law."
rationale: The claim is too vague and lacks verifiable context (which school, when, and what charge). There is no general, documented policy that students nationwide were systematically 'overcharged' specifically 'to help pay for the health care law'; universities sometimes raise student fees or health insurance premiums for many reasons, but tying those increases uniformly to paying for a health-care law is not supported by clear evidence.

claim: "Coolmath Games is being taken down cause it was run by the Mexican drug cartel?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that Coolmath Games was owned or run by a Mexican drug cartel, nor that the site is being taken down for that reason. The claim appears to be a baseless internet rumor or meme rather than a factual report. Official statements and mainstream news outlets have not corroborated any such allegation.

claim: The United States has experienced "40 straight months of unemployment at 8 percent or higher."
rationale: Monthly U.S. unemployment (the official U-3 rate) did reach very high levels during the Great Recession, peaking at 10% in late 2009, but Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly data do not show a continuous 40-month stretch at 8.0% or higher. The high-unemployment period lasted multiple years spanning 2009–2012, but the uninterrupted span at or above 8% was shorter than 40 months.

claim: "West Linn has one of the highest per capita rates of home-based businesses in the United States."
rationale: I am unaware of any authoritative national data or reputable rankings showing West Linn as having one of the highest per-capita rates of home-based businesses in the United States. Claims like this are often made in local promotional materials but are not substantiated by national sources such as the U.S. Census Bureau or SBA statistics.

claim: "Gov. Scott Walker (is) more than halfway to (his) 250,000 jobs goal."
rationale: The claim is unqualified and lacks a start date or definition of what counts as a ‘job,’ so it cannot be verified as stated. Public reporting and official labor statistics require a baseline and end date to assess progress toward a numeric goal; available historical summaries of Wisconsin job growth under Gov. Walker do not clearly support an unqualified statement that he had already passed half (125,000+) of a 250,000-job goal at a specific point. Without those specifics the assertion is misleading.

claim: "Our jobless rate, our unemployment rate, is the lowest of all of the big cities in New Jersey."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits which city is meant and what time period is referenced; unemployment rates vary over time and across New Jersey's large cities. Without a specific city and date, one cannot confirm it truly had the lowest jobless rate among all big NJ cities, so the claim is treated as false pending precise data.

claim: Says Jimmy Carter was the last "U.S. president to say flat out those (Israeli) settlements are illegal."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. While Jimmy Carter and his administration criticized settlements, later U.S. administrations and senior officials have described Israeli settlements as inconsistent with or violating international law — notably the Obama administration and Secretary of State John Kerry — and the UN Security Council in 2016 characterized settlements as a violation of international law. Although some presidents did not always use the exact word "illegal," the U.S. position after Carter was not uniformly to refrain from calling settlements unlawful.

claim: "After Texas defunded Planned Parenthood, both the unintended pregnancy and abortion rates dropped."
rationale: Research on Texas’s removal of Planned Parenthood from state family‑planning programs found contraceptive visits declined and Medicaid-financed births increased, consistent with more unintended pregnancies rather than fewer. While abortion counts later fell in Texas, that decline is attributable to separate clinic restrictions and closures, so both unintended pregnancy and abortion rates did not drop together after the defunding.

claim: Twenty million Americans are "out of work."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and misleading without a date or definition. The count of "out of work" depends on whether you mean officially unemployed, not in the labor force, or temporarily furloughed; only during the COVID-19 peak in spring 2020 did combined measures approach roughly 20–23 million people, while in most periods the number is substantially lower.

claim: After Fahrenheit 9/11 came out, "Bush's approval rating never was better, it only got worse."
rationale: Fahrenheit 9/11 premiered in June 2004, but President George W. Bush's approval ratings fluctuated after that date rather than only declining. He experienced periods of modest improvement (including around the 2004 election and into early 2005) before suffering larger drops later (notably after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 and as the Iraq war continued).

claim: "Throughout his time in elected office, Barack Obama has taken multiple positions on banning handguns and the D.C. handgun ban."
rationale: Public records and reporting show Obama expressed different stances on handguns over his years in office and campaigning — earlier statements indicated support for stricter handgun limits (including acceptance of the D.C. handgun ban) while later as a U.S. senator and presidential candidate he framed his positions differently after the Supreme Court's Heller decision and emphasized regulation rather than outright reinstating a ban. These shifts constitute multiple positions over time.

claim: If sea levels rise six feet due to climate change, Waterplace Park in Providence and Wickford village would be swamped
rationale: Both Waterplace Park in downtown Providence and Wickford village lie at very low elevations along tidal waterways. Sea level rise of about six feet (≈1.8 m) is widely projected to inundate large portions of low-lying Narragansett Bay shoreline, making flooding of those specific locations very likely absent major protective measures.

claim: "We are now, for the first time ever, energy independent."
rationale: The statement is false as an absolute claim: it lacks definition of who "we" are and what "energy independent" means. Some countries (notably the U.S.) have recently been net energy or petroleum exporters for the first time in many decades, but that is not the same as complete, permanent energy self-sufficiency and is not accurately described as "for the first time ever."

claim: No one "with a concealed carry permit ever committed a mass shooting."
rationale: The claim is an absolute universal negative but is contradicted by documented counterexamples. Public reporting and law-enforcement records indicate at least some perpetrators of incidents commonly categorized as mass shootings did hold concealed-carry permits, so the statement that no one ever did is false.

claim: It "is estimated that as many as 300,000 auto workers may be out of a job before the end of the year."
rationale: The statement provides no source or jurisdiction and I could not find authoritative estimates from government agencies, industry groups, unions, or major news outlets projecting up to 300,000 auto workers to be unemployed by the end of the year. Reported auto-sector layoffs in recent coverage have been in the tens of thousands and typically tied to specific companies or regions, so the 300,000 figure as stated is unsupported. Without clear sourcing or context the claim is not substantiated.
cited_knowledge: General knowledge of media and official reporting on auto-sector layoffs, typical scales of announced plant closures/layoffs, and absence of a widely reported 300,000-worker projection.
safety_notes: The claim is ambiguous (no country, year, or source). A credible estimate could be true for a different scope (global, multi-year) or if sourced; verify with a named source and timeframe.

claim: Says county parties representing more than half the state’s Republican voters approved resolutions "demanding changes" in Texas House leadership.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and public tallies show many Texas county Republican parties adopted resolutions calling for changes in House leadership, but those counties do not together encompass more than half of the state’s Republican primary electorate. Major population centers and several large counties did not adopt such resolutions, so the claim that the county parties representing a majority of Republican voters approved the demand is not supported.

claim: More private-sector jobs were created in the second year of the Obama administration than in the eight years of the Bush administration.
rationale: This claim is not supported by official employment data. Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll series show that private-sector job gains in President Obama’s second year (2010) were positive but far smaller than the cumulative private-sector job change across the full eight years of the Bush administration; comparing a single year to an entire eight-year span therefore misstates the relative magnitudes.

claim: "Senator Robert Hurt voted for a bill that’s raised your electric rates seven times."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and too vague: there is no well-documented, specific bill tied to Senator Robert Hurt that can be shown to have directly caused electricity rates to be raised seven times. 'Senator Robert Hurt' is ambiguous (he served in the Virginia state senate years earlier and later as a U.S. Representative), and public records and reporting do not link a particular Hurt vote to seven distinct rate increases for constituents.

claim: "Governor (Perry), you were a Democrat, having worked for Al Gore as his campaign manager..."
rationale: The statement conflates two claims: Rick Perry did begin his political career as a Democrat and later became a Republican, but he did not work as Al Gore's campaign manager. There is no credible record of Perry serving on Gore's campaign staff and Gore's campaigns were run by other Democratic operatives.

claim: "The median income in America has dropped by 10 percent in the last four years."
rationale: Available U.S. income data through mid-2024 show that median household income did not fall by as much as 10% over a four-year span; incomes rose to record (inflation-adjusted) levels around 2021 and any declines since have been modest and well under 10% in typical measures. The claim lacks specificity (household vs individual, nominal vs real) and is inconsistent with Census/BLS trend summaries.

claim: Orrin Hatch co-sponsored a 1993 health care bill that had an individual mandate.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Senator Orrin Hatch co-sponsored any 1993 federal health-care bill that included an individual mandate. The major 1993 health-care effort was the Clinton plan (and related congressional proposals) which did not impose a federal individual mandate, and historical sponsorship records do not show Hatch signing on to a 1993 mandate bill. Claims that Hatch co-sponsored such a measure appear to conflate different bills and years.

claim: "Voting in the wrong precinct led to over 14,000 registered voters statewide to lose their vote in 2008."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated because it gives no state or source and I could not verify any official 2008 election report showing over 14,000 registered voters statewide lost their vote specifically for voting in the wrong precinct. Provisional ballot rejection and ballot-cancellation data from states show rejections for many reasons (registration issues, ID, wrong precinct) and numbers vary widely by state; a single statewide loss figure of >14,000 for just wrong-precinct errors in 2008 is not supported by known election records. Without a named state and source, the assertion is likely misleading or incorrect.

claim: "About halfway through fiscal year 2009, Washington has run out of money."
rationale: The U.S. federal government did not "run out of money" about halfway through fiscal year 2009 (around spring 2009). The government continued to fund operations, there was no shutdown or default then, and the higher-profile U.S. debt-ceiling crises and payment standoffs occurred in later years (notably 2011).

claim: "Forty-seven percent of Americans pay no income tax."
rationale: The 47% figure is misleading as a blanket statement. It originated from analyses of a specific year and referred to the share of households with no federal individual income tax liability under the tax code at that time; many in that group still pay payroll, state, and local taxes or receive refundable credits, and the percentage varies by year and by whether you count households, filers, or individuals.

claim: "1 in 4 Rhode Islanders under the age of 65 does not have health insurance."
rationale: Rhode Island's uninsured rate for people under 65 is much lower than 25%; recent U.S. Census and state data show single-digit uninsured rates for the state driven by Medicaid expansion and ACA marketplace coverage. Saying 1 in 4 Rhode Islanders under 65 lack insurance significantly overstates the documented uninsured population.

claim: "59 percent of Americans today believe that Barack Obama is still a Muslim."
rationale: No reputable national poll indicates 59% of all Americans believe Barack Obama is still a Muslim. Most national surveys over the past decade have found much lower overall rates (typically in the teens or low twenties), though higher percentages have appeared within specific partisan subgroups at times.

claim: Photo shows Ice Cube and 50 Cent wearing Donald Trump hats.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting showing an authentic photo of Ice Cube and 50 Cent together wearing Donald Trump hats; circulated images appear to be digitally edited or misattributed. Both artists have public histories and statements that make such a joint pro-Trump image unlikely, and fact-checkers have debunked similar viral manipulations.

claim: "You said you went to Delaware State but you forgot the name of your college."
rationale: There is no supporting evidence provided that the person both asserted they attended Delaware State and at the same time forgot the name of their college. The claim is ambiguous and self-contradictory as presented, and cannot be verified without a source (e.g., a transcript, recording, or reliable citation).

claim: "Kim Martin Morrow the CEO of Netflix has just been charged with 15 charges for child pornography"
rationale: There are no credible reports that anyone named Kim Martin Morrow is the CEO of Netflix or has been charged with child pornography. Netflix's leadership is publicly known and a high-profile criminal charge against a CEO would be widely reported; no such reporting exists.

claim: Common Core is "education through Washington D.C."
rationale: The Common Core State Standards were developed in 2009 through a state-led effort by the National Governors Association and the Council of Chief State School Officers, not by the federal government in Washington D.C. While the U.S. Department of Education provided incentives and grant programs (e.g., Race to the Top) that encouraged some states to adopt the standards, the federal government did not create or legally mandate Common Core.

claim: Says "I never billed a single hour of my time to the City of Portland in the last 10 years -- so, no revolving door."
rationale: The claim that the speaker "never billed a single hour... in the last 10 years" is unverifiable without citing payroll, contract, or disclosure records; publicly available evidence would be required to establish a zero billing history. The added conclusion "so, no revolving door" does not follow reliably even if billing were absent, since revolving-door relationships can involve other forms of compensation or employment and require investigation of employment, lobbying, and contracting history.

claim: The "3 red stripes" in Joe Biden’s campaign logo refer to a Chinese socialist slogan.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the three red stripes in Joe Biden’s campaign logo were intended to reference a Chinese socialist slogan. The logo is widely described by the campaign and designers as a stylized representation of the American flag and the letter 'E' in 'Biden.' Assertions tying it to a Chinese slogan appear to be speculative or conspiratorial without supporting documentation.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: House committees routinely conduct closed-door depositions under their investigatory authority and, in 2019, Speaker Pelosi authorized an impeachment inquiry that empowered the committees; Rep. Schiff, as Intelligence Committee chair, presided over such depositions. While some House Republicans argued a separate full-House floor vote was required, longstanding House practice and rules give committees investigatory powers and permit the Speaker to authorize an inquiry, so the closed-door hearings were not clearly inconsistent with House rules.

claim: Says Dennis Miller said that if he didn’t see women protesting the Ghislaine Maxwell trial verdict "you're all frauds. This isn't justice for those women, this is a joke."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Dennis Miller making this specific statement about the Ghislaine Maxwell verdict in major media coverage or in his known public posts. The quote appears to be unverified and likely misattributed or fabricated rather than a documented public remark from Miller.

claim: "We know dangerous criminals can slip through immigration at airports just like ours. Yet Joe Donnelly stood right here with the radical left against all efforts to secure our most vulnerable entry points."
rationale: The claim bundles a plausible general concern (border/airport screening can sometimes fail) with an unsubstantiated, sweeping accusation that Joe Donnelly "stood with the radical left against all efforts" to secure entry points. There is no reliable evidence that Donnelly categorically opposed every security measure at airports or consistently voted against all such efforts; the language is hyperbolic and lacks specific votes or policies to support it.

claim: "U.S. military at the White House arresting Congress."
rationale: There are no credible reports or evidence that U.S. military forces have been at the White House arresting members of Congress. Such an action would be unprecedented, would violate domestic law and norms governing military involvement in civilian law enforcement, and would have been widely and unmistakably reported by major media and official sources.

claim: "Jim Justice is the first West Virginia governor to fight for pay raises for educators."
rationale: This claim is false because multiple West Virginia governors before Jim Justice have advocated for, proposed, or signed measures that increased teacher pay. Justice is notable for his role in the 2018 teacher pay dispute and subsequent raises, but he was not the first governor in the state to push for educator pay increases.

claim: Says a video shows a "gay party in Italy few weeks before COVID-19."
rationale: The claim assigns a specific time and place to an unspecified viral video without verifiable provenance. Similar viral clips have repeatedly been misdated or misattributed (often from other countries or earlier years), and absent original video metadata or independent reporting this specific 'gay party in Italy few weeks before COVID-19' claim cannot be substantiated and is likely false.

claim: "But for immigrants, we would have a contracting population..."
rationale: The statement is too general to be true as written: whether population would contract without immigrants depends on the country and timeframe. In many high‑income, low‑fertility countries immigration is essential to prevent decline, but other countries (or some time periods) have enough natural increase that population would not contract even with no immigration.

claim: "CBO reports that delaying the Obamacare individual mandate will reduce the deficit by $35 billion over ten years."
rationale: This claim misstates CBO's finding. The approximately $35 billion 10-year reduction figure reported in 2013 referred to delaying the employer mandate, not the individual mandate; delaying the individual mandate would primarily reduce penalty revenue and tend to increase deficits. CBO analyses distinguish the employer and individual mandate effects, and the $35 billion saving is tied to the employer-side delay.

claim: Says Tim Tebow wrote, "The government might be preparing us for a cashless society, but it was predicted by the Bible."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Tim Tebow authored that specific sentence; it appears to be a misattributed or fabricated quote circulated online. Tebow is a public Christian figure who posts faith-based commentary, but searches of his verified accounts and reputable news archives do not show this phrasing.

claim: "Smartmatic and Dominion systems ... were built to do this very thing, for changing the results of elections."
rationale: Multiple independent audits, hand recounts, security analyses, and statements from U.S. election officials and cybersecurity agencies found no evidence that Dominion or Smartmatic systems were designed to alter election results. Investigations into 2020 election claims repeatedly debunked assertions that the machines were built to flip votes, and courts have rejected related conspiracy allegations. While isolated software bugs or operator errors have occurred, those are not the same as systems being intentionally engineered to change outcomes.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "knows full well I voted for his amendment to increase military spending to $697 billion."
rationale: The claim presents a quoted statement without identifying who said it or providing a source; I could not verify any public record or reputable reporting showing someone saying verbatim that Rubio 'knows full well I voted for his amendment to increase military spending to $697 billion.' Without attribution or supporting evidence the assertion is unverified and treated as false.

claim: "There's no court session between now and the end of this election."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that cannot be verified as true without specifying which court, which jurisdiction, and which election timeline. Courts at various levels commonly hold sessions and can schedule emergency or expedited hearings related to elections, and historically litigation often occurs close to or during election periods, so it is unlikely that no court sessions will occur everywhere before the election ends.

claim: "More Texans have jobs today than ever before in the history of our state."
rationale: Texas has experienced sustained population and labor-force growth and state and federal employment series have recorded successive all-time highs in recent years, so the absolute number of Texans working is higher now than at most prior points in history. This conclusion rests on commonly used employment series that have recently hit record levels.

claim: Says that singer Dolly Parton said, "Trump in one year is already better than 16 years of Bush, Obama put together."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or record that Dolly Parton ever made this specific statement praising Trump as "better than 16 years of Bush, Obama put together." Her public comments on politics have generally avoided explicit endorsements or sweeping comparative claims of that form, and a remark this sensational would have been widely reported but is not found in news or interview archives.

claim: "A portion of everything you pay A.A.R.P goes directly to the Democratic Party."
rationale: AARP does not automatically route a portion of every membership payment to the Democratic Party. Political donations associated with AARP come from a separate, voluntary AARP PAC and other designated advocacy funds; while the PAC has at times given more to Democratic candidates, dues are used for operations and nonpartisan advocacy, not direct party contributions.

claim: "More than 20 million people are at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months in 4 nations."
rationale: This wording matches repeated warnings from the United Nations and humanitarian agencies that more than 20 million people in four areas—Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northeastern Nigeria—were at imminent risk of starvation within months. The claim reflects those official assessments that identified an immediate famine risk across those four countries/regions.

claim: "In March 2020 the United States deployed 30,000 troops to Europe to ... free child-trafficked children and arrest deep state cabal members."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the United States deployed 30,000 troops to Europe in March 2020 to free child-trafficked children or arrest a so-called 'deep state cabal.' Department of Defense announcements and major news outlets from that time do not record any such operation, and the claim aligns with debunked conspiracy narratives rather than documented military activity. U.S. military forces do not conduct extrajudicial mass arrests or unilateral law-enforcement raids in allied countries without clear legal authorization and public reporting.

claim: Says more Austinites voted in the city’s 1973 election featuring a mayor’s race than in the city’s most recent mayoral election.
rationale: Austin's population and registered voter base have grown substantially since the 1970s, so recent mayoral elections have tended to produce higher absolute vote totals than elections from 1973. Without specific turnout figures showing the 1973 raw vote exceeding the most recent mayoral election, the claim is unlikely to be correct.

claim: Says David Jolly’s former firm lobbied "for hundreds of millions (of dollars) for a dictator in Pakistan."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that David Jolly’s former firm arranged or lobbied to obtain "hundreds of millions" of dollars for a Pakistani dictator. Public lobbying disclosures and contemporary news coverage do not support a claim that his employer brokered multi‑hundred‑million dollar payments on behalf of any Pakistani autocrat; the statement appears to mischaracterize or exaggerate routine foreign representation or aid-related advocacy.

claim: Mitt Romney "said it was 'tragic' to end the war in Iraq."
rationale: I find no clear evidence Romney explicitly said it was "tragic to end the war in Iraq." Romney did criticize the troop withdrawal and called aspects of the pullout a mistake or lamented how it was handled, but the exact quoted wording appears to be a mischaracterization or out-of-context paraphrase. Without a direct reliable source for that precise quote, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "We have more hospitals that are children’s hospitals than any other state in the union." 
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify which state 'we' refers to; without a specific state, it cannot be confirmed. Additionally, counts of children's hospitals vary by definition and over time, and larger states such as California, Texas, and New York commonly have the highest numbers, so a blanket statement is unlikely to be true without supporting data.

claim: The U.S. spends "57 cents on the dollar on defense."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While defense constitutes about half of federal discretionary spending, discretionary spending is only about 25–35% of the total federal budget, so defense outlays equal roughly 15–20 cents of each total federal dollar, not 57 cents. Without specifying ‘of what dollar’ (total federal spending, discretionary spending, or tax dollars) the claim is inaccurate.

claim: Photos show "diesel generators" at the COP26 climate change conference.
rationale: Viral posts claiming photos showed diesel generators at COP26 were investigated by independent fact‑checkers and reporters and found to be misattributed or misleading; the organisers stated the conference was powered from mains/grid supplies and the pictured units were not large diesel powerplants supplying the summit. The images either showed other kinds of temporary event equipment or were taken out of context, so the blanket claim is false.

claim: "A law enforcement officer is more likely to commit a crime than a CWP (concealed weapons permit) holder."
rationale: There is no clear, generalizable evidence that law enforcement officers are more likely to commit crimes than concealed-weapons-permit (CWP) holders. Multiple studies and government analyses have found that CWP holders have very low arrest and conviction rates relative to the general population, while officer misconduct exists but is relatively rare and unevenly reported; direct comparisons are confounded by differences in screening, duties, reporting, and jurisdictional data. Without consistent, comparable nationwide data showing higher offending among officers, the blanket claim is not supported.

claim: Wall Street megabanks that received bailouts in 2009 now get taxpayer-funded advantages not available to community banks in Ohio.
rationale: Large Wall Street banks that were rescued in 2008–09 continue to enjoy taxpayer-backed advantages that community banks typically do not, including an implicit "too-big-to-fail" subsidy that lowers their funding costs and preferential access to Federal Reserve emergency liquidity facilities and capital-market privileges (e.g., primary-dealer roles). Academic and policy analyses have documented a measurable funding-cost advantage for systemically important banks and the U.S. resolution and Fed tools are structured to protect large interconnected institutions rather than small community banks in Ohio.

claim: "Less mass shootings under Trump!"
rationale: Available data sources and reporting show that mass shootings (by common public definitions such as four or more people shot) did not decrease during Donald Trump's presidency; counts rose in several years of his term and were higher than many prior years. The claim lacks a specified baseline and ignores variation by definition and year, but the overall trend across commonly used datasets is not consistent with a blanket "less" statement.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said: "While there may have been an age difference, Josh Duggar’s transgressions are far less an affront to God than what gays do to each other."
rationale: There is no reputable record or contemporaneous news reporting attributing that quote to Ted Cruz; such an explicit, inflammatory comparison would have been widely covered and sourced. Available public statements from Cruz about the Josh Duggar case do not contain that language, making this specific quotation a likely misattribution or fabrication.

claim: Terry McAuliffe favors "taking the Pledge of Allegiance and the 4th of July out of the (school) curriculum."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and fact-checking found that McAuliffe did not propose an official policy to remove the Pledge of Allegiance or the Fourth of July from school curricula; quotes used in attacks were taken out of context or referred to loosening prescriptive statewide mandates, not banning those civic practices. He has repeatedly denied advocating a removal and emphasized support for civic education.

claim: "There has never been an alderman who has defeated an incumbent mayor in the history of this great city."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it omits the city's name and time frame, and it asserts a universal negative across an entire city's history. In general, municipal histories often include cases where sitting council members or aldermen have run for and defeated incumbent mayors, so the blanket statement is unlikely to be true without precise context.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings are up.
rationale: The statement is misleading because Rick Scott is not currently a governor (he has served as Florida governor in the past and has been a U.S. senator since 2019), and the claim provides no timeframe or poll source showing his approval ratings increasing. Approval ratings are poll-dependent and can only be judged with a specified poll and period; absent that context there is no verifiable basis for asserting they are "up."

claim: "Like every budget passed by the Senate since I have been lieutenant governor, Senate Bill 1 is within the spending limit set by the Texas Constitution."
rationale: The claim makes a blanket assertion that every Senate budget since the speaker became lieutenant governor, including Senate Bill 1, complied with the Texas Constitution's spending limits; I find insufficient public evidence to verify that universal claim. Texas budgets must be measured against comptroller revenue certifications and sometimes required revisions or trigger cuts when estimates change, and specific certification or legal findings would be needed to prove SB1 and every prior Senate budget were within the constitutional limit.

claim: "Pre-existing conditions are covered under my (health care) plan."
rationale: The statement is not universally true: whether pre-existing conditions are covered depends on the specific health plan and the laws that govern it. For example, in the U.S. the Affordable Care Act generally prohibits exclusions for pre-existing conditions in most individual and small-group plans since 2014, but some plans (short-term limited-duration policies, certain grandfathered plans, and specific limited products) may not provide that protection; rules differ in other countries.

claim: Arnold Schwarzenegger slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself because he had been turned away from a hotel.
rationale: No reliable contemporary sources corroborate the anecdote and established fact-checkers have found the story to be fabricated. Biographical records of Schwarzenegger note other early hardships (sleeping in cars or gyms) but not an incident of being turned away from a hotel and sleeping in front of a bronze statue of himself, and the claimed timeline is inconsistent with when such statues were installed.

claim: "If Sen. Hillary Clinton could enact all of her campaign proposals, taxpayers would be faced with financing more than $777.6-billion in new spending over one White House term."
rationale: No authoritative, nonpartisan source supports the precise figure that Sen. Hillary Clinton’s campaign proposals would require $777.6 billion in new spending over one term. Cost estimates for Clinton’s various proposals (from different years) were produced piecemeal by different analysts and partisan groups and vary widely depending on which items and offsets are included; there is no consensus single-score that yields that exact number. The claim appears to be a partisan aggregation rather than a verified, comprehensive budget scoring by an impartial budget office.

claim: Actions by Joe Biden left "10,000 - 15,000 American citizens abandoned to terrorists in Afghanistan."
rationale: Contemporary U.S. government statements and reporting showed the number of U.S. citizens left in Afghanistan after the 2021 withdrawal was in the low hundreds or fewer, not 10,000–15,000. The much larger figures often cited (tens of thousands) referred to Afghans eligible for visas, interpreters, or other at-risk evacuees—not U.S. citizens abandoned to terrorists.

claim: "The pension fund in the city of Providence is only 30 percent funded, about the same level as when he [Taveras] took office."
rationale: Public records and news reporting show Providence's pension funded ratio has varied depending on the valuation method and year, and it is inaccurate to state flatly that it was 'only 30 percent' and 'about the same' as when Taveras took office. Available budget and actuarial reports indicate the funded level changed over the 2010s and the exact percentage depends on whether actuarial assumptions or market value are used, so the claim's absolute comparison is misleading.

claim: "We got a million jobs."
rationale: The claim "We got a million jobs." lacks any context about who "we" refers to, the time period, or the data source, so it is not verifiable as stated. Without specifying a country, employer, or official labor report showing an increase of one million jobs, the assertion cannot be confirmed and is treated as false for lack of evidence.

claim: An independent payment advisory board created by the health care reform law "can ration care and deny certain Medicare treatments."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act’s Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) was statutorily barred from recommending policies that would ration care, restrict benefits, limit eligibility, or deny Medicare coverage for specific treatments. IPAB’s role was to recommend cost-saving payment and delivery system changes; while those recommendations could indirectly affect access through payment incentives, the law explicitly prohibited direct denial of treatments or benefit cuts as recommendations.

claim: The United States is "the only advanced country on Earth" that doesn’t guarantee "paid maternity leave to our workers."
rationale: At the national (federal) level the United States does not guarantee paid maternity or parental leave, only unpaid leave under the FMLA for eligible workers. Comparative data from OECD and other summaries of developed-country policies show the U.S. is the only major developed/OECD country lacking a statutory national paid maternity/parental leave program.

claim: "We have the lowest beer tax in the nation."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unlikely to be true without specifying which jurisdiction 'we' refers to and the date of comparison. Beer excise taxes vary widely by state and local jurisdiction and several states have extremely low or even zero beer excise rates, so an unqualified statement that 'we have the lowest' cannot be verified as true. To validate, one must compare current per‑volume excise rates for the named jurisdiction against all others.

claim: President Joe Biden withdrew troops from Afghanistan "simply because of Trump Derangement Syndrome and they wanted to reverse any policy that Trump had implemented."
rationale: The claim that Biden withdrew troops "simply" out of "Trump Derangement Syndrome" and to reverse Trump policies is inaccurate. The U.S. withdrawal followed the February 2020 U.S.-Taliban agreement that set a timeline for troop exit, and the Biden administration publicly cited strategic, national security, and political reasons for completing that withdrawal rather than solely partisan animus. Multiple documented policy, legal, and operational factors influenced the decision.

claim: "Over 60 percent of the provisional ballots cast in [the 2012] election were disqualified because those folks were not duly registered as voters."
rationale: Nationwide data for the 2012 U.S. general election do not support a claim that over 60% of provisional ballots were disqualified for lack of registration. Federal and media analyses of Election Assistance Commission and state data show a substantially lower overall rejection rate and that rejected provisional ballots were dismissed for multiple reasons (wrong precinct, duplicate voting, ineligibility), not solely for not being registered. Therefore the specific claim is inaccurate as stated.

claim: Insulin prices have "gone THRU THE ROOF for patients/taxpayers bc of manufacturer, health plan & PBM biz practices."
rationale: Insulin prices have risen substantially over recent decades, with list and net prices climbing and patient out‑of‑pocket costs increasing for many. Independent investigations and reporting have repeatedly identified manufacturer list‑price increases, PBM rebate structures and insurer/health‑plan benefit design (which can shift costs to patients) as major contributors to higher prices and greater taxpayer spending through public programs.

claim: Says TriMet spends "$10.3 million in police contracts" a year for 56 transit police who must respond to non-transit calls
rationale: Public reporting and TriMet budget documents have shown roughly $10.3 million annually in law-enforcement contracts to fund about 56 sworn transit officers. Those officers are commissioned through local police/sheriff agencies and, under their agency duties and mutual-aid/dispatch systems, can be required to respond to non‑transit calls or be reassigned away from transit work.

claim: Paul Ryan "is one of only six House Republicans who voted for Teddy Kennedy's bill to force Christian employers to hire LGBT employees."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. Paul Ryan was not one of only six House Republicans who voted for a Teddy Kennedy 'force Christian employers to hire LGBT employees' bill — Ryan's Congressional record shows he opposed federal mandates of this kind, and he was not a supporter of the Employment Non-Discrimination Act as characterized. The statement also misstates the bill: ENDA was designed to prohibit employment discrimination and the extent of religious exemptions was debated, so describing it as 'forcing Christian employers to hire LGBT employees' is misleading.

claim: Romney refused to pardon "a decorated soldier" returning from Iraq who had been charged with a crime involving a BB gun when he was 13.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Mitt Romney refused to pardon a 'decorated soldier' returning from Iraq for a BB-gun incident when he was 13. Romney's gubernatorial pardon and commutation record and national fact-checking coverage do not show a widely reported case matching that description, suggesting the claim conflates or invents events.

claim: "Military tribunals start Jan. 20, 2021."
rationale: There is no evidence that any nationwide military tribunals were scheduled to begin on January 20, 2021, and no official orders instituting such tribunals were issued. The U.S. presidential inauguration took place that day and civilian legal processes continued as normal. Claims that military tribunals would start that date were part of unsubstantiated political rumors and conspiracy theories.

claim: The United States "is the only major country that taxes its own exports."
rationale: The United States does not impose export duties: the U.S. Constitution forbids taxes or duties on exports. Many countries likewise do not levy export taxes, while a minority (often resource-exporting states) impose specific export duties on certain commodities. Therefore the claim that the U.S. is the only major country that taxes its own exports is incorrect.

claim: We live in "a time of historically low violent crime rates and historically high gun ownership rates nationally."
rationale: Violent crime in the U.S. is well below its early‑1990s peak, but it has risen in recent years (notably around 2020–2021), so it is not uniformly at an all‑time low today. Likewise, firearm sales and the number of guns in circulation surged recently, but survey measures of household gun ownership remain below some historical peaks and vary by source, so the claim that ownership is 'historically high' nationally is misleading.

claim: "Welders make more money than philosophers."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement without context and therefore false as stated. Wages vary by country, experience, and specific role: many welders earn solid middle-income wages and can out-earn low-paid adjunct or nonacademic philosophy positions, but philosophy professors and some industry-employed philosophers can earn more than many welders. Because earnings overlap and depend on definitions (median vs top earners, location, experience), the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Donald Trump "himself has a financial stake in the French company that makes the brand-name version of hydroxychloroquine."
rationale: The brand-name hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) is produced by Sanofi, a French company, but there is no credible evidence that Donald Trump personally owned stock or had a direct financial stake in Sanofi. Public disclosures and contemporary fact-checking found no record of Trump holding Sanofi shares; at most any exposure would be indirect (e.g., via mutual funds) which is not the same as a personal stake in the company.

claim: "While Exxon Mobil has 40 pages on its media response strategy, its plan for resource protection is only five pages long and its plan for oil removal is just nine pages long."
rationale: The claim asserts specific page counts for ExxonMobil’s media, resource protection, and oil removal plans, but I find no verifiable public source that confirms those exact numbers. Major oil companies do maintain detailed response and media plans that vary by region and revision, so the cited page counts appear to be an unverified or cherry-picked characterization rather than a documented fact.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s polling numbers show that he’s "the highest with Hispanics that any Republican has ever been."
rationale: The claim is absolute but not supported by the historical record: various Republicans (notably George W. Bush and in some eras Ronald Reagan) have received comparable or higher shares of the Hispanic vote in national exit polls and surveys. Trump’s Hispanic support has risen in some polls, but it is variable by poll, state, and voter sample and does not clearly exceed every prior Republican peak across history.

claim: "Only five Texas counties account for almost 90 percent of the (state’s) cattle industry."
rationale: Cattle in Texas are widely distributed across many counties and historical USDA/NASS county data show that the top few counties do not account for anywhere near 90% of the state's cattle inventory or production. While a handful of counties have large herds, the industry is spread across hundreds of counties, so the claim that only five counties account for almost 90% is inconsistent with typical agricultural statistics.

claim: "In campaigns in the past with Sen. McCain and President George W. Bush and others, they have tended to release tax records in April."
rationale: There is no consistent pattern showing that Sen. McCain, President George W. Bush, and other candidates routinely released tax records in April; release timing has varied across different campaigns and years. Historical disclosures occurred in different months depending on campaign strategy and filing schedules, so saying they 'tended' to release in April is misleading.

claim: Most of Kathy Manning’s donors are from out-of-state.
rationale: Public campaign finance patterns for Kathy Manning show substantial fundraising from North Carolina individuals and local supporters, so the categorical claim that most donors are out-of-state is not clearly supported. The statement also depends on definitions (individual vs PAC donors) and the specific election cycle, which changes the in-state vs out-of-state split.

claim: "There's not a major bill I know with Hillary's name on it."
rationale: There is no widely recognized major U.S. federal law commonly known by Hillary Clinton's name. While Hillary Clinton has sponsored and advocated for legislation during her Senate and policy career, major statutes are not commonly titled with her name in the way some commemorative laws are named for other figures.

claim: The Obama administration "raised discretionary spending by 24 percent from President George W. Bush's last full-year budget and will run up more debt by October than Bush did in eight years."
rationale: The statement mixes incomparable baselines and timeframes. Independent fact-checkers and federal budget data show the cited 24% jump depends on cherry-picked comparisons (including or excluding wartime and stimulus spending and using different fiscal years), and when comparable years are used the discretionary increase is much smaller; likewise, the claim that Obama 'will run up more debt by October than Bush did in eight years' misstates timing and totals — Bush-era deficits over eight years were larger in aggregate than the short early-Obama period the statement implicitly references.

claim: A Fox News affiliate reported on a shooting before it happened.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated: there is no widely verified example showing a Fox News affiliate definitively reporting a shooting before it actually occurred. Instances that circulate online are typically misinterpretations of time stamps, prewritten alerts, or premature live updates, not confirmed evidence of clairvoyant reporting.

claim: Says BLM activist Sasha Johnson tweeted, "The white man will not be our equal but our slave."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Sasha Johnson posted that tweet; versions of the quote circulated as screenshots on social media but fact-checkers and archive searches found no matching post on her verified accounts. The claim appears to be a fabricated or misattributed social-media image rather than an authentic tweet.

claim: "The claim ... that we plan to set up panels of bureaucrats with the power to  kill off senior citizens ... is a lie, plain and simple."
rationale: The allegation that policymakers planned to create 'panels of bureaucrats' with the power to kill off senior citizens has been repeatedly debunked. Major U.S. health reform proposals discussed (notably the Affordable Care Act) contained no provisions authorizing such panels; debates referenced reimbursement for advance care planning, not authorization of killing.

claim: Says only about 250 Texans have been killed in action since 9/11.
rationale: Public casualty tallies and Department of Defense totals for post‑9/11 combat (Iraq, Afghanistan and related operations) show several thousand U.S. combat deaths overall; Texas, as a large contributor of service-members, accounts for far more than ~250 KIA. State-by-state casualty lists and memorial databases record many hundreds of Texans killed in action since 2001, so the claim understates the true number.

claim: Before COVID-19, "Iowa had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the country, and many employers were scrambling to find qualified employees to fill their job openings."
rationale: In the months before the COVID-19 pandemic (late 2019–early 2020) Iowa's unemployment rate was below the national average and ranked among the lower rates across states. At the same time multiple state workforce reports and news accounts documented labor shortages and employers in sectors like manufacturing, healthcare, and agriculture struggling to find qualified workers.

claim: "In (Sen. Marco) Rubio's state of Florida alone, Social Security lifts more than -- count it -- a million people out of poverty."
rationale: State- and national-level analyses by Social Security and policy researchers show Social Security substantially reduces poverty, and Florida's large retiree population means the program lifts well over one million Floridians out of poverty in recent years. State-by-state breakdowns from reputable analyses produce figures consistent with the senator's claim.

claim: "The Parole Board operates with Mark Herring’s advice and consent."
rationale: The phrase 'advice and consent' refers to a legislative confirmation role, not to an attorney general. Parole board members are appointed and/or confirmed through the executive and legislative processes (e.g., governor appointments and legislative confirmation) rather than by the attorney general, so the board does not operate with Mark Herring's 'advice and consent.'

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: I cannot confirm the statement as presented because it omits the jurisdiction, the exact tax metric (rate, bill, or revenue), and the date Sharpe first took office. Without those specifics and supporting official budget or assessor/treasurer data, the 18% figure is unverified and therefore should be treated as false. To substantiate it would require comparing official historical property tax rates or typical homeowner tax bills from when Sharpe began his term to the present.

claim: "We have laws on the books where people can walk right up to our ports of entry, say ‘I have a credible fear of persecution,’ and we bring them in. We don’t send them back."
rationale: U.S. immigration law provides a credible-fear screening for noncitizens who express fear of return at ports of entry or after initial encounter; those who demonstrate a credible fear are referred into full asylum proceedings rather than being summarily returned. In practice such people may be detained or released on parole/bond, and if they ultimately fail their claims they can later be removed, so the statement is broadly correct but omits important procedural nuances.

claim: Florida drivers who have their cell phones "in hand" can be ticketed $250 and sent to "driving school."
rationale: This statement overstates Florida law. Florida has laws restricting texting while driving and special rules for novice drivers, but there is not a uniform rule that simply having a cellphone "in hand" automatically results in a $250 ticket and mandatory "driving school." Fines and penalties vary by offense, driver age, and local enforcement, and court-ordered driving school is not a standard automatic sanction for handheld phone use.

claim: "George Bush never suggested that we eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement of 'never,' which is difficult to prove true without exhaustive historical records for both George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush. Public Republican policy debates and statements over the years show at least efforts by GOP leaders to restrict or withdraw federal funding tied to abortion providers, and the blanket claim that neither George Bush ever suggested eliminating Planned Parenthood funding cannot be verified and is therefore unreliable.

claim: Iowa has "the highest high-school graduation rate in the country."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute but graduation-rate rankings change year to year and Iowa is not consistently the single highest state. Federal data (NCES/adjusted cohort graduation rates) show several states — e.g., New Jersey, Massachusetts, Vermont — have often reported equal or higher on-time graduation rates than Iowa in recent years.

claim: "In 2010, everybody said you can't dare let guns go into the national parks, and of course the rapes, murders, robberies and assaults are down about 85 percent since we did that."
rationale: While a 2010 National Park Service policy change and/or reinterpretation made carrying firearms in many park units consistent with state concealed-carry laws, there is no evidence that rapes, murders, robberies and assaults in national parks fell by about 85% as a result. Official NPS crime reports and independent fact-checks do not support an 85% decline and show much smaller, mixed changes in crime rates; the claim conflates events, overstates consensus about the policy, and asserts a large causal effect without supporting data.

claim: "The average Republican voter thinks there should be some revenue as part of this deal."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it names no specific deal and cites no polling. Claims about the 'average Republican voter' require representative, current survey data; views among Republican voters vary by the issue, timing, and question wording, so the blanket assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says Jeb Bush "said he would take his pants off and moon everybody ... Nobody reports that."
rationale: There is no credible record—no news reports, video, debate transcripts, or campaign statements—showing Jeb Bush saying he would "take his pants off and moon everybody." The phrase appears to be a misattribution or fabrication rather than a documented public remark by Bush.

claim: Four million women have fallen into poverty in the last six years.
rationale: The claim is underspecified: it gives no country, region, or source and simply states a numeric change over six years, so it cannot be verified as presented. Poverty statistics depend on the country, timeframe, and definition used, and global or national data sets (World Bank, national statistical offices) do not support a universal, context-free statement like this without a cited source. If a specific country and data source were provided the claim could be checked.

claim: If COVID-19 was real, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge wouldn’t have been "allowed to join 50,000 other football fans inside a stadium."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute consequence (that if COVID-19 were real, royals could not have attended a large stadium), which is false. Whether public figures attended large events depended on the time, local public-health rules, vaccination and testing status, and mitigation measures; many jurisdictions permitted large crowds at various stages of the pandemic. Attendance at a crowded event does not demonstrate that the disease was not real.

claim: Hillary Clinton wants to "wave the white flag of surrender and set a date for withdrawal."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton advocated a policy of 'waving the white flag of surrender' or unconditionally setting a fixed withdrawal date; throughout her public career she has generally opposed arbitrary timetables and favored conditions-based or phased drawdowns. The quoted language is rhetorical and more consistent with critics' characterizations than with her documented policy statements.

claim: Water rates in Manila, Philippines, "were raised up to 845 percent" when a subsidiary of the World Bank became a partial owner.
rationale: The claim greatly exaggerates and misattributes rate changes. After the 1997 privatization of Manila water services there were substantial, regulator-approved tariff increases over time, but independent reviews and domestic data do not support a general ‘‘up to 845%’’ increase tied directly to a World Bank subsidiary taking partial ownership. The World Bank Group’s private arm (IFC) had limited investment roles, and tariff adjustments followed contractual and regulator processes rather than a single owner decision.

claim: Forty percent of union members voted Republican in 2008.
rationale: 2008 presidential exit-poll data indicate that roughly four-in-ten union members or union-household voters supported the Republican nominee, John McCain (McCain's share among union voters is commonly reported around 39–41%). Obama received the majority of union votes, but the Republican share was close to 40%.

claim: Says Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ted Cruz "opposes the DREAM Act, which is supported by 85% of Latinos."
rationale: The claim bundles two points. Ted Cruz did oppose the DREAM Act during his 2012 Senate campaign and in his public statements, but the precise figure '85% of Latinos' depends on the specific poll and timing. While many polls have shown very high Latino support for the DREAM Act (often in the 70–90% range), the blanket ‘‘85%’’ number is not reliably verifiable without citing a particular survey.

claim: "Over the past decade, drug prices have risen at three times the rate of inflation."
rationale: The statement is too broad and not supported by aggregate price data: while some specific drugs (notably certain brand drugs and insulin) have risen far faster than inflation, overall prescription drug price growth in major datasets over the past decade has not uniformly been three times the consumer inflation rate. Differences in definitions (list price vs. net price after rebates), the country and exact ten-year window chosen, and large offsets from generic competition make the blanket claim inaccurate.

claim: "Already this calendar year, since January 1, we have had more than 20,000 people come across the border, apprehended, unauthorized."
rationale: The claim lacks necessary context (which country/border and which year) so it cannot be verified as stated. Without a specified year or border, the statement is ambiguous; while many national borders (including the U.S. southern border) have seen far more than 20,000 apprehensions in a calendar year, the assertion as phrased is not verifiable and therefore not supported.

claim: "Barron Trump was born in March 2006 and Melania wasn’t a legal citizen until July 2006. So under this executive order, his own son wouldn’t be an American citizen."
rationale: Barron Trump was born on March 20, 2006, and Melania Trump became a U.S. citizen in 2006; even if her naturalization occurred after March, birthright citizenship is governed by the 14th Amendment. A president cannot strip or override constitutional birthright citizenship for someone born in the United States by executive order. Therefore the claim that an executive order would make Barron non‑citizen is incorrect.

claim: "The public option is not funded with public money. It's funded with private insurance premiums."
rationale: That statement is too categorical. While many public option proposals envision enrollee premiums covering claims and administration, actual legislative designs often include public funding elements such as start‑up money, subsidies, reinsurance, government payments to providers, or a federal backstop for losses. Whether a particular public option is exclusively financed by private premiums depends on the specific bill.

claim: "Why was there no news coverage of this raid on the Arizona border? … Seizure was just five days ago. Right on the Arizona border!"
rationale: The claim asserts there was no news coverage of a recent raid/seizure on the Arizona border five days ago, but as stated it is unverifiable and unlikely. Border raids and seizures near Arizona are routinely reported by local and national media; without a specific date, location, and incident reference one cannot confirm an absence of coverage. If a significant seizure occurred very recently it would typically generate at least local reporting.

claim: Says Alex Sink "failed Florida homeowners by using predatory lending practices."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Alex Sink personally engaged in or promoted predatory lending practices that 'failed Florida homeowners.' Sink served as Florida Chief Financial Officer and previously worked in banking leadership, but public records and reporting do not show she ran predatory-lending programs or directly used such practices. Claims like this typically arise as political accusations without substantiating facts.

claim: "The Democrat controlled House never even asked John Bolton to testify."
rationale: During the 2019–2020 impeachment inquiry House Democrats sought John Bolton's testimony; his lawyer publicly said Bolton had volunteered to testify but the White House prevented it, and Democratic committees pursued subpoenas/requests for his testimony and manuscript. Therefore the blanket statement that the Democrat-controlled House "never even asked" him is incorrect.

claim: Says Donald Trump said, "Make no mistake: They’re not after me. They are after you; your guns, your Christian values, your freedom. I’m just in their way."
rationale: Donald Trump has repeatedly framed legal actions against him as attacks on his supporters' guns, religion, and freedoms, but there is no verified record of him uttering this precise, punctuated sentence. The wording appears to be a paraphrase or amalgam of his common rhetoric rather than a documented verbatim quote.

claim: "I investigated Abramoff and people ended up in jail."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it uses an unidentified first person — there is no evidence here linking the speaker personally to the Abramoff investigation or to causation of any jailings. It is true as background that investigations into Jack Abramoff led to convictions and prison terms for Abramoff and several associates, but the claim that a specific "I" conducted that investigation cannot be confirmed from this statement alone.

claim: "We cut taxes for 95 percent of working families."
rationale: The statement is vague and not verifiable as written; major U.S. tax changes reviewed by nonpartisan analysts typically show a substantially smaller share of households receiving net, permanent tax cuts than 95%, and benefits vary by income and over time. Without specifying which law, year, and the definition of "working families," the claim overstates what independent analyses have found.

claim: The city of Richmond "built the second richest team in the NFL a $14 million stadium."
rationale: This claim is incorrect or highly misleading: no city named Richmond built an NFL franchise a $14 million stadium, and Richmond has not hosted an NFL team. Modern NFL stadiums cost hundreds of millions to over a billion dollars, so a $14 million facility would not be an NFL stadium for a top-valued team.

claim: "Greenland's ice sheet isn't shrinking any more rapidly today than it was 80 years ago."
rationale: Multiple independent lines of evidence show Greenland's ice sheet mass loss has accelerated in recent decades. Satellite gravimetry (GRACE), altimetry, and in situ mass-balance studies indicate current annual losses (hundreds of gigatons) and a clear acceleration since the 1990s/2000s, far greater than mid-20th-century rates.

claim: The people who want President Barack Obama impeached "are all white, they're all older, and guess what, they're in the far right wing of the Republican Party."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While calls to impeach Obama were concentrated among conservative and Tea Party-aligned Republicans, they were not exclusively white, uniformly older, or confined solely to the far-right—public petitions, commentators, and at least some political figures who supported inquiries or impeachment efforts included a range of ages and some non-white individuals, and many mainstream Republicans did not endorse impeachment.

claim: Wisconsin sold fresh water to California, helping that state's dairy industry, and "lost a bunch of jobs (and) a bunch of farmland."
rationale: There is no evidence that Wisconsin sold bulk fresh water to California in any way that materially supplied California’s dairy industry or caused widespread loss of jobs and farmland in Wisconsin. Large-scale transfers of Great Lakes basin water to the West are legally and logistically constrained (Great Lakes Compact and long-distance transport), and California dairies rely on in-state surface and groundwater supplies. While private bottled-water shipments from Wisconsin may reach many states, those volumes are trivial compared with agricultural needs and would not cause the claimed economic impacts.

claim: "We only have 2 percent of the oil reserves in the world, and we consume 25 percent of the world's oil on a daily basis."
rationale: The claim bundles two precise percentages without a timeframe. The United States holds roughly 2–3% of global proven oil reserves (so '2%' is plausible), but U.S. daily oil consumption in recent years has been nearer 20% of global consumption, not 25%; the U.S. share did peak around 25% in the mid-2000s. As stated without a date and using current-context numbers, the claim is misleading/outdated.

claim: Says Joe Biden talked about eating wooden corn dog sticks.
rationale: There is no reliable, verifiable record that Joe Biden said he ate wooden corn-dog sticks; viral posts that make this claim have typically been shown to misquote or take remarks out of context. Biden has told anecdotes about eating corn dogs, but credible reporting and available clips do not support the assertion that he said he ate the wooden sticks themselves.

claim: "We are No. 1 among all large states in having fully vaccinated teenagers. We are No. 2 in all large states for having fully vaccinated five- to 11- year-olds."
rationale: The statement gives no date, definition of 'large states,' or source for the rankings, and vaccination coverage by age group and state changes over time. Without a time-stamped, cited dataset (for example CDC/state dashboard figures) the claim cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false.

claim: Says "Christine Blasey Ford’s letter to Sen. Dianne Feinstein revealed to be a total FAKE… contains 14 glaring errors that could only be committed by a poorly educated writer." ​
rationale: The claim that Christine Blasey Ford’s letter to Sen. Dianne Feinstein was revealed to be a “total FAKE” with 14 glaring errors is unsupported. The letter was submitted confidentially to Feinstein, Ford subsequently identified herself and testified under oath before the Senate Judiciary Committee, and mainstream reporting and committee records treated the letter as a genuine allegation; no credible forensic analysis has established it as fabricated. The specific viral list of “14 errors” circulated on partisan sites and was debunked by journalists and experts who found the assertions misleading or inaccurate.

claim: As a result of Roe vs. Wade, "America’s maternal mortality rate dropped dramatically."
rationale: After Roe v. Wade (1973) legalizing abortion nationwide, abortion-related maternal deaths fell sharply and overall U.S. maternal mortality declined during the 1970s. Legal access to safe abortion is widely credited with reducing deaths from unsafe procedures, though concurrent improvements in obstetric and prenatal care also contributed, so Roe was a major but not sole cause of the decline.

claim: "The race will tighten, just because that's what happens at the end of campaigns. They always have."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute rule ('They always have'), but historical election data and polling show that races sometimes tighten near the end of campaigns and sometimes do not; some races widen, others remain stable or move unpredictably. Therefore the universal phrasing is incorrect.

claim: "Middle-class income rose to a record level in 2017 as the strong economy lifted the fortunes of more Americans."
rationale: The U.S. Census Bureau reported that real median household income rose in 2017 to the highest level on record for the series, and contemporaneous news coverage credited the stronger economy with lifting incomes. The statement's phrasing uses 'middle-class income' as a shorthand for median household income, which did reach a record in 2017, though gains were modest and uneven.

claim: "Two-thirds of our kids can’t read at grade level."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and lacks key context (which country, which grades, which assessment, and which year). In the U.S., national NAEP reading results show roughly one-third of 4th graders reach the NAEP 'proficient' level (implying about two-thirds are below that particular benchmark), but state assessments and grade-level standards produce widely different proficiency rates, so the blanket statement 'two-thirds of our kids can't read at grade level' is misleading and unsupported as written.

claim: Dave Aronberg's career legal experience is "less than two years as Asst. AG/private attorney."
rationale: Public biographical information and news profiles indicate Dave Aronberg worked for multiple years in legal roles rather than less than two years; he served as an assistant prosecutor and later held other legal positions and private-practice work spanning several years. Therefore the claim that his career legal experience is under two years in those capacities is inaccurate.

claim: In Arizona, "there are only one and a half (Border Patrol) agents per every 10 square miles."
rationale: Interpreting the claim literally (1.5 agents per 10 square miles statewide) implies about 17,100 Border Patrol agents in Arizona (Arizona ≈114,000 sq mi), which is inconsistent with known Border Patrol staffing and sector counts. In reality Border Patrol staffing is on the order of ~18–20k nationwide and far fewer are assigned to Arizona, with deployment concentrated unevenly by sector, so the stated uniform density is incorrect.

claim: "At the Democratic convention, the Pledge of Allegiance was read with the words 'under God' removed."
rationale: There was no official change by the Democratic Party to remove 'under God' from the Pledge at its national convention. Fact-checking and contemporary news coverage found reports of individual recitations that omitted the phrase or were not clearly audible, but no formal policy or blanket removal was enacted.

claim: "Barack Obama will somehow manage to add more than $8 trillion to the national debt, which is more debt than the 43 presidents who held office before him compiled together."
rationale: Barack Obama presided over an increase in the federal debt of roughly $8–9 trillion over his two terms, but the total national debt that existed before he took office (around $10–11 trillion in January 2009) was larger than his addition. Therefore his increase was not greater than the debt accumulated under the previous 43 presidents combined. The claim misstates the relationship between the increment during his presidency and the historical total.

claim: Says for every dollar the state spent on audits last year, it delivered $64 in cost savings.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which state, which audits, or provide a source or methodology for the $64-per-$1 figure. Audit return-on-investment ratios vary widely by jurisdiction and how savings are calculated (gross vs. net, recurring vs. one-time), so a blanket statement cannot be confirmed. Without specific documentation showing that every dollar spent produced $64 in documented, realized cost savings for a named state and year, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: There is a Republican "plan to end Medicare."
rationale: There is no single, official Republican plan to abolish Medicare outright; major Republican proposals in recent years have instead proposed restructuring the program (for example, shifting to premium-support/voucher models, increasing means-testing or raising the eligibility age) rather than immediate termination. Democratic critics commonly describe those reforms as a plan to “end Medicare,” but that characterization overstates the explicit intent to eliminate the program entirely.

claim: "Joe Biden tells voters he's 'going to beat Joe Biden.'"
rationale: There is no credible record or reputable news/fact-check report showing Joe Biden told voters "I'm going to beat Joe Biden." The claim is self-contradictory and appears to stem from a misquote, out-of-context editing, or manipulated media rather than an actual statement by Biden.

claim: "Together we added more jobs than any other area" while I was Dane County executive.
rationale: The claim omits a specific timeframe and comparator (e.g., other counties, metro areas, or states), so it is unverified as stated. Absolute job additions depend on the period and metric used, and larger metropolitan areas or counties typically record higher total job gains than Dane County. Without precise data from labor statistics for the executive's tenure, the blanket claim that 'we added more jobs than any other area' cannot be substantiated.

claim: "Here in Pennsylvania, the annual cost for infant childcare is over $10,000 per child, which is more than most families pay in rent and almost the same cost as in-state college tuition."
rationale: While average infant childcare costs in Pennsylvania commonly run around or slightly above $10,000 per year for center-based care, the rest of the claim is misleading. Median rent/gross housing costs in PA are in the same ballpark or higher depending on area, so infant care is not clearly "more than most families pay in rent." In-state public college tuition in Pennsylvania also varies widely (many four‑year programs cost more than $10k annually, community colleges less), so saying childcare is "almost the same" as in‑state tuition overgeneralizes.

claim: Says a mall Santa beat up a child molester.
rationale: The claim provides no specifics (time, place, identities) and there is no known, widely reported verified incident of a mall Santa beating up a child molester. Stories of vigilante Santas circulate frequently on social media but are typically unverified or debunked by local news outlets. Without corroborating credible reporting, the claim should be treated as false or unsubstantiated.

claim: "Parents in Vail, Arizona just took over the school board — all according to the rules. Voted in a whole new board, and immediately removed the mask mandate."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific, recent claim that parents in Vail, Arizona 'just took over' the entire school board and that the new board immediately removed a mask mandate. News about school-board changes in Vail has included contested elections and some board turnover in the past, but replacing an entire board at once and instantly rescinding district-wide health policy is unlikely without documented local reporting. Because the claim is specific and time-sensitive but lacks corroborating public records or credible reports, it should not be treated as true without verification.

claim: Henry Kissinger "said that we should meet with Iran — guess what — without precondition."
rationale: There is no reliable public record of Henry Kissinger uttering that exact line. While Kissinger has long advocated diplomatic engagement with adversaries (including arguments for talking to Iran), the quoted phrasing appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution rather than a documented Kissinger quote.

claim: Says she "called for addressing risks of derivatives, cracking down on subprime mortgages and improving financial oversight" early on in the financial crisis.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because the pronoun "she" is unspecified and no timing or source is provided. While many public figures did call for tighter oversight of derivatives, subprime lending, and financial regulation around the crisis, without an identified person or citation this specific attribution cannot be confirmed.

claim: "We must deal with the here and now and assure affordable fuel for America by increasing domestic production."
rationale: Saying increased domestic production will "assure" affordable fuel is false because global fuel prices are set by international markets and influenced by demand, geopolitics, refinery capacity, and taxes.
